The use of the word 'seizure' (أخذ) conveys a sense of sudden, overwhelming divine intervention, reminding humanity that no society, no matter how powerful or prosperous, is beyond accountability. The verse invites reflection on collective moral responsibility, urging communities to self-correct before the point of no return, as the punishment described is not gentle or gradual, but painful and severe — a testimony to the gravity with which God views injustice perpetrated at a societal level.

translation: Indeed in that is a sign for those who fear the punishment of the Hereafter. That is a Day for which the people will be gathered, and that is a Day [that will be] witnessed.
interpretation: This verse speaks to those whose hearts are alive with the awareness of divine accountability. The 'sign' mentioned is not merely an intellectual pointer, but a wake-up call directed specifically at those who already carry within them a consciousness of the Hereafter. This selectivity is profound — only a heart softened by the fear of God can truly perceive and benefit from the signs of God. The description of the Day of Judgment as 'witnessed' (mash-hud) suggests its absolute, undeniable reality; it will be a moment beyond all denial, attended by all of creation, angels, humans, and the divine presence, making it the most consequential moment in existence. The verse thus urges believers to allow their fear of that Day to sharpen their perception of divine signs in this world, so that worldly life becomes a conscious preparation for the inevitable gathering.

translation: And We delay it only for a fixed term.
interpretation: This verse reminds us that divine judgment and consequence are never arbitrary or forgotten — they operate according to a precise and predetermined wisdom that transcends human understanding. The delay in punishment or reckoning should not be mistaken for absence or indifference on God's part, but rather understood as a manifestation of His perfect order and mercy, giving souls time to reflect and return. Every moment of respite is itself a gift, yet the appointed time, when it arrives, is absolute and inevitable.

translation: The Day it comes, no soul will speak except by His permission. Among them will be the wretched and the blessed.
interpretation: This verse draws our attention to the absolute sovereignty of God on the Day of Judgment, a day so overwhelming that even speech itself will be subject to divine permission. The division of humanity into the wretched and the blessed is not arbitrary, but rather the culmination of each soul's own choices in this worldly life. It serves as a profound reminder that our current freedom to speak, choose, and act is itself a divine gift — and that how we use this freedom will ultimately determine which of the two eternal destinations we belong to. The silence imposed on that Day stands in stark contrast to the noise and argumentation of this world, signifying that all pretense, debate, and self-justification will fall away, leaving only the truth of what each soul has done.

translation: As for those who were wretched, they will be in the Fire, for them therein is exhaling and inhaling (of agonized breath).
interpretation: This verse speaks to the irreversible consequence of a life lived in spiritual ruin and rejection of divine guidance. The specific mention of 'zafeer' (exhaling) and 'shaheek' (inhaling) — the labored, agonized breathing of one in extreme distress — is not merely a description of physical suffering, but a profound metaphor for the complete and total consumption of one's being by regret and despair. It suggests that even the most involuntary, unconscious act of existence — breathing itself — becomes an expression of torment for those who chose wretchedness. This serves as a stark reminder that our choices in this life penetrate so deeply into our very nature that they shape the character of our existence in the next, even down to the most basic biological reflex.

translation: Abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except as your Lord wills. Indeed, your Lord is an effecter of what He intends.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the absolute and unlimited sovereignty of God over all matters, including the eternal fate of souls. While the phrase 'as long as the heavens and the earth endure' is used to convey a sense of permanence and eternity in human terms, the exception 'except as your Lord wills' serves as a profound reminder that nothing — not even eternity itself — falls outside the dominion of God. It is not suggesting that punishment or reward will end, but rather that the concept of everlastingness itself is subject to divine will. God is not bound by His own creation, including the framework of time and existence. The closing affirmation that God 'does what He wills' is a call to humility, urging us to recognize that human understanding of divine matters is inherently limited, and that ultimate authority rests solely with God, whose wisdom and will transcend all comprehension.

translation: And as for those who were blessed, they will be in Paradise, abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills — a gift uninterrupted.
interpretation: This verse conveys that the reward of the righteous in Paradise is eternal and without end, emphasizing the absolute sovereignty of God over all things. The exception 'except what your Lord wills' is not a suggestion that Paradise may come to an end, but rather a reminder that its permanence is itself contingent upon God's will and sustained by His grace — it is not inherent to creation but is a continuous divine gift. The phrase 'a gift uninterrupted' seals this meaning, affirming that God's bestowal of eternal bliss upon the faithful is an act of endless, unbroken generosity that flows from His mercy rather than from any entitlement. The verse thus invites the believer to understand that salvation is ultimately rooted in trust in God's boundless grace, not merely in human deeds.

translation: So do not be in doubt about what these people worship. They worship nothing but what their fathers worshipped before them. And indeed, We will give them their full share without any reduction.
interpretation: This verse addresses the Prophet (peace be upon him) — and by extension all believers — urging him not to waver or feel uncertainty in the face of the polytheists' persistence in their false worship. The idolatry of the Quraysh was not a reasoned, spiritually grounded practice, but merely an inherited tradition blindly passed down from generation to generation, devoid of divine authority or rational foundation. The verse then delivers a solemn warning: Allah will hold every person fully accountable for their deeds. The phrase 'their full share without reduction' implies that no wrongdoer will escape the precise and complete consequence of their actions. It is a reminder that divine justice is absolute and unfailing — no deed, however ancient or habitual, will be overlooked on the Day of Reckoning.

translation: And We certainly gave Moses the Scripture, but it was differed over. And if not for a word that preceded from your Lord, it would have been concluded between them. And indeed they are, concerning it, in disquieting doubt.
interpretation: This verse draws a profound parallel between the reception of previous revelations and the revelation of the Qur'an, serving as a consolation and warning to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). The deeper message is that human division and doubt over divine truth is a recurring pattern in history — not a sign of the truth's weakness, but of human weakness. God's mercy and wisdom deliberately delays final judgment, allowing humanity time to reflect and return to truth. The 'word that preceded' refers to God's pre-ordained decree of granting humanity a period of respite before ultimate accountability. The doubt described is not mere intellectual uncertainty, but a deeply unsettling, self-generated skepticism born from ego, tradition, and desire rather than from any genuine ambiguity in the revelation itself.

translation: And indeed, your Lord will fully compensate them for their deeds. Indeed, He is Acquainted with what they do.
interpretation: This verse serves as a profound reminder of divine justice and accountability. Allah's complete awareness of every human action — no matter how hidden or seemingly insignificant — ensures that no deed, whether virtuous or sinful, will go unrecorded or unrewarded. The emphasis on God's full recompense speaks to the perfection of divine justice, offering both comfort to the oppressed and a warning to the wrongdoer. It invites the believer to cultivate a constant consciousness of God in all their actions, knowing that ultimate judgment belongs solely to Him, and that worldly outcomes are never the final measure of a soul's worth.

translation: So remain steadfast as you have been commanded, and those who have turned back with you, and do not transgress. Indeed, He is All-Seeing of what you do.
interpretation: This verse calls the Prophet and his followers to a life of unwavering moral and spiritual uprightness, not merely as an act of ritual compliance, but as a conscious and sustained orientation of the entire self toward God. The command to 'be steadfast' implies that righteousness is not a single moment of decision but a continuous, active discipline of the soul. The warning against transgression reminds us that even those on the righteous path can drift into excess — whether in pride, in the treatment of others, or in the distortion of divine boundaries. The concluding reminder that God sees all that we do serves not as a threat, but as a source of moral grounding: our actions carry weight precisely because they are witnessed by One whose knowledge is infinite and whose justice is perfect.

translation: And do not incline toward those who do wrong, lest the Fire touch you, and you would have no protectors other than Allah, and then you would not be helped.
interpretation: This verse is a profound warning against moral compromise and the subtle danger of sympathizing with or leaning toward oppressors and wrongdoers, even without actively participating in their wrongdoing. The Arabic word 'tarkanu' implies a gentle inclination or a soft leaning, suggesting that even a passive alignment with injustice — whether through silence, admiration, or seeking favor from the unjust — is enough to incur divine displeasure. The verse teaches that true protection and ultimate victory come solely from Allah, and that abandoning one's moral integrity by allying with the oppressors severs one's connection to that divine protection, leaving the believer utterly alone and without aid on the Day of Judgment.

translation: And establish prayer at the two ends of the day and in the early hours of the night. Indeed, good deeds remove evil deeds. That is a reminder for those who remember.
interpretation: This verse calls us to anchor our lives around regular prayer — at dawn, at dusk, and in the early night — as a divine rhythm that continuously purifies the soul. The deeper message is one of immense hope and mercy: no matter how heavily sin weighs upon a person, the consistent practice of good deeds, especially prayer, acts as a spiritual cleanser that washes away wrongdoing. This is not merely a mechanical transaction, but a transformation of character — each act of worship reshapes the heart, drawing it further from sin and closer to God. The verse ends by reminding us that this gift of renewal through righteous action is only truly grasped by those who remain mindful and reflective, suggesting that awareness itself is the key that unlocks the purifying power of good deeds.

translation: And be patient, for indeed Allah does not allow the reward of the doers of good to be lost.
interpretation: This verse calls us to understand that patience is not merely passive endurance, but an active form of excellence and worship. The linking of patience with the reward of 'the doers of good' (al-muhsineen) reveals that true patience itself is an act of ihsan — of striving for the highest standard of conduct. When we remain steadfast in difficulty without complaint or despair, we are not simply waiting for relief; we are actively earning a divine reward that Allah, in His justice and faithfulness, guarantees will never be diminished or forgotten. The verse thus reframes hardship: it is not a sign of abandonment, but an opportunity to rise to the level of those whom Allah honors most.

translation: If only there had been among the generations before you people of lasting virtue, forbidding corruption on earth — except a few of those whom We saved from among them. But the wrongdoers pursued the luxury they were given, and they were criminals.
interpretation: This verse serves as a profound moral warning across time: the downfall of past civilizations was not merely due to the presence of evil, but due to the absence of righteous people who actively stood against corruption. The rare few who did speak out were the ones saved. This calls upon believers not to be passive observers of wrongdoing but to be those courageous voices of moral conscience in their societies. Silence and complicity in the face of injustice and corruption, especially when driven by comfort and material indulgence, is itself a path to collective ruin. The verse implicitly demands that we ask ourselves whether we are among the complacent majority or the steadfast few.

translation: And your Lord would never destroy the towns unjustly while their people were reformers (acting righteously).
interpretation: This verse affirms the absolute justice of God, emphasizing that divine punishment is never arbitrary or capricious. Destruction only comes as a consequence of a people's own moral corruption and wrongdoing. As long as a community upholds righteousness and strives for reform, God's mercy protects them. This serves as both a reassurance to the believers and a warning to the unjust — that accountability is rooted in one's own choices, and that God never wrongs His creation, even when He holds them to account.

translation: And if your Lord had willed, He could have made mankind one community; but they will not cease to differ.
interpretation: This verse reveals a profound divine wisdom: human diversity and disagreement are not failures of creation, but a deliberate feature of it. God, in His absolute power, chose not to impose uniformity upon humanity. This tells us that the freedom to differ — in belief, thought, and choice — is itself a gift and a test. The existence of difference is the very arena in which human moral agency, responsibility, and the search for truth become meaningful. A world of forced unity would have no room for genuine faith, virtue, or the exercise of free will.

translation: Except those upon whom your Lord has mercy - and for that He created them. And the word of your Lord is to be fulfilled: 'I will surely fill Hell with jinn and people all together.'
interpretation: This verse reveals the profound tension between divine mercy and divine justice that lies at the heart of human existence. The phrase 'for that He created them' refers not to the creation of people for punishment, but rather for the reception of mercy - mercy being the very purpose and telos of creation. Human beings are endowed with free will, and it is through the exercise of that will that some choose to reject divine guidance and thus bring judgment upon themselves. Allah's mercy is the default and intended state, while the filling of Hell is the consequence of human and jinn choices, not a predetermined fate imposed upon them. The verse thus serves as both a warning and an invitation - a warning that divine justice is absolute and inescapable, and an invitation to seek the mercy for which humanity was originally and fundamentally created.

translation: And all that We relate to you of the news of the messengers is so that We may strengthen your heart thereby. And there has come to you in this [surah] the truth, and an instruction and a reminder for the believers.
interpretation: This verse reveals the profound psychological and spiritual purpose behind the Qur'anic narratives of the prophets. The stories of past messengers were not merely historical accounts, but were deliberately revealed as a divine source of emotional and spiritual fortification for the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) during times of hardship, rejection, and persecution. By learning that previous prophets endured similar trials and ultimately prevailed through steadfast faith, the Prophet's heart was continuously renewed with patience and resolve. This speaks to a universal truth: that the remembrance of those who remained firm in righteousness before us has the power to anchor our own souls in moments of doubt and difficulty. The verse thus affirms that divine guidance is not cold doctrine, but a living mercy, personally tailored to the human need for consolation, strength, and reminder.

translation: And say to those who do not believe: 'Act according to your position; indeed, we are acting.'
interpretation: This verse reflects a profound spiritual confidence and unwavering commitment. Rather than engaging in futile argument or confrontation with those who reject faith, the believer is directed to simply proceed with conviction on their own path. It is a declaration of mutual accountability — each party will bear the consequences of their own choices. The verse teaches that the believer's role is not to force or coerce, but to remain steadfast in righteous action, trusting that the ultimate judgment belongs to God alone. It is a reminder that certainty in one's faith requires no validation from disbelievers, and that patience and purposeful action are the most dignified responses to rejection.

translation: And wait; indeed, we are waiting.
interpretation: This verse serves as a powerful declaration of divine confidence and certainty. It challenges those who oppose the truth to await their fate, while simultaneously asserting that the believers and Allah Himself are also waiting — not out of uncertainty or fear, but out of absolute assurance that the outcome has already been determined. It is a rhetorical dismissal of the disbelievers' plots and a reminder that history and ultimate judgment belong to Allah, and that no amount of opposition can alter what has been decreed.

translation: And to Allah belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth, and to Him all matters are returned. So worship Him and put your trust in Him. And your Lord is not unaware of what you do.
interpretation: This verse calls the believer to a complete surrender of the ego — recognizing that all hidden realities belong exclusively to Allah liberates us from the anxiety of the unknown. Since ultimate control rests with Him alone, worship and tawakkul (trust) are not merely acts of piety but the most rational response to human limitation. The closing reminder that Allah is never heedless of our actions is not merely a warning but a profound comfort: every effort, every sacrifice, every silent struggle made in His path is seen, recorded, and accounted for, even when ignored by the world.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Alif Lam Ra. These are the verses of the clear Book.
interpretation: The mysterious disjointed letters 'Alif Lam Ra' at the opening of this verse serve as a divine reminder of the miraculous and inimitable nature of the Qur'an. Though the Arabic alphabet belongs to the people, no human being can assemble these letters into anything comparable to the Word of God. By then immediately declaring these to be the verses of 'the clear Book,' Allah draws attention to the paradox of divine clarity: that which is composed of the simplest, most familiar elements — letters known to every Arab — transcends human comprehension in its depth, wisdom, and guidance. The Qur'an is 'clear' not only in its language and eloquence, but in its purpose — it leaves no ambiguity in its mission to illuminate the path of truth for humanity.

translation: Indeed, We have sent it down as an Arabic Qur'an so that you may understand.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the divine wisdom behind the choice of Arabic as the language of revelation. God did not choose Arabic arbitrarily, but rather because it was the living tongue of those first addressed by the message, giving them no excuse for misunderstanding. The deeper implication is that revelation is always contextually grounded — God meets humanity in its own linguistic and cultural reality. The phrase 'so that you may understand' suggests that comprehension is not merely an intellectual exercise but a moral responsibility; to be given clarity is to be held accountable for how one responds to it. The verse thus frames the Qur'an not just as a text, but as an act of divine mercy and purposeful communication aimed at awakening human reason and conscience.

translation: We relate to you the best of stories through what We have revealed to you this Qur'an, although you were, before it, among the unaware.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the transformative power of divine revelation, emphasizing that the Qur'an is not merely a collection of narratives, but the finest and most purposeful of all stories, chosen and crafted by God Himself. The acknowledgment that the Prophet was previously unaware of these accounts serves to affirm the miraculous nature of the revelation — it was not drawn from human learning or prior knowledge, but was purely a gift from the Divine. This underscores the idea that true wisdom and guidance do not originate from worldly experience or intellectual pursuit alone, but can only be perfected through divine illumination. The verse invites the believer to approach the Qur'anic stories not as mere history, but as a living source of moral and spiritual insight, granted by God to elevate the human condition.

translation: When Joseph said to his father, 'O my father, indeed I have seen eleven stars and the sun and the moon; I saw them prostrating to me.'
interpretation: This verse marks the beginning of the divine plan unfolding in Joseph's life. The vision is not merely a dream of grandeur, but a sacred covenant between God and His chosen servant. The prostration of the celestial bodies — symbolizing his brothers, mother, and father — reveals that true leadership and honor are not seized through ambition, but are divinely ordained and granted to those whom God selects. The verse teaches us that God plants the seeds of destiny early in the lives of His prophets, and that the trials which follow are not obstacles to that destiny, but the very path through which it is realized.

translation: He said, 'O my son, do not relate your vision to your brothers, lest they devise a plan against you. Indeed, Satan is to man a clear enemy.'
interpretation: This verse reminds us that wisdom sometimes requires discretion in sharing our blessings and divine gifts, even with those closest to us. Jacob's warning to Joseph reflects the profound spiritual insight that envy can corrupt even the bonds of brotherhood, and that Satan exploits human weaknesses — particularly jealousy — to sow discord and destruction among people. The verse teaches us that protecting a God-given blessing may sometimes mean guarding it in silence, and that awareness of Satan's machinations is itself a form of spiritual intelligence and precaution.

translation: And thus will your Lord choose you and teach you the interpretation of narratives and complete His favor upon you and upon the family of Jacob, as He completed it upon your two forefathers before, Abraham and Isaac. Indeed, your Lord is Knowing and Wise.
interpretation: This verse reveals that divine selection is not arbitrary but purposeful — God's choosing of a soul is always accompanied by the bestowal of a corresponding gift that enables that soul to fulfill its destiny. In the case of Joseph, the gift of interpreting dreams and narratives was not merely a personal talent but the very instrument through which God's larger plan for an entire lineage would unfold. The verse invites us to understand that every blessing granted to an individual carries within it a responsibility toward a wider community, as Joseph's gift ultimately served to preserve the family of Jacob. Furthermore, by connecting Joseph's election to that of Abraham and Isaac, the verse reminds us that divine grace moves through generations — it is not exhausted but rather accumulates and flows forward, suggesting that faithfulness in one generation plants seeds of mercy that bloom in the next.

translation: Indeed, in the story of Joseph and his brothers were signs for those who ask.
interpretation: This verse invites the believer to look beyond the surface narrative and engage actively with divine wisdom. The phrase 'for those who ask' suggests that the signs embedded within this story are not passively received but must be sought through reflection and inquiry. It implies that spiritual insight is a reward for the sincere seeker — those who approach the Qur'an with genuine curiosity and humility will find in the trials of Joseph and his brothers profound lessons about patience, divine providence, jealousy, forgiveness, and the ultimate unfolding of God's plan. The verse thus positions the believer as an active participant in understanding revelation, rather than a passive listener.

translation: When they said, 'Joseph and his brother are more beloved to our father than we are, though we are a group. Indeed, our father is in clear error.'
interpretation: This verse reveals the dangerous nature of envy and how it can corrupt the heart and distort one's perception of reality. The brothers' jealousy led them to view their father's natural affection as a moral failing or misjudgment, labeling it 'clear error.' This illustrates how envy blinds a person to truth and justice, causing them to rationalize their resentment by casting blame on others rather than examining their own souls. The verse serves as a warning that when the heart is consumed by jealousy, it loses its capacity for sound judgment and can lead a person to commit grave injustices against their own kin.

translation: Kill Joseph or cast him into some land, so that your father's attention will be free for you, and after that you may become righteous people.
interpretation: This verse reveals the dangerous self-deception that envy can produce in the human heart. The brothers of Joseph, consumed by jealousy, rationalize an act of great evil — murder or abandonment — by promising themselves righteousness afterward. This exposes a profound spiritual warning: that the ego, when driven by envy, can construct elaborate justifications for wrongdoing while simultaneously entertaining fantasies of future virtue. True repentance and righteousness cannot be built upon a foundation of deliberate sin; one cannot plan a crime and redemption in the same breath. The verse invites us to examine the ways in which we deceive ourselves, dressing our worst impulses in the clothing of reason and future good intentions.

translation: One of them said, 'Do not kill Joseph, but throw him into the bottom of a well — some travellers will pick him up — if you must do something.'
interpretation: This verse reveals a profound truth about divine providence operating through human conscience. Even in the darkest of conspiracies, God plants a voice of mercy — here, one brother's reluctance to commit murder becomes the instrument through which God's greater plan unfolds. The suggestion to cast Joseph into the well, while still an act of cruelty, inadvertently sets in motion a chain of events leading to Joseph's elevation and ultimate destiny. It teaches us that Allah's decree cannot be thwarted; even the schemes of those who oppose His will become the very means by which His will is accomplished.

translation: They said, 'O our father, why do you not trust us with Joseph, while indeed we are his well-wishers?'
interpretation: This verse reveals the dangerous subtlety of deception cloaked in the language of sincerity. The brothers of Joseph appeal to their father Jacob through a combination of emotional manipulation and false assurance, using the very vocabulary of trustworthiness and care to conceal their jealousy and ill intent. It is a reminder that the most perilous forms of betrayal often arrive dressed in the garments of love and concern, and that true wisdom, as embodied by Jacob, lies in the discernment of the heart beneath the words spoken by the tongue.

translation: Send him with us tomorrow that he may enjoy himself and play, and indeed we will be his guardians.
interpretation: This verse captures the deceptive persuasion used by the brothers of Prophet Yusuf (Joseph) to convince their father Ya'qub (Jacob) to let him go with them. The verse serves as a warning about how sincere-sounding promises and reassurances can be used to manipulate, and how a loving parent's trust can be exploited by those with ill intentions. It reminds us to be discerning about the motives of those who make grand promises, as words of protection and care can sometimes be a veil for betrayal and deception.

translation: He said, 'It truly saddens me that you should take him away, and I fear that the wolf may eat him while you are inattentive to him.'
interpretation: This verse reveals the profound vulnerability of parental love and the nature of grief and premonition. Jacob's hesitation is not merely a practical concern about physical safety, but reflects a deep spiritual intuition — a father's heart sensing danger beyond what logic can articulate. His fear of the wolf is symbolic of his awareness that the world holds unseen threats to those we cherish most. The verse teaches us that true love is inseparable from anxiety and protective sorrow, and that sometimes our deepest fears, even when dismissed by others, carry within them a prophetic truth. Jacob's grief begins before the loss itself, demonstrating that the heart of a believer can perceive what the eye has not yet witnessed.

translation: They said, 'If the wolf were to eat him while we are a group, indeed we would then be losers.'
interpretation: This verse reveals the subtle art of self-incrimination used as a rhetorical device to manipulate. The brothers of Joseph, in constructing their alibi before the fact, actually expose the weakness of their own argument. By acknowledging that it would be a great failure and disgrace for a whole group of strong men to allow a wolf to take a child, they unknowingly highlight the implausibility of their later story. The verse invites the reader to see through the facade of their words — their very protestation of strength and unity is the seed of their own contradiction. It teaches us that those who plan deception often leave traces of truth in their speech, and that falsehood carries within it the evidence of its own unraveling.

translation: And when they took him away and agreed to put him at the bottom of the well, We revealed to him: 'You will surely inform them of this deed of theirs while they do not perceive.'
interpretation: This verse reveals the divine protection and foreknowledge granted to Prophet Yusuf (Joseph) at his most vulnerable moment. When he was cast into the darkness of the well by his own brothers, abandoned and seemingly powerless, Allah did not abandon him. The revelation given to the young Yusuf in the depths of the well serves as a profound reminder that moments of greatest human weakness can be the very moments of greatest divine closeness. The promise that he would one day confront his brothers with their own betrayal — while they remain unaware of his identity — points to the grand, unfolding nature of divine justice. It teaches us that Allah's plan operates on a timeline and with a wisdom far beyond human comprehension, and that no act of injustice escapes His awareness or goes unaddressed in His perfect arrangement of events.

translation: And they came to their father in the evening, weeping.
interpretation: This verse reveals a profound truth about the nature of deception: that wrongdoers often use outward expressions of grief and sorrow as a tool to mask their guilt and manipulate those who trust them. The brothers of Prophet Yusuf (Joseph) crafted their tears as a shield, demonstrating that the appearance of emotion can be weaponized to cloud the judgment of even the most loving and trusting of hearts — in this case, a father's. It serves as a warning to be discerning, as not all displays of emotion reflect genuine remorse or truth.

translation: They said, 'O our father, indeed we went racing with one another and left Joseph with our belongings, and a wolf ate him. But you would not believe us, even if we were truthful.'
interpretation: This verse reveals the profound guilt embedded within deception itself. The brothers, having committed a grave sin against Joseph, preemptively acknowledge that their father will not believe them — not merely because their story is implausible, but because on some level they know that truth carries its own recognizable weight, and lies carry their own shadow. Their admission that 'you would not believe us even if we were truthful' is a subconscious confession of their own dishonesty, as though the lie itself has already undermined any credibility they might have claimed. It speaks to the spiritual reality that those who betray trust cannot easily reclaim it, and that a guilty conscience often projects its own unworthiness onto others' perceptions.

translation: And they came with false blood on his shirt. He said, 'Rather, your souls have enticed you to something, so patience is most fitting. And Allah is the one sought for help against what you describe.'
interpretation: This verse reveals a profound spiritual truth about the nature of deception and the proper response to betrayal. Jacob's immediate discernment — seeing through the fabricated evidence despite his grief — illustrates that true wisdom is not blinded by emotion. More significantly, his response of 'beautiful patience' (sabrun jameel) teaches us that the believer's first resort in the face of injustice is not rage or despair, but dignified surrender to Allah. By declaring 'Allah is the one sought for help,' Jacob models that human scheming, no matter how elaborate, ultimately falls under Divine sight, and that our only true refuge when confronted with the treachery of others — even those closest to us — is to turn wholly toward God rather than seeking revenge or validation from the world.

translation: And there came a caravan of travellers, and they sent their water-drawer, and he let down his bucket. He said, 'Oh, what good news! This is a boy!' And they concealed him as merchandise. And Allah was All-Knowing of what they did.
interpretation: This verse illustrates how divine providence works through seemingly random and even unjust human events. Joseph, abandoned in a well by his own brothers, is discovered not by a rescuer but by a passing caravan seeking only water. The water-drawer's cry of joy — treating the child as a fortunate find rather than a soul in distress — and the decision to conceal him as trade goods reveals human shortsightedness and moral failure. Yet Allah's omniscience frames the entire scene: those who acted with greed and deception believed they were in control of events, but they were unknowingly serving a far greater divine plan. The verse invites the believer to trust that even in moments of vulnerability, exploitation, and apparent abandonment, Allah sees all and is orchestrating a purpose beyond what any human actor can perceive or intend.

translation: And they sold him for a cheap price, a few dirhams, and they were of those who had little interest in him.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the tragic reality of how humanity often fails to recognize the true worth and divine potential within one another. Just as the brothers of Joseph reduced his immeasurable value to a handful of coins, we too are guilty of diminishing the worth of those around us — whether through indifference, envy, or short-sighted greed. The 'few counted dirhams' serve as a powerful symbol of how material thinking blinds us to spiritual and human value. The verse is a profound warning against the zuhd — the disinterest — we show not toward worldly things (which would be praiseworthy), but toward our fellow human beings, reminding us that such indifference to the dignity of others is a grave moral failing.

translation: And the one from Egypt who bought him said to his wife, 'Make his stay comfortable. Perhaps he will benefit us, or we will adopt him as a son.' And thus We established Joseph in the land that We might teach him the interpretation of events. And Allah is predominant over His affair, but most of the people do not know.
interpretation: This verse reveals the profound and subtle workings of divine providence. What appears to be a series of human misfortunes — Joseph being thrown into a well and sold into slavery — is in reality the carefully orchestrated unfolding of God's plan. The Egyptian's seemingly mundane decision to treat Joseph with kindness becomes the very instrument through which God's will is realized. The verse invites us to recognize that divine wisdom operates through the ordinary decisions and circumstances of human life, often hidden from our perception. Most people see only the surface of events — the hardship, the coincidence, the chance encounter — without perceiving the deeper divine purpose threading through them. The statement that 'Allah is predominant over His affair' is a reminder that no human scheming, whether malicious like that of Joseph's brothers or well-intentioned like that of the Egyptian, can ultimately derail what God has decreed. True wisdom lies in trusting that every twist of fate, however painful, may be a step in a divinely guided journey toward a purpose greater than we can currently comprehend.

translation: And when he reached his full maturity, We gave him wisdom and knowledge. And thus do We reward the doers of good.
interpretation: This verse teaches us that divine wisdom and true knowledge are not merely the products of human effort or intellectual pursuit alone, but are sacred gifts bestowed by Allah upon those who demonstrate excellence of character and righteous conduct throughout their formative years. The verse implies that the spiritual and moral preparation of youth — the struggles, the patience, and the uprightness maintained during the journey to maturity — is itself a form of ihsan (excellence) that invites the grace of Allah. It is a reminder that when a person strives sincerely to do good at every stage of life, Allah elevates them with inner light and discernment that transcends ordinary learning, making their maturity not just physical but profoundly spiritual.

translation: And she, in whose house he was, sought to seduce him. She locked the doors and said, 'Come to me.' He said, 'I seek refuge in Allah! Indeed, he is my master who has made my stay comfortable. Indeed, wrongdoers never succeed.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the supreme moral integrity of Prophet Yusuf (Joseph) when faced with the most intimate and powerful of human temptations. Despite being in a position of vulnerability — a slave in a foreign land with no witness present — Yusuf's first instinct was to seek refuge in Allah rather than in his own willpower. His refusal was not merely about personal virtue or social consequence, but was rooted in gratitude and loyalty to his earthly master and, more profoundly, in his consciousness of Allah. The verse teaches that true moral strength comes not from suppressing desire through ego, but from a deep awareness of divine presence that makes transgression feel spiritually impossible. It also affirms a universal truth: that injustice and betrayal, however momentarily tempting or advantageous, ultimately lead to failure, because the moral order of the universe is aligned with righteousness.

translation: And she certainly desired him, and he would have desired her, had he not seen the proof of his Lord. And thus it was that We might avert from him evil and immorality. Indeed, he was of Our sincere servants.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the nature of human temptation and divine protection. The acknowledgment that even a Prophet-to-be, Joseph, stood at the precipice of human desire illustrates that spiritual greatness does not exempt one from the pull of temptation. The profound lesson lies in what follows — it was the vision of his Lord's proof, an inner spiritual illumination, that redirected him. This teaches us that sincere servitude to God is not the absence of temptation, but the presence of divine consciousness strong enough to overcome it. The phrase 'of Our sincere servants' (al-mukhlaseen) implies that God Himself had chosen and purified Joseph, suggesting that divine selection carries with it a form of protection — not by removing the human experience of desire, but by fortifying the soul with the light of God-consciousness (taqwa) so that the servant can rise above it. True sincerity in devotion thus becomes both a shield and a distinction.

translation: And they raced to the door, and she tore his shirt from the back, and they found her husband at the door. She said, 'What is the punishment for one who intended evil toward your wife except that he be imprisoned or a painful punishment?'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the desperate nature of guilt and how the wrongdoer, when cornered, instinctively resorts to accusation as a shield. The tearing of the shirt from the back is not merely a physical detail but a profound symbolic clue — it is the evidence that speaks truth even when the human tongue lies. The wife of Al-Aziz, caught in her transgression, immediately inverts the narrative and positions herself as the victim, demonstrating how power and social standing can be weaponized to distort justice. The verse teaches us that deception may momentarily succeed in human courts, but the truth always leaves its mark — here, literally woven into the fabric of a torn garment — awaiting the moment of its revelation.

translation: He said, 'It was she who sought to seduce me.' And a witness from her own household testified: 'If his shirt is torn from the front, then she has told the truth and he is of the liars.'
interpretation: This verse reveals a profound moment of divine intervention in the form of human wisdom. When Joseph breaks his silence to proclaim his innocence, the truth is not left to mere accusation and counter-accusation. Instead, God arranges for a wise witness from within the very household to provide an objective, physical standard of judgment — the direction of the torn garment. This teaches us that God does not abandon the righteous when they are falsely accused; He provides a means for truth to emerge even from within the circles of those who conspire against the innocent. It also demonstrates that integrity and truth carry their own evidence, and that those who walk in righteousness will find that reality itself bears witness on their behalf.

translation: And if his shirt was torn from the back, then she has lied, and he is of the truthful ones.
interpretation: This verse highlights the divine wisdom embedded in physical evidence as a means of establishing truth and justice. It teaches us that Allah has ordained ways — even through seemingly mundane material clues — by which falsehood is exposed and innocence is vindicated. The tearing of the shirt from the back serves as a symbol that truth, no matter how concealed by powerful forces or false accusations, will ultimately be revealed through signs that Allah places in the world. It is a reminder that the righteous who are patient in the face of slander will be defended, and that justice is never truly beyond reach when one trusts in Allah's wisdom.

translation: And when he (the husband) saw that his shirt was torn from the back, he said, 'Indeed, this is of the plot of you women. Indeed, your plot is great.'
interpretation: This verse reveals a profound truth about how accusations and blame can be deflected even in the face of clear evidence. The tearing of the shirt from behind was irrefutable proof of Joseph's innocence, yet rather than condemning his wife directly, her husband generalizes the deception to all women. This deflection is itself a kind of moral cowardice — an unwillingness to confront the specific wrong committed by someone close to him. The verse invites us to reflect on how those in positions of power or intimacy often rationalize wrongdoing by those they love, broadening blame to avoid personal accountability and the pain of direct confrontation with the truth.

translation: 'Joseph, turn away from this! And you [woman], ask forgiveness for your sin. Indeed, you were of the wrongdoers.'
interpretation: This verse reveals a profound moment of moral reckoning in which truth asserts itself with undeniable clarity. The husband's command to Joseph to 'turn away' — meaning to keep silent about the matter — alongside his rebuke of his own wife, illustrates how power and social standing can attempt to suppress truth even when guilt is openly established. Yet the significance lies in the fact that innocence does not need to defend itself; it is self-evident. The verse invites us to reflect on the nature of justice within systems of power, and how those who hold authority may seek to manage scandal rather than fully confront wrongdoing. It also subtly affirms that God's protection of the righteous operates independently of human institutions, for even in a household of privilege and concealment, the truth of Joseph's integrity could not ultimately be buried.

translation: And women in the city said: 'The wife of al-'Azeez is seeking to seduce her slave boy. He has inflamed her heart with love. Indeed, we see her in clear error.'
interpretation: This verse reveals the timeless human tendency toward gossip and social judgment. The women of the city, while outwardly condemning the wife of al-'Azeez, are themselves engaged in the morally questionable act of spreading rumors and passing harsh judgment. There is a subtle irony embedded here — those who speak of another's 'clear error' are themselves not free from fault, as they indulge in slander and self-righteousness. The verse invites the reader to reflect on how communities often project moral outrage publicly while harboring the same weaknesses privately, a dynamic that will be further exposed when these very women are themselves overcome by the beauty of Yusuf. It is a divine setup that unmasks human hypocrisy and illustrates that no soul should be quick to declare another lost, for the same temptations may await the one who judges.

translation: And when she heard of their scheming, she sent for them and prepared for them a banquet, and she gave each one of them a knife and said, 'Come out before them.' And when they saw him, they were greatly struck by him and cut their hands and said, 'Perfect is Allah! This is not a human being; this is none but a noble angel.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the overwhelming and almost supernatural power of true beauty — not merely physical, but as a reflection of divine grace. The women who had mocked Zulaikha for her infatuation with Yusuf were instantly overtaken by the same awe upon seeing him, cutting their own hands without even feeling the pain. This serves as a divine vindication of Zulaikha's helplessness, while simultaneously pointing to a deeper truth: that beauty of the highest order is a manifestation of God's light, and when a soul encounters it, rational self-control can be momentarily overwhelmed. The exclamation 'Perfect is Allah!' acknowledges that such perfection can only originate from the Divine, reminding us that all beauty in creation is ultimately a reflection of its Creator.

translation: She said, 'So this is the one you blamed me for! And I did indeed try to seduce him, but he firmly restrained himself. And if he does not do what I command him, he will surely be imprisoned and will be of those brought low.'
interpretation: This verse reveals the nature of unchecked worldly power and desire: when confronted with truth and exposed before others, the ego does not repent but instead doubles down, using coercion and threat to bend the righteous to its will. Zulaikha's confession is remarkable in its honesty — she admits her own wrongdoing openly — yet she immediately follows it with a threat, demonstrating that the acknowledgment of sin does not always lead to repentance, but can instead escalate into tyranny. The verse serves as a spiritual warning that those who walk the path of righteousness must be prepared to face worldly punishment and humiliation, as the forces of this world often respond to moral resistance not with respect, but with persecution. True spiritual integrity, as embodied by Prophet Yusuf, sometimes demands accepting worldly loss in order to preserve divine closeness.

translation: He said, 'My Lord, prison is more dear to me than what they invite me to. And if You do not avert their scheme from me, I might incline toward them and be among the ignorant.'
interpretation: This verse reveals the profound spiritual maturity and self-awareness of Prophet Yusuf (Joseph), who does not merely resist temptation through personal willpower, but openly acknowledges his human vulnerability before Allah. Rather than claiming moral superiority, he surrenders completely to divine protection, recognizing that without God's grace, even the most righteous soul can fall. His preference for imprisonment over sin illustrates that true freedom lies not in physical liberty but in the liberation of the soul from moral corruption. The verse teaches that genuine piety is rooted not in arrogance about one's own strength, but in humble dependence on Allah, understanding that it is ultimately God who guards the believer's heart against what it cannot withstand alone.

translation: So his Lord responded to him and turned away their plot from him. Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.
interpretation: This verse teaches us that sincere supplication to Allah is never in vain. When a believer turns to Allah in a moment of vulnerability and temptation, as Prophet Yusuf did, divine protection becomes a certainty. The attributes of Allah mentioned here — Al-Sami' (the All-Hearing) and Al-'Alim (the All-Knowing) — are not merely descriptive but carry a deeply reassuring message: Allah hears every whisper of the heart and knows the full weight of every trial we face. The verse thus invites the believer to place complete trust in Allah during moments of weakness, affirming that true refuge from corruption and harm lies not in one's own strength, but in one's connection with the Divine.

translation: Then it appeared to them, after they had seen the signs, that they should imprison him for a time.
interpretation: This verse reveals a profound truth about the nature of those in power: that even when confronted with clear and undeniable evidence of innocence and truth, they will still choose to suppress and silence it for the sake of preserving their own interests and reputation. The 'signs' had made the truth plain — Joseph was innocent — yet the powerful chose persecution over justice. It is a timeless warning that worldly authority, when corrupted by ego and self-interest, will always seek to bury the truth rather than confront it, and that the righteous must be patient in their trials, for such oppression is never the final word.

translation: And there entered the prison with him two young men. One of them said, 'Indeed, I see myself pressing wine.' And the other said, 'Indeed, I see myself carrying upon my head bread, from which the birds are eating. Inform us of its interpretation; indeed, we see you to be of those who do good.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates how even in the darkest circumstances of imprisonment, God's wisdom and purpose are at work. Joseph's reputation for righteousness and goodness preceded him even within the prison walls, such that his fellow inmates naturally turned to him for guidance. The two contrasting dreams — one of life and productivity, the other foreshadowing death — remind us that divine destiny is woven into the fabric of our subconscious experiences. The verse teaches us that true excellence of character (ihsan) is not diminished by adversity or unjust confinement, but rather shines more brightly, drawing others toward the light of wisdom and truth. Joseph's gift was not merely one of dream interpretation, but of being a vessel of divine knowledge that transforms suffering into a platform for spiritual service.

translation: He said, 'No food will come to you as your provision, but I will inform you of its interpretation before it comes to you. That is from what my Lord has taught me. Indeed, I have left the religion of a people who do not believe in Allah, and they, in the Hereafter, are disbelievers.'
interpretation: This verse reveals the profound connection between divine knowledge and the responsibility of the believer to proclaim it. Joseph uses his God-given gift of interpreting dreams not merely as a personal talent but as a doorway to dawah — calling others to Allah. By promising his fellow prisoners that he will interpret their visions before they are fulfilled, Joseph demonstrates that his knowledge is rooted in divine revelation, not occult or worldly wisdom. More significantly, he seizes the opportunity to distance himself from polytheism and disbelief, making clear that this knowledge is inseparable from his faith in the One God. The verse teaches us that a true believer must never compartmentalize their gifts from their faith; every ability is an occasion to bear witness to the truth of Allah and to clarify the distinction between belief and disbelief, particularly regarding accountability in the Hereafter.

translation: And I follow the religion of my fathers - Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. It was not for us to associate anything with Allah. That is from the favor of Allah upon us and upon the people, but most of the people are not grateful.
interpretation: This verse, spoken by Prophet Joseph (Yusuf), teaches us that true faith is not merely an individual achievement but a divine gift passed down through generations of righteous predecessors. By attributing his monotheism to both his lineage and the grace of Allah, Joseph reminds us that guidance is ultimately granted by God, not earned solely through personal merit. The concluding observation — that most people fail to show gratitude — serves as a profound rebuke of human negligence: the greatest blessing a person can receive is the light of true faith, yet it is precisely this blessing that most take for granted or squander, failing to recognize it as the extraordinary and undeserved mercy that it truly is.

translation: O two companions of prison, are many different lords better, or Allah, the One, the Prevailing?
interpretation: This verse, spoken by Prophet Yusuf (Joseph) while in prison, uses a rhetorical question not merely to argue monotheism intellectually, but to awaken the innate human disposition toward truth. By addressing his companions directly and personally, Yusuf seizes a moment of vulnerability — imprisonment — to redirect the human soul toward its natural inclination to seek the one true source of power and refuge. The contrast between 'many fragmented lords' and 'the One Who overwhelms all things' implies that polytheism scatters the human heart, leaving it enslaved to multiple fears and desires, while true monotheism unifies and liberates the soul by anchoring it to the only true and absolute authority.

translation: You worship besides Him nothing but names which you have named, you and your forefathers, for which Allah has sent down no authority. The command belongs to none but Allah. He has commanded that you worship none but Him. That is the right religion, but most people do not know.
interpretation: This verse challenges the very foundation of idolatry and false worship by exposing it as a purely human invention — a linguistic and cultural construct devoid of divine sanction. The gods people worship outside of Allah are not real sovereign powers; they are mere labels, stories, and traditions passed down through generations, carrying the weight of habit and ancestral loyalty rather than divine truth. The verse then asserts the absolute and exclusive sovereignty of Allah — not just in worship, but in governance, judgment, and authority over all affairs. True religion, al-deen al-qayyim, is therefore not merely a ritual practice but a comprehensive submission to the one legitimate authority in existence. The tragedy highlighted at the end is not simply ignorance, but willful or inherited blindness — most people follow what they know rather than seeking what is true.

translation: O two companions of prison! As for one of you, he will pour wine for his lord; but as for the other, he will be crucified, and the birds will eat from his head. The matter has been decreed about which you both inquired.
interpretation: This verse reveals the absolute certainty and finality of divine decree. Joseph, having been granted the gift of interpreting dreams, delivers two contrasting fates to his prison companions — one of liberation and service, the other of death and disgrace. The stark contrast between the two outcomes serves as a reminder that divine knowledge encompasses all things, and that no human being, regardless of their circumstances, can alter what has been ordained. The phrase 'the matter has been decreed' underscores that God's will is not speculative or conditional — it is settled and inevitable. The verse also subtly affirms the prophethood and wisdom granted to Joseph, as his interpretation comes not from personal intuition but from divine guidance, reinforcing that true knowledge of the unseen belongs solely to God, who reveals it to whom He wills.

translation: And he said to the one whom he thought would be saved among the two: 'Mention me to your master.' But Satan made him forget to mention it to his master, so Joseph remained in prison for several years.
interpretation: This verse reminds us that true deliverance comes only from Allah, not from human intermediaries. Joseph's mistake was placing his hope in a fellow prisoner rather than directing his plea solely to Allah. The intervention of Satan, causing the man to forget, was a divine correction — a means by which Allah taught Joseph that reliance on creation over the Creator leads only to prolonged suffering. The years spent in prison were not a punishment, but a purification and a preparation, stripping Joseph of any dependence on other than Allah, so that when his liberation finally came, it came through divine will alone, untainted by worldly scheming or human favor.

translation: And the king said, 'Indeed, I see seven fat cows being eaten by seven lean ones, and seven green ears of grain and others dry. O eminent ones, explain to me my vision, if you should interpret visions.'
interpretation: This verse invites us to reflect on the nature of worldly cycles and the importance of seeking wisdom and knowledge. The king's dream, with its imagery of abundance and scarcity, reminds us that prosperity and hardship are transient phases ordained by Allah. The king's humility in consulting his advisors teaches us that true leadership involves recognizing the limits of one's own understanding and actively seeking guidance from those with knowledge and insight. It is a reminder that wisdom is not the exclusive domain of the powerful, but may be found in the most unexpected of places, as demonstrated by the subsequent role of Prophet Yusuf in interpreting the dream.

translation: They said, 'These are confused dreams, and we have no knowledge of the interpretation of dreams.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the human tendency to dismiss or minimize what we cannot understand or explain. When faced with something beyond their knowledge, the advisors of the king retreated into denial and ignorance rather than admitting their limitations honestly or seeking deeper wisdom. It serves as a reminder that true intellectual humility requires us not only to acknowledge what we do not know, but also to remain open to those who may possess knowledge we lack — as was demonstrated when Joseph, despite being imprisoned, possessed the divine insight that the learned men of the court did not. Proximity to power or status does not guarantee wisdom, and sometimes truth comes from the most unexpected and marginalized of sources.

translation: And the one who was saved of the two said, remembering after a period of time: 'I will inform you of its interpretation, so send me forth.'
interpretation: This verse highlights the nature of human forgetfulness and the way divine providence works through seemingly coincidental moments of recollection. The survivor's sudden remembrance after a long period is not merely a narrative detail, but a reminder that truth and knowledge cannot be indefinitely suppressed — they resurface at precisely the moment they are needed most. It suggests that God orchestrates the timing of events so that the right person, with the right knowledge, steps forward at the right moment, demonstrating that what appears to be chance or coincidence is in reality part of a greater, carefully arranged plan.

translation: 'Joseph, O man of truth! Explain to us the meaning of seven fat cows being devoured by seven lean ones, and seven green ears of grain and others dry, so that I may return to the people that they may know.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates that truth and integrity earn lasting respect, as even the king's cupbearer — once freed — returned to Joseph not merely because of his interpretive gift, but because Joseph had earned the title 'man of truth' (al-Siddiq) through his uncompromising honesty. The verse teaches that a person of genuine virtue and knowledge becomes an indispensable source of guidance for entire communities and nations, and that worldly power ultimately seeks wisdom rooted in moral uprightness rather than political authority.

translation: He said, 'You will sow for seven consecutive years, and whatever you harvest, leave it in its ear, except for a little of what you eat.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates the divine wisdom embedded in long-term planning and resource management. The instruction to leave the grain in its husk is a profound lesson in preservation and foresight — that in times of abundance, one must resist the temptation of overconsumption and instead safeguard resources for the inevitable hardships ahead. It teaches that true wisdom lies not in enjoying the fullness of the present moment, but in disciplined stewardship that secures the well-being of future generations. The believer is thus called to balance immediate needs with long-term responsibility, recognizing that blessings are not merely for present enjoyment but are also a trust to be carefully managed.

translation: Then after that will come seven difficult (years) which will consume what you put forth for them, except a little from what you store.
interpretation: This verse, part of the story of Prophet Yusuf (Joseph) and his interpretation of the king's dream, reminds us that periods of hardship and scarcity inevitably follow times of abundance. It teaches us the divine wisdom of planning ahead and practicing prudence during times of plenty, so that we may endure the trials that are to come. The verse underscores that foresight, guided by God's wisdom, is an essential virtue, and that even in the most difficult of times, God leaves a remnant of mercy and provision for those who are prepared and patient.

translation: Then after that will come a year in which the people will be given rain and in which they will press [olives and grapes].
interpretation: This verse, part of the interpretation of the king's dream by Prophet Yusuf (Joseph), carries a deeper spiritual message beyond its immediate prophetic context: that hardship and suffering, no matter how prolonged, are always followed by relief and divine mercy. The mention of rain — a symbol of God's sustenance and blessing — alongside the act of pressing, which requires effort and labor, reminds us that the restoration of good times is not merely passive but involves human engagement and gratitude. God's mercy ultimately prevails, and no period of trial is permanent, urging believers to remain patient and hopeful in times of difficulty.

translation: And the king said, 'Bring him to me.' But when the messenger came to him, [Joseph] said, 'Return to your master and ask him about the women who cut their hands. Indeed, my Lord is well aware of their scheme.'
interpretation: This verse reveals the profound moral integrity and spiritual dignity of Prophet Joseph (Yusuf). Despite having endured years of unjust imprisonment, he does not rush toward freedom out of desperation or self-interest. Instead, he insists on his innocence being publicly established before he steps out of prison. This teaches us that a believer of true character does not compromise their honor merely to escape hardship, and that justice must be acknowledged openly, not quietly swept aside. Joseph's patience and restraint here are not weakness but a demonstration that his trust is ultimately in Allah, who knows all schemes and deceptions, and that divine vindication, when it comes, must be complete and unambiguous.

translation: He said, 'What was your business when you sought to seduce Joseph?' They said, 'God forbid! We know no evil against him.' The wife of al-'Aziz said, 'Now the truth has come to light: it was I who sought to seduce him, and he is indeed one of the truthful.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates that truth, no matter how long it is suppressed or obscured, will ultimately manifest and prevail. Joseph's steadfast integrity and patience in maintaining his truthfulness, even while imprisoned, is ultimately vindicated not by his own insistence but through the confession of those who wronged him. It teaches us that genuine virtue does not require self-defense or self-promotion — Divine justice ensures that the righteous are eventually exonerated, and those who have sinned are compelled, in their own conscience and in moments of clarity, to acknowledge the truth they once concealed.

translation: That is so he may know that I did not betray him in his absence, and that Allah does not guide the scheming of those who betray.
interpretation: This verse, spoken by Zulaykha (or according to some interpretations by Yusuf himself), reveals a profound spiritual truth: true integrity is not merely about outward behavior when observed, but about remaining faithful and honest even in secret. The acknowledgment that Allah does not guide the plots of traitors serves as a reminder that deception and betrayal are ultimately self-defeating paths, for divine guidance and support are reserved only for those who maintain honesty and fidelity even when no human eye is watching. It is a call to align one's inner reality with one's outer conduct, knowing that Allah is ever-aware of what is concealed.

translation: And I do not acquit myself. Indeed, the soul is a persistent enjoiner of evil, except those upon which my Lord has mercy. Indeed, my Lord is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: This verse teaches us the profound spiritual wisdom of self-awareness and humility before God. No matter how righteous one may appear, the human soul is inherently inclined toward base desires and wrongdoing. True piety begins not with self-congratulation, but with honest acknowledgment of one's own weakness and vulnerability to sin. The only escape from this inward pull toward evil is through divine mercy and grace — not through personal virtue alone. This should instill in the believer both a vigilant watchfulness over their own soul and a deep, ongoing dependency on God's forgiveness, preventing arrogance and fostering a state of perpetual humility and turning toward the Divine.

translation: And the king said, 'Bring him to me; I will select him exclusively for myself.' And when he spoke to him, he said, 'Indeed, you are today established [in position] and trusted with us.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates that true integrity and wisdom cannot remain hidden forever. Joseph's steadfast commitment to honesty and moral uprightness, even through years of imprisonment and hardship, ultimately elevated him to a position of great authority and trust. The verse teaches us that those who maintain their character and truthfulness in times of trial will inevitably be recognized and rewarded, for God orchestrates circumstances to honor those who remain faithful to their principles. The king's immediate recognition of Joseph's trustworthiness upon merely speaking with him underscores the profound spiritual truth that genuine virtue radiates through one's words and presence, commanding respect without the need for self-promotion.

translation: He said, 'Put me in charge of the storehouses of the land. I am indeed a knowledgeable guardian.'
interpretation: This verse reflects the Islamic principle that it is not only permissible but sometimes necessary for a person of integrity and competence to seek a position of authority when they know they are the most qualified for it. Yusuf's request was not an act of arrogance or worldly ambition, but rather a recognition of his unique God-given abilities in administration and foresight. The verse teaches us that placing the right person in the right position is an act of justice and wisdom, and that a true believer may actively seek responsibility when they are confident they can serve the greater good — combining both moral trustworthiness (hifz) and practical knowledge ('ilm) as the twin pillars of righteous leadership.

translation: And thus We established Joseph in the land to settle therein wherever he willed. We bestow Our mercy on whom We will, and We do not allow to be lost the reward of those who do good.
interpretation: This verse invites the believer to trust in the long arc of divine justice and providence. Joseph's journey — marked by betrayal, slavery, and imprisonment — appeared to be one of unrelenting suffering, yet every hardship was quietly being woven into a tapestry of elevation and honor. The verse teaches that God's mercy does not always arrive on the timetable we expect, nor through the paths we anticipate, but it arrives nonetheless for those who remain steadfast in righteousness. The concluding declaration — that God never wastes the reward of those who excel in goodness — is an eternal covenant of reassurance: no act of patience, integrity, or moral excellence, however unseen by the world, is ever lost before God. It calls the soul to focus not on immediate outcomes but on the quality of one's conduct, trusting that divine accounting is both perfect and unfailing.

translation: And the reward of the Hereafter is better for those who believed and used to fear Allah.
interpretation: This verse serves as a profound reminder that no matter how abundant worldly gains may appear, they are fleeting and insignificant when compared to the eternal reward awaiting the believers. It calls the faithful to maintain their perspective and priorities, encouraging them not to be seduced by the temporary pleasures of this world. True success is measured not by what one accumulates in this life, but by the degree of one's faith and God-consciousness (taqwa), which together form the foundation upon which the eternal reward of the Hereafter is built.

translation: And the brothers of Joseph came and entered upon him, and he recognized them, but they did not recognize him.
interpretation: This verse highlights the profound reversal of power and knowledge that God orchestrated in Joseph's story. Joseph, once thrown into a well by these very brothers, now holds complete authority over them while possessing full awareness of who they are — yet they remain ignorant of his identity. This asymmetry is a divine reminder that those who wrong others may one day find themselves utterly dependent on the very person they harmed, and that God's plan unfolds in ways that transcend human calculation. The one who was made vulnerable is now the one with power, and the ones who once held power are now the ones in need — a testament to God's ultimate justice and the elevation of the patient and righteous.

translation: And when he had furnished them with their provisions, he said, 'Bring me a brother of yours from your father. Do you not see that I give full measure and that I am the best of hosts?'
interpretation: This verse reveals Joseph's masterful use of his position of power not for revenge, but as a divine instrument of reunion and healing. By conditioning further provisions on the arrival of his full brother Benjamin, Joseph is carefully orchestrating a reunion that serves a higher purpose — the fulfillment of God's plan. His emphasis on being a fair dealer and a generous host is not merely a negotiating tactic, but reflects the integrity of a man shaped by his trials. The verse teaches that those who are tested and remain faithful are ultimately entrusted with both worldly authority and the moral wisdom to use it righteously, serving as instruments of divine will rather than personal ambition.

translation: But if you do not bring him to me, there shall be no measure of grain for you from me, nor shall you come near me.
interpretation: This verse, spoken by Joseph (Yusuf) to his brothers, illustrates how divine orchestration works through seemingly ordinary human negotiations and conditions. The withholding of sustenance serves as a divinely arranged mechanism to compel the brothers to bring Benjamin, ultimately leading to the reunion of the family and the fulfillment of Joseph's earlier dream. It teaches that Allah's plans unfold through worldly means and circumstances, and that hardship and conditions placed upon people may in fact be instruments of mercy and reunion rather than punishment.

translation: They said, 'We will try to persuade his father to send him with us, and indeed we will do it.'
interpretation: This verse reflects the sincerity and determination of the brothers of Joseph when they pledged to convince their father, Jacob, to allow Benjamin to travel with them to Egypt. It illustrates how the divine plan was unfolding — the brothers, though unaware, were becoming instruments through which God's greater design would be fulfilled. Their confident promise, 'we will surely do it,' reveals a human assertiveness that, when aligned with God's will, becomes part of a larger providential scheme. The verse invites reflection on how human resolve and commitment, even when made in ordinary circumstances, can serve as vehicles for extraordinary divine purposes.

translation: And he said to his attendants, 'Put their merchandise back into their saddlebags so that they may recognize it when they return to their family, so that they might come back.'
interpretation: This verse reveals the magnanimity and subtle wisdom of Joseph (Yusuf), who secretly returned the payment of his brothers without their knowledge. By doing so, he created a compelling reason for them to return, knowing that men of honor would feel obligated to come back upon discovering they had received goods without paying for them. This act reflects the divine wisdom operating through Yusuf — his generosity was not merely material, but strategically compassionate, designed to draw his brothers back so that the unfolding of God's greater plan could continue. It illustrates how God's providence works through the thoughtful and merciful actions of the righteous, turning seemingly ordinary gestures into instruments of divine will.

translation: And when they returned to their father, they said, 'O our father, measure has been withheld from us, so send with us our brother that we may obtain measure, and indeed, we will be his guardians.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates a pivotal moment where the brothers of Joseph use material necessity — the withholding of grain — as leverage to persuade their aging father Jacob to part with his youngest son Benjamin. The deeper spiritual lesson lies in how divine providence orchestrates circumstances to bring about what has already been decreed. Jacob, who had already suffered the loss of Joseph, is now being asked to trust the very brothers who had previously betrayed that trust. The verse invites reflection on how trials are layered upon one another in a believer's life, and how the fulfillment of God's plan often requires human beings to act within seemingly difficult circumstances, unknowingly moving toward a reunion and mercy that only God has foreseen.

translation: He said, 'Shall I trust you with him as I trusted you with his brother before? But Allah is the best guardian, and He is the most merciful of the merciful.'
interpretation: This verse captures the profound tension between human helplessness and divine trust. Jacob's words reveal a heart torn between the trauma of past loss and the necessity of surrender to God's will. Rather than expressing bitterness or accusation toward his sons, he ultimately transcends his grief by anchoring his trust not in human promises — which have failed him before — but in Allah, the supreme Protector. The verse teaches that true faith is not the absence of fear or sorrow, but the conscious choice to place one's most precious concerns in the hands of the Most Merciful, even when worldly circumstances offer no guarantees. It is a model of tawakkul — complete reliance on God — born not from naivety, but from a wisdom deepened by suffering.

translation: And when they opened their baggage, they found their merchandise returned to them. They said, 'O our father, what more could we want? Here is our merchandise returned to us, and we will obtain provision for our family, and protect our brother, and obtain an extra camel's load. That is an easy measure.'
interpretation: This verse illustrates how divine providence orchestrates events to serve a higher purpose, working through seemingly ordinary circumstances. The return of the brothers' payment was not merely an act of generosity from Joseph, but a carefully arranged sign meant to persuade their father Jacob to allow Benjamin to travel with them. The verse teaches that when Allah wills something to occur, He arranges the material and emotional conditions that make it inevitable, using worldly incentives — the returned goods, the promise of more provisions, and the protection of Benjamin — as instruments of His greater plan. The ease and bounty of the situation was a divinely arranged circumstance meant to move the hearts of those involved toward the fulfillment of a purpose they could not yet fully comprehend.

translation: He said, 'I will never send him with you until you give me a solemn oath by Allah that you will surely bring him back to me, unless you are yourselves encompassed.' And when they gave him their solemn oath, he said, 'Allah is witness over what we say.'
interpretation: This verse reveals the profound wisdom of a father who has been tested by loss.
