It exposes the hollowness of their assertions by demanding accountability — highlighting that bold claims made without basis cannot be backed by any individual willing to stake their honor or their fate upon them. It is a rhetorical device that silences opposition by revealing the absence of any real foundation for their arguments.

translation: Or do they have partners [with Allah]? Then let them bring their partners, if they should be truthful.
interpretation: This verse issues a direct challenge to those who associate partners with Allah, exposing the emptiness of their polytheistic claims. The rhetorical demand to produce these so-called partners serves as an intellectual confrontation, revealing that idols and false deities have no real existence or power that can be demonstrated. It is an invitation to honest reflection: if one truly believes in these partners, let them be presented as genuine, tangible sources of divine authority. The challenge cannot be met, and in that silence lies the proof of Tawhid — the absolute oneness of Allah. The verse strips away the illusions of false worship and calls humanity back to reason and truth.

translation: The Day when the shin will be uncovered, and they will be invited to prostrate but they will not be able to.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the irreversible spiritual consequence of a life lived in deliberate rejection of God. The 'uncovering of the shin' is a moment of ultimate, undeniable Divine revelation — a Day when all concealment is stripped away and truth stands bare. Those who refused to bow in worship during their earthly lives, when prostration was still possible and meaningful, will find themselves paralyzed, physically and spiritually incapable of performing the very act that could have saved them. The verse is a profound warning that the opportunity for sincere submission is bound to this life alone; habitual arrogance and neglect of worship harden the soul to such a degree that, when the moment of absolute truth arrives, the ability to respond has already been forfeited. The body itself becomes a testament to the choices of the soul.

translation: Their eyes humbled, overwhelmed by disgrace. And they had already been invited to prostrate while they were sound and unharmed.
interpretation: This verse serves as a profound warning about the consequence of spiritual arrogance in this life. The humiliation that will befall the disbelievers on the Day of Judgment is directly tied to their deliberate refusal to bow in prostration to God when they were healthy, free, and fully capable of doing so. The contrast is striking: in this world, they had every physical and circumstantial ability to submit, yet they chose pride over surrender. On that final Day, the very eyes that once looked upon the world with haughtiness will be cast down in shame, and the dignity they sought to preserve through their refusal will be replaced by utter disgrace. The verse thus teaches that true honor lies not in resisting submission to God, but in embracing it willingly while one still has the opportunity, for the chance to bow in worship is itself a gift that, if squandered, leads to eternal regret.

translation: So leave Me with whoever denies this message. We will gradually lead them on from where they do not know.
interpretation: This verse conveys a profound warning about divine justice operating through a mechanism that is imperceptible to the wrongdoer. Allah instructs the Prophet not to grieve excessively over those who reject the truth, for their punishment is already set in motion. The most striking aspect of this verse is the concept of 'istidraj' — a gradual drawing in — suggesting that those who deny God's word are not immediately struck down, but are instead lured deeper into their transgression through worldly comforts, success, and ease. This false sense of security becomes their undoing, as they mistake divine forbearance for divine approval. The verse thus warns that prosperity in the absence of faith can itself be a form of punishment, a silent and invisible snare that tightens without the victim's awareness, ultimately leading them to a reckoning they never anticipated.

translation: And I will give them respite. Indeed, My plan is firm.
interpretation: This verse serves as a profound reminder that divine wisdom operates on a timescale and through mechanisms beyond human comprehension. When wrongdoers appear to prosper and escape consequence, it is not a sign of divine indifference, but rather a deliberate and measured allowance — a rope being extended. The apparent delay in divine retribution should not be mistaken for weakness or absence. Rather, it reflects the absolute certainty and inescapability of divine justice. The firmness of Allah's plan means that no scheme of the ungrateful or the arrogant can ultimately succeed, no matter how sophisticated or powerful it may appear. True security lies not in worldly cunning or power, but in alignment with divine will.

translation: Or do you ask them for a payment, so they are burdened by debt?
interpretation: This verse challenges the disbelievers by pointing out that their rejection of the Prophet's message cannot be justified by any financial burden placed upon them. The Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) sought no material compensation for delivering the divine message, making their resistance entirely without practical excuse. The rhetorical question exposes the irrationality of their opposition — if the message costs them nothing, their refusal to accept it stems purely from arrogance and spiritual blindness, not from any worldly hardship imposed upon them.

translation: Or do they have knowledge of the unseen, so they write it down?
interpretation: This verse challenges the arrogance of those who make claims about divine matters without any authority or revelation. It is a rhetorical rebuke directed at those who presume to know what only Allah knows — the unseen realities of existence, destiny, and judgment. The verse exposes the absurdity of their certainty, reminding us that no human being possesses access to the hidden knowledge of the universe unless Allah has granted it. True knowledge of the unseen belongs solely to Allah, and any claim to it without divine sanction is nothing but conjecture dressed as truth.

translation: So be patient for the judgment of your Lord, and do not be like the companion of the whale, when he called out while he was distressed (swallowed with grief).
interpretation: This verse draws a profound lesson from the story of Prophet Jonah (Yunus), who abandoned his mission prematurely without divine permission, leading to his confinement in the belly of the whale in a state of overwhelming anguish. The command directed at the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is not merely about enduring hardship, but about the quality and nature of that patience — it must be rooted in complete trust and surrender to Allah's timing and wisdom. True steadfastness means remaining at one's post of duty without letting frustration or despair push one into hasty action. The verse teaches that impatience in the face of divine decree, even from a prophet of great stature, carries consequences, and that the servant's role is to hold firm with dignified perseverance until Allah's judgment unfolds in its perfect time.

translation: Had it not been that a favor from his Lord reached him, he would have been cast onto the open shore while he was blameworthy.
interpretation: This verse reminds us that no matter how far a person strays or falls into error, divine mercy remains available to rescue them. It teaches that God's grace is not contingent on our perfection, but rather intervenes precisely at the moment of our greatest failure. The implication is that human beings should never despair of God's mercy, nor should they become arrogant in their righteousness, for it is ultimately God's favor alone that saves any soul from ruin and disgrace.

translation: Then his Lord chose him and made him of the righteous.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the profound mercy and grace of Allah, illustrating that divine selection is not merely a reward for prior perfection, but rather a transformative act of God's will. It reminds us that Allah's choosing of a soul elevates and purifies it, suggesting that righteousness itself can be a gift bestowed by God rather than solely a product of human effort. The verse invites the believer to remain open to God's grace, understanding that His favor can lift a person from their lowest state to the highest ranks of spiritual virtue.

translation: And indeed, those who disbelieve would almost make you slip with their eyes when they hear the message, and they say, 'Indeed, he is mad.'
interpretation: This verse speaks to the intense hatred and spiritual malice of the disbelievers, whose very gazes were filled with such envy and ill-will that they could cause harm — a recognition of the reality of the evil eye (al-'ayn). Yet the deeper message is one of divine protection and reassurance to the Prophet ﷺ: no matter how fiercely his enemies stared at him with contempt, jealousy, or the desire to destroy him, Allah's protection rendered their malice ineffective. Their accusation of madness is itself a sign of their own spiritual blindness — for the one they called mad was the most balanced, noble, and guided of all human beings. The verse thus invites us to recognize that truth-bearers throughout history have always faced such psychological and spiritual warfare, and that reliance on Allah is the only shield against the hostility of those who refuse the light.

translation: And it is not except a reminder to the worlds.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the universal nature of the Qur'an's message, affirming that its guidance transcends the boundaries of time, culture, and people. It is not limited to any one nation or era, but is a reminder for all of creation — a call to consciousness and reflection that speaks to the innate nature of every soul, inviting humanity and all beings to return to an awareness of their Creator and their purpose in existence.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. The Inevitable Reality.
interpretation: The opening of Surah Al-Haqqah confronts the human soul with the certainty of the Day of Judgment by using one of its most striking names: Al-Haqqah, meaning the Inevitable or the Undeniable Truth. This single word serves as a profound spiritual warning — that no matter how much one may deny, delay, or dismiss the idea of ultimate accountability, its occurrence is as certain as existence itself. The invocation of God's names of mercy before this reminder of judgment is itself deeply significant: it tells us that the announcement of this inevitable reality is not an act of divine threat, but an act of divine compassion, giving humanity fair warning so that they may turn back and reflect before it is too late.

translation: What is the Inevitable Reality?
interpretation: This opening verse employs a rhetorical question not to seek information, but to provoke deep reflection and awe in the listener. The repetition of the word 'Al-Haqqah' serves as a dramatic device to emphasize that the Day of Judgment is a truth so overwhelming and momentous that the human mind, in its current state, cannot fully grasp its magnitude. God is essentially saying that this event transcends ordinary human comprehension, preparing the listener for the vivid and sobering description that follows.

translation: And what will make you realize what the Inevitable Hour is?
interpretation: This rhetorical question is not merely asking for information — it is a divine declaration that the magnitude of the Day of Judgment surpasses all human comprehension. By posing this question, Allah emphasizes that no human mind, no matter how knowledgeable or perceptive, can fully grasp the true nature and weight of that inevitable moment. It is a call to humility before the unknown, reminding us that there are realities beyond the limits of our perception and imagination, and that we must approach the concept of accountability with awe, seriousness, and sincere preparation.

translation: Thamud and 'Aad denied the Striking Calamity.
interpretation: This verse serves as a solemn warning to those who reject divine truth by invoking the fates of two ancient and powerful civilizations. The mention of Thamud and 'Aad — peoples of great strength and prosperity — is a reminder that no civilization, regardless of its power or achievements, is immune to divine justice when it persistently denies the truth. The 'Striking Calamity' (Al-Qari'ah) refers not only to the physical destruction that befell these peoples, but also to the ultimate cosmic reckoning on the Day of Judgment. By recalling their denial, the verse implicitly challenges the listener to reflect on their own stance toward divine revelation, warning that denial carries consequences that no human power can avert.

translation: As for Thamud, they were destroyed by the overwhelming [blast].
interpretation: This verse serves as a divine warning that arrogance, transgression, and the rejection of God's messengers inevitably lead to destruction. The fate of Thamud is presented not merely as a historical event, but as a timeless reminder that no civilization, no matter how powerful, can escape the consequences of moral corruption and defiance against divine guidance. The use of the word 'al-Taghiyah' — the overwhelming or exceeding force — suggests that the punishment was proportionate to their own excess and transgression, reflecting a cosmic principle of justice wherein the nature of one's downfall mirrors the nature of one's sin.

translation: As for 'Aad, they were destroyed by a furious, roaring wind.
interpretation: This verse serves as a powerful warning to all of humanity by recounting the fate of the ancient people of 'Aad, who were known for their great strength and civilization. Despite their worldly power, they were utterly helpless before the divine decree. The use of a wind — something invisible and uncontrollable by human hands — as the instrument of their destruction underscores the absolute sovereignty of Allah and the complete insignificance of human pride and arrogance when set against divine will. The lesson is that no amount of physical strength, wealth, or civilization can protect a people who turn away from truth and persist in transgression.

translation: He unleashed it upon them for seven nights and eight days in succession, so you would have seen the people lying prostrate within it, as if they were hollow trunks of palm trees.
interpretation: This verse calls upon the reader to reflect on the absolute powerlessness of human arrogance when confronted with divine will. The vivid image of people fallen like hollow palm trunks is a profound metaphor: just as a palm tree may appear strong and towering from the outside yet be empty and structurally void within, so too were the people of 'Ād — outwardly mighty, boastful of their physical strength and civilizational achievements, yet inwardly hollow in their spiritual and moral substance. The precision of 'seven nights and eight days' emphasizes that divine punishment, when decreed, is measured and deliberate — not chaotic — reminding us that every moment of suffering has a purpose within a greater cosmic order. The verse ultimately warns that worldly strength, without spiritual integrity and submission to God, is as fragile as a dead tree standing only until the wind comes.

translation: So do you see any remnant of them?
interpretation: This rhetorical question serves as a profound reminder of the absolute and total annihilation that befalls those who defy divine will. It invites the reader to reflect on the transience of worldly power and arrogance, emphasizing that no matter how mighty a civilization or individual may seem, defiance of truth and justice leads to complete obliteration — leaving behind not even a trace. It is a call to humility and a warning that the legacy one truly leaves behind is determined not by power or wealth, but by righteousness and submission to God.

translation: And Pharaoh came, and those before him, and the overturned cities, with sin.
interpretation: This verse serves as a powerful warning by invoking the historical examples of those who committed grave sins and faced divine punishment. The mention of Pharaoh, the ancient nations before him, and the destroyed cities (referring to the people of Lot) collectively illustrates that no power, civilization, or community is immune from divine accountability when they persist in transgression and corruption. The verse reminds humanity that arrogance, oppression, and moral depravity inevitably lead to ruin, urging reflection on the consequences of turning away from righteousness.

translation: They disobeyed the messenger of their Lord, so He seized them with a severe seizure.
interpretation: This verse serves as a profound warning about the consequences of rejecting divine guidance. The use of the word 'rābiya' (increasing, surpassing) to describe the seizure suggests that the punishment was not merely proportional to the transgression, but exceeded it in severity as a demonstration of divine authority and justice. The verse implies that the greatest act of disobedience is not merely a moral failing, but a rejection of the mercy that God extends through His messengers. In sending messengers, God offers humanity a way out of destruction, and so to reject the messenger is to actively choose one's own ruin. The verse thus calls the believer to reflect on the gravity of turning away from divine guidance, understanding that such rejection carries consequences both in this world and the next.

translation: Indeed, when the water overflowed, We carried you in the sailing ship.
interpretation: This verse draws the believer's attention to the profound mercy and providence of Allah, reminding humanity that even in moments of catastrophic destruction — when divine punishment overwhelms the earth — Allah preserves those who believe and trust in Him. The reference to carrying 'you' rather than 'your ancestors' collapses the distance of time, making the salvation of Noah's people a living, personal reminder that every human being alive today is a descendant of those who were saved. It is an invitation to gratitude and humility, urging us to recognize that our very existence is a testament to Allah's mercy and His will to preserve the faithful.

translation: That We might make it a reminder for you and that attentive ears might retain it.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the divine intentionality behind preserved historical lessons and revelations. Allah affirms that the events and truths communicated through scripture are not merely historical records, but living reminders designed to penetrate the hearts of those who are truly receptive. The phrase 'attentive ear' suggests that not all hearing is equal — true comprehension requires a heart that is spiritually awake, humble, and oriented toward Allah. It is a call to move beyond passive listening to active, transformative engagement with divine guidance, implying that the responsibility to internalize truth lies with the individual believer.

translation: Then when the Trumpet is blown with a single blast,
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the absolute certainty and swiftness of the Day of Resurrection. The use of 'single blast' highlights that the end of this world requires no prolonged effort — it will occur in an instant by the will of Allah, reminding humanity that all of creation is utterly dependent on and subservient to His command. It serves as a profound warning to not be deceived by the apparent permanence of this worldly life.

translation: And the earth and the mountains are lifted and leveled with a single blow.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the absolute and total transformation of the physical world at the moment of the Day of Resurrection. The imagery of the earth and mountains — the most stable and immovable structures known to humanity — being crushed and leveled in a single strike is a powerful reminder that nothing in creation is permanent or indestructible. What humans perceive as unshakeable certainties will be rendered utterly insignificant before the power of Allah. The verse invites us to reconsider our attachments to the material world and to recognize that true stability lies only in the eternal, not in the transient physical realm we inhabit.

translation: So on that Day, the Event will come to pass.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the absolute certainty and inevitability of the Day of Judgment. The use of the word 'al-Waqi'ah' (the Event) refers back to the trumpet blast mentioned earlier in Surah Al-Haqqah, and its repetition here serves as a powerful rhetorical device to underscore that when the first trumpet is blown, the second shall inevitably follow, and the resurrection and reckoning will be set into irreversible motion. No force in existence can delay or prevent it, reminding humanity to take the promise of accountability seriously.

translation: And the sky will split apart, for on that Day it will be frail.
interpretation: This verse draws our attention to the fragility of what we consider permanent and immovable. The heavens, which we perceive as an eternal and unshakeable canopy above us, will on the Day of Judgment prove to be as delicate and transient as everything else in creation. This serves as a profound reminder that nothing in existence possesses inherent permanence or strength — all solidity and stability are gifts granted by Allah, and on that ultimate Day, the illusion of permanence will be stripped away entirely. It invites human beings to redirect their trust and reliance away from the apparent structures of the material world and toward the only true constant: Allah Himself.

translation: And the angels will be at its edges, and above them eight will carry the Throne of your Lord that Day.
interpretation: This verse draws our attention to the absolute and uncontested sovereignty of Allah on the Day of Judgment. The imagery of angels stationed at the edges of the sky and eight mighty bearers carrying the Divine Throne is not merely a description of cosmic architecture, but a powerful reminder that all grandeur, power, and authority belong solely to Allah. Everything in existence — angels, creation, and the very fabric of the universe — is subservient to Him. On the most critical day humanity will ever face, this scene is presented first, before any reckoning begins, to establish that there is no refuge, no intercession, and no escape except through the mercy and justice of the One whose Throne is carried above all. It is an invitation to reflect on one's relationship with that sovereign power while there is still time to do so.

translation: On that Day, you will be presented [before Allah], and nothing hidden among you will remain hidden.
interpretation: This verse reminds us that on the Day of Judgment, every soul will stand utterly exposed before Allah, with no secret deed, hidden intention, or concealed thought escaping His complete and perfect knowledge. It serves as a profound moral warning urging believers to purify not only their outward actions but also their innermost intentions, knowing that true accountability encompasses the totality of one's being — seen and unseen — in this life.

translation: As for he who is given his record in his right hand, he will say, 'Here, read my record!'
interpretation: This verse speaks to the joy and relief of the righteous on the Day of Judgment. Receiving one's book of deeds in the right hand is a symbol of success and divine approval. The eager invitation to others to read one's record reflects the confidence and happiness of a soul that has lived a life of faith and good deeds — one who has nothing to hide and everything to celebrate. It is a moment of ultimate vindication, where a person's entire life of devotion is laid bare before all, not with shame, but with pride and gratitude toward Allah.

translation: Indeed, I was certain that I would meet my account (reckoning).
interpretation: This verse reflects the profound spiritual state of a believer who lived with constant awareness of the Hereafter. The use of 'zanantu' (I thought/was certain) here does not imply doubt, but rather a deep, motivating conviction — a lived certainty that shaped every action in this life. The believer is not surprised by the reckoning; they anticipated it, prepared for it, and are now at peace standing before it. This is the fruit of taqwa: not fear that paralyzes, but awareness that purifies. The verse invites us to examine whether our own lives are lived with this same conscious anticipation of standing before Allah, for it is that awareness which transforms mundane deeds into acts of worship and gives ultimate meaning to our existence.

translation: He will be in a pleasing life.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the profound spiritual reward that awaits the believer in the Hereafter. The 'pleasing life' is not merely one of material comfort, but rather a state of complete inner contentment and divine satisfaction. It suggests that true fulfillment comes not from worldly pursuits, but from living a life aligned with God's will, which ultimately leads to an eternal existence of joy and peace. The use of 'راضية' (pleasing/satisfied) implies a reciprocal contentment — not only is the person pleased with their life, but their life itself reflects a state of divine approval and grace.

translation: In a lofty Garden
interpretation: This verse points to the elevated and exalted nature of Paradise, suggesting that true spiritual fulfillment and reward are not found in the lowly pursuits of worldly life, but are reserved for those who raise themselves through faith and righteous deeds. The 'loftiness' of the Garden is not merely physical but symbolic of the supreme dignity and honor that God bestows upon the souls who strived for something higher than the material world.

translation: Its fruits are within close reach.
interpretation: This verse invites the believer to reflect on the effortless abundance of Paradise, suggesting that spiritual reward is not something distant or difficult to attain for those who have lived righteously — just as the fruits of Paradise hang low and accessible, the mercy and generosity of God draw near to those who sincerely seek Him, removing all struggle and strain in the ultimate abode of rest.

translation: Eat and drink with ease for what you put forth in the days gone by.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the profound relationship between our earthly deeds and our ultimate reward. It is a divine invitation to the believers in the hereafter, reminding us that every act of worship, sacrifice, and righteousness performed in this transient world is never lost. The pleasures of Paradise are not arbitrary gifts but are deeply personal — they are the fruit of one's own spiritual labor. The use of the word 'هنيئا' (with ease, wholesomely) suggests that the enjoyment in the hereafter carries no guilt, no consequence, and no limitation, unlike the pleasures of this world. It is an encouragement to invest in our spiritual accounts today, for the days of this life are fleeting, and what we send ahead of us will define the eternity that awaits us.

translation: But as for him who is given his record in his left hand, he will say: 'Oh, I wish I had not been given my book!'
interpretation: This verse speaks to the profound and inescapable nature of divine accountability. The left hand, in the Qur'anic worldview, symbolizes disgrace and failure, and receiving one's book of deeds in it signifies a life spent in transgression and heedlessness. The anguished cry of regret — wishing the record had never been revealed — reflects the ultimate tragedy of a soul that had every opportunity in the worldly life to reform, yet squandered it. The verse serves as a powerful warning to the living: the record of our deeds is being written now, and the moment of reckoning will come when regret will be utterly useless. True wisdom lies not in wishing to escape accountability in the Hereafter, but in living consciously and righteously in the present so that one may receive their book with joy rather than despair.

translation: And I had no idea what my account would be!
interpretation: This verse captures the profound moment of a believer's astonishment and humility upon receiving their record of deeds on the Day of Judgment. It reflects the soul's recognition that divine accounting surpasses all human comprehension and expectation, reminding us that no person can fully anticipate the extent of God's mercy or justice. It serves as a call to remain conscious of our actions in this life, knowing that every deed, however small, is recorded and will be brought to account in ways beyond our imagination.

translation: 'Oh, would that it (death) had been the decisive one!'
interpretation: This verse captures the desperate cry of a disbeliever or wrongdoer on the Day of Judgment, who, upon witnessing the terrifying reality of divine reckoning and the consequences of their deeds, wishes that death had been the final end — that there had been no resurrection, no accountability, and no eternal consequence. It is a moment of profound regret and despair, revealing that those who denied the afterlife in their worldly life will, at the moment of ultimate truth, wish their denial had been correct. The verse serves as a powerful warning to humanity: death is not the end, and the soul's journey continues beyond it into a realm of perfect justice.

translation: My wealth has not availed me.
interpretation: This verse serves as a profound reminder that material wealth, no matter how vast, holds no power or influence in the face of divine judgment. It underscores the ultimate futility of placing one's trust and identity in worldly possessions, warning humanity that on the Day of Reckoning, only one's deeds and faith will matter. True security lies not in the accumulation of riches, but in spiritual preparation for the eternal life to come.

translation: My power (authority) has perished from me.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah Al-Haqqah (69:29), captures the desperate cry of a soul on the Day of Judgment who realizes that all worldly power, status, and authority they once possessed have utterly vanished. It serves as a profound reminder that the dominion, influence, and prestige that humans accumulate in this life are entirely temporary and illusory. On the Day of Reckoning, no amount of worldly power can shield a person from divine accountability. True sovereignty belongs only to Allah, and the verse urges us to invest in deeds of righteousness rather than in the fleeting pursuit of worldly power and authority.

translation: 'Seize him and shackle him!'
interpretation: This verse, addressed to the angels, reflects the ultimate consequence of rejecting divine guidance. It serves as a powerful reminder that the freedom granted to human beings in this worldly life is temporary and conditional. The one who misused their free will and turned away from truth will find that freedom utterly stripped away on the Day of Judgment. The command is sharp and immediate, signaling that divine justice, though delayed, is absolute and inescapable — a moment where no intercession, wealth, or influence can alter one's fate.

translation: Then burn him in Hellfire.
interpretation: This verse serves as a divine warning and a declaration of ultimate justice. It signifies that no act of arrogance, denial, or transgression against God's truth goes unanswered. The command to cast the condemned into Hellfire reflects the absolute authority of God as the final Judge, reminding humanity that worldly power and defiance hold no weight in the face of divine accountability. It is a call for reflection — urging the living to consider the consequences of rejecting faith and persisting in wrongdoing before it is too late to turn back.

translation: Then in a chain the length of which is seventy cubits, insert him.
interpretation: This verse conveys the ultimate humiliation and confinement that awaits the arrogant disbeliever in the Hereafter. The imagery of a chain measuring seventy cubits symbolizes the totality of bondage — a punishment that is not merely physical restraint, but a complete stripping away of the freedom and pride that the disbeliever exercised in this world when he rejected God and oppressed others. The enormity of the chain reflects the enormity of the sin of rejecting divine truth, suggesting that those who bind themselves spiritually to arrogance and disbelief in this life will find themselves literally and inescapably bound in the next.

translation: Indeed, he used to not believe in Allah, the Most Great.
interpretation: This verse serves as a profound warning about the ultimate consequence of a life lived in denial of the Divine. The emphasis on 'the Most Great' (Al-Azeem) is deliberate — it underscores the magnitude of the transgression. To reject belief in Allah is not merely an intellectual misstep, but a fundamental turning away from the very source of existence and majesty. The verse invites reflection on the gravity of disbelief, reminding us that faith is not a peripheral matter but the very foundation upon which a meaningful and accountable life is built.

translation: And does not encourage the feeding of the poor.
interpretation: This verse serves as a profound moral indictment, suggesting that true faith is not merely expressed through ritual worship but must manifest in active concern for the vulnerable. The failure to urge others to feed the poor reveals a heart disconnected from compassion and communal responsibility. Islam teaches that social conscience is inseparable from spiritual integrity — one who does not feel moved to advocate for the hungry has failed to internalize the core message of faith, which demands that believers be agents of mercy and justice in the world.

translation: So he has here today no devoted friend.
interpretation: This verse serves as a profound warning about the ultimate isolation that awaits the heedless soul on the Day of Judgment. It reminds us that the social bonds, friendships, and alliances we rely upon in this worldly life will dissolve completely in the Hereafter. No companion, no ally, no intercessor will be present to offer comfort or rescue. The verse urges us to invest in the only relationship that truly endures beyond death — our relationship with Allah — rather than placing false hope in the fleeting connections of this world.

translation: And no food except from the foul discharge of wounds.
interpretation: This verse serves as a stark warning about the consequences of a life lived in rejection of divine guidance. The ghisleen — the filthy, scalding fluid that oozes from the wounds and bodies of those in Hellfire — represents the ultimate inversion of nourishment. Just as sustenance in this world is a sign of God's mercy and blessing, the absence of true nourishment in the Hereafter is a sign of divine justice. The verse compels the reader to reflect on the blessings they take for granted, urging gratitude and righteous action before the moment when such blessings are irrevocably lost.

translation: None shall eat it except the sinners.
interpretation: This verse serves as a stark warning about the consequences of sin and transgression. The exclusivity of this punishment — that only the wrongdoers will be subjected to it — underscores the divine principle of perfect justice. God does not punish the innocent; every soul is held accountable only for its own deeds. The verse invites the believer to reflect on their own conduct and to fear a day when one's moral failures become the very sustenance of their suffering, turning the natural act of eating — a source of life and nourishment in this world — into a symbol of torment and degradation in the next.

translation: So I swear by what you see
interpretation: Allah draws attention to the totality of observable reality as a witness to divine truth. By swearing an oath upon everything that is visible to human beings, the verse invites deep reflection on the created world as a sign of God's power and existence. The use of 'فلا' before the oath intensifies its solemnity, suggesting that the evidence surrounding humanity is so overwhelming and self-evident that creation itself stands as testimony to the truth of what is being conveyed.

translation: And what you do not see
interpretation: This phrase alludes to the existence of unseen realms and realities beyond human perception, reminding us of the limitations of our senses and the vast dimensions of existence that lie beyond our comprehension. It calls us to humility, acknowledging that our knowledge is finite while Allah's knowledge encompasses all things, seen and unseen.

translation: Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger.
interpretation: This verse affirms the divine authenticity of the Qur'an by emphasizing that it was conveyed through a noble and trustworthy messenger — whether referring to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) or the Angel Jibreel (Gabriel). The use of the word 'noble' (كريم) is deliberate, reminding us that the channel through which revelation flows is pure and honorable, and therefore the message itself is beyond doubt or corruption. It calls upon the listener to receive the Qur'an not with skepticism, but with the reverence owed to a communication that originates from God and was delivered through the most trustworthy of bearers.

translation: And it is not the word of a poet; little do you believe.
interpretation: This verse serves as a divine rebuttal to one of the central accusations made by the Quraysh against the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, who dismissed the Qur'an as mere poetry. The verse challenges the spiritual blindness of those who refuse to recognize the divine origin of the Qur'an, suggesting that their rejection is not rooted in genuine intellectual inquiry but rather in a deliberate unwillingness to open their hearts to faith. The phrase 'little do you believe' is a rebuke that points to a deeper moral and spiritual failure — the capacity for faith exists within them, yet they suppress it out of pride, stubbornness, or worldly attachment. The Qur'an, unlike poetry, does not serve the ego of a human composer; it transcends human artistry and speaks to the eternal truths of existence, urging those who hear it to reflect sincerely rather than dismiss it through convenient labels.

translation: Nor is it the word of a soothsayer; little do you reflect.
interpretation: This verse challenges those who dismissed the Qur'an as mere fortune-telling or divination. The rebuke 'little do you reflect' points to a deeper spiritual failure: the unwillingness to engage one's reason and conscience. True reflection would make it evident that the Qur'an's wisdom, coherence, and guidance far transcend anything a soothsayer could produce. The verse thus invites humanity to move beyond superficial rejection and engage seriously with the divine message, suggesting that disbelief often stems not from rational inquiry but from a lack of genuine contemplation.

translation: A revelation from the Lord of the worlds.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the divine origin and supreme authority of the Qur'an, reminding the reader that its source is not human but the Lord who sustains and governs all of creation. It calls upon us to approach the scripture with humility and reverence, recognizing that its guidance transcends human wisdom and is suited for all peoples across all times.

translation: And if he (the Prophet) had fabricated against Us some sayings,
interpretation: This verse serves as a powerful divine guarantee of the authenticity of the Qur'an. God is establishing that the Prophet Muhammad could not have invented or altered the revelation, because the consequences would have been severe and immediate. It underscores that the Qur'an is not a human composition but a divinely protected message, and that the Prophet had no personal agency in shaping its content. The verse invites the reader to trust in the integrity and purity of the revelation they are receiving.

translation: We would have seized him by the right hand.
interpretation: This verse conveys the absolute power and authority of Allah over all creation, including the Prophet himself. The 'right hand' symbolizes the seat of power and control. The verse serves as a profound reminder that no one, regardless of their status or closeness to Allah, is beyond divine accountability. Even the most beloved of messengers is ultimately subject to Allah's supreme authority, reinforcing the principle that prophethood is a sacred trust, not a personal privilege, and that any deviation from the revealed message would invite immediate and decisive divine intervention.

translation: Then We would have cut from him the aorta.
interpretation: This verse serves as a solemn divine warning emphasizing that God's relationship with the Prophet, and by extension with all people, is not one of favoritism or unconditional privilege. Even the most beloved and trusted of God's messengers would face severe divine retribution if he were to fabricate or distort the revelation. The imagery of severing the aorta — the vital vessel of life — conveys that God's justice is absolute and uncompromising, transcending all personal bonds and social hierarchies. It underscores that the authority of the Qur'an is not a human construction but a sacred trust, and any corruption of divine truth would be met with immediate and certain destruction, no matter who the perpetrator might be.

translation: And there is not among you anyone who could prevent [Us] from [punishing] him.
interpretation: This verse serves as a profound reminder of human vulnerability and absolute dependence on Allah. It dismantles any illusion of self-sufficiency or protection that a person might cling to, emphasizing that no worldly power, wealth, status, or relationship can shield a soul from divine accountability. The verse invites deep humility, urging believers to recognize that their only true refuge lies in turning sincerely to Allah, as no intercessor or protector exists independently of His will.

translation: And indeed, it is a reminder for the righteous (those who are mindful of God).
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that the Qur'an is not merely a book of information, but a living reminder that awakens the hearts of those who have already cultivated a sense of God-consciousness within themselves. True benefit from divine guidance requires a prepared and receptive heart — one softened by taqwa (mindfulness and fear of God). The verse suggests that spiritual readiness is a prerequisite for receiving divine wisdom, implying that the more one nurtures their taqwa, the deeper their connection to and benefit from the Qur'anic message becomes.

translation: And indeed, We know that among you are those who deny.
interpretation: This verse serves as a divine warning that God's omniscience encompasses even the hidden intentions of disbelievers. It is not merely an observation, but a subtle reminder that denial of the truth is not hidden from God, and that such denial carries consequence. The verse implies that accountability is inevitable, as nothing — not even the quiet rejection held within one's heart — escapes divine awareness.

translation: And indeed, it will be a cause of regret for the disbelievers.
interpretation: This verse serves as a profound warning about the spiritual consequences of rejecting divine truth. The regret spoken of here is not merely an emotion, but an existential reckoning — a moment when those who turned away from guidance will fully comprehend the magnitude of what they lost. The use of the word 'hasra' (حسرة), meaning deep regret or anguish, suggests an irreversible sorrow that comes from a missed opportunity that can never be reclaimed. It reminds the believer that faith is not simply a theological position, but a mercy and a gift, and its rejection leads ultimately to a grief that transcends the temporal world.

translation: And indeed, it is the truth of certainty.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that the divine revelation is not merely probable or speculative knowledge, but represents the highest and most absolute form of truth — a certainty that transcends all doubt. It calls the believer to anchor their faith not in conjecture or inherited tradition alone, but in a deeply verified and unshakeable conviction about the reality of God's word and the ultimate nature of existence.

translation: So glorify the name of your Lord, the Most Great.
interpretation: This verse is a divine command urging the believer to continuously engage in the remembrance and glorification of Allah, acknowledging His absolute greatness and transcendence above all imperfection. It reminds us that the tongue, the heart, and the entire being should be oriented toward magnifying God, as true spiritual fulfillment lies not in worldly pursuits but in the constant awareness of and surrender to the magnificence of the Creator.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. A questioner asked about a punishment bound to happen.
interpretation: This verse addresses those who mockingly or skeptically demanded to see the divine punishment that the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) warned about. The use of 'bound to happen' (waqi') emphasizes the absolute certainty and inevitability of divine retribution. The verse serves as a profound warning that the disbelievers' dismissal of punishment as impossible or distant is a grave error in judgment, for what God has decreed cannot be averted or delayed beyond its appointed time. Their very questioning of it does not diminish its reality, but rather reflects their own spiritual blindness and arrogance in the face of divine truth.

translation: For the disbelievers, there is no one to repel it.
interpretation: This verse serves as a stern warning that the punishment destined for those who reject faith is absolutely inevitable and unstoppable. No power in existence — no intercessor, no wealth, no worldly authority — can shield a person from divine retribution when they have persistently turned away from truth. It emphasizes the absolute sovereignty of Allah, reminding humanity that accountability is inescapable, and that the only true protection lies in sincere belief and righteous action before that day arrives.

translation: From Allah, the Lord of the Ascending Stairways
interpretation: This phrase emphasizes the supreme and transcendent nature of Allah, whose dominion extends across all levels of existence and spiritual elevation. The 'ascending stairways' or 'Ma'arij' symbolize the infinite degrees of nearness to the Divine, reminding us that all revelation, mercy, and authority descend from a source so exalted that it transcends human comprehension. It calls the believer to humility, recognizing that whatever reaches us of guidance or blessing must travel, in a sense, from an incomprehensibly high station down to our limited earthly reality.

translation: The angels and the Spirit ascend to Him in a day whose measure is fifty thousand years.
interpretation: This verse invites the believer to contemplate the infinite and transcendent nature of Allah, whose reality exists entirely beyond the boundaries of human time and perception. The staggering figure of fifty thousand years is not meant to be taken as a literal astronomical measurement, but rather as a device to shatter our earthly conception of time and impress upon us the absolute majesty and otherness of the Divine. Just as the angels — beings of pure light and obedience — must traverse an incomprehensible span to reach Him, so too must the human soul recognize the vast distance between the created and the Creator. This distance, however, is not one of abandonment, but of awe, reminding the believer that to draw near to Allah requires humility, patience, and a willingness to surrender one's small and finite self to the One who is boundless and eternal.

translation: So be patient with beautiful patience.
interpretation: This verse calls the believer to a form of patience that is not merely passive endurance, but an active, graceful, and dignified acceptance of hardship. 'Beautiful patience' implies bearing trials without complaint, without despair, and without losing one's inner composure or faith in God's wisdom. It is a patience that is free of bitterness and resentment, one that reflects a deep trust in the divine plan and an understanding that all difficulty is temporary and purposeful. True patience, in this sense, becomes a form of worship and a mark of spiritual maturity.

translation: Indeed, they see it as far away.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the spiritual blindness of those who deny the Day of Judgment. Their disbelief causes them to perceive the inevitable reckoning as a distant, almost impossible reality. It is a reflection of how the human heart, when veiled by arrogance and worldly attachment, fails to grasp the nearness of accountability. What they dismiss as remote, Allah sees as imminent, reminding us that our perception of time and consequence is limited, while divine knowledge and justice are absolute and ever-present.

translation: And We see it near.
interpretation: This verse reminds us that what human beings perceive as distant or delayed — particularly the Day of Judgment — is, from Allah's perspective, already imminent and close at hand. It is a call to spiritual urgency, urging believers not to be deceived by the apparent passage of time, for Allah's perception of time transcends all human understanding, and what seems far off to us is already within His immediate sight and grasp.

translation: The Day when the sky will be like murky oil (or molten brass)
interpretation: This verse evokes the terror and upheaval of the Day of Judgment by describing the dissolution of the very heavens, which humanity has always perceived as a symbol of permanence, order, and divine majesty. The sky transforming into something molten and unstable serves as a powerful reminder that nothing in creation is eternal or immovable, and that all familiar structures of existence will ultimately collapse before the absolute reality of God's dominion on that Day.

translation: And the mountains will be like wool
interpretation: This verse evokes the absolute powerlessness of even the mightiest of earthly structures on the Day of Judgment. Mountains, which we regard as symbols of permanence, stability, and overwhelming strength, will be rendered as light and scattered as carded wool. This imagery serves as a profound reminder that nothing in this world, no matter how grand or immovable it may appear, holds any permanence before the power of Allah. It invites the believer to reconsider where they place their trust and sense of security, redirecting it away from the material world and toward the eternal.

translation: And no close friend will ask [anything of] a close friend.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the absolute terror and self-absorption of the Day of Judgment. Despite the deep bonds of love and friendship that connect people in this world, on that Day every soul will be so overwhelmed by its own fear and accountability before Allah that it will be utterly indifferent to even its dearest companion. The verse serves as a powerful warning that the relationships and social bonds we rely upon in this life will be of no use in the Hereafter, urging us to focus on our individual relationship with Allah rather than placing false hope in worldly connections for our ultimate salvation.

translation: They will be made to see each other. The criminal will wish that he could ransom himself from the punishment of that Day by his children,
interpretation: This verse reveals the profound terror and desperation of the Day of Judgment, where even the most sacred of human bonds — the love of one's children — becomes something a sinner would willingly sacrifice to escape divine punishment. It serves as a stark warning that no worldly attachment, no matter how dear, will hold any value on that Day. The verse compels us to reflect on our priorities in this life: rather than placing ultimate reliance on family ties or material bonds, we should focus on building a relationship with Allah that will truly protect us when all else fails.

translation: And his companion and his brother
interpretation: This verse, likely part of a larger passage describing the Day of Judgment, reminds us that on that momentous Day, even the closest and most cherished human bonds — those of a spouse and a sibling — will be of no avail. It serves as a profound warning that ultimate accountability before Allah is a deeply personal and individual matter, and that no worldly relationship, no matter how intimate, can shield a soul from divine reckoning. The verse calls us to focus on our own deeds and our own relationship with Allah, rather than placing false hope in the intercession of loved ones.

translation: And his kindred who sheltered him
interpretation: This verse highlights the profound isolation that will befall the sinner on the Day of Judgment. Despite the deep bonds of family and clan that defined social identity and protection in Arabian culture, even these ties will be severed. The verse implies that the very relationships a person relied upon in this world for refuge, support, and identity will be rendered utterly meaningless in the Hereafter, emphasizing that no worldly connection or loyalty can substitute for one's personal accountability before God.

translation: And everyone on earth entirely, then it would save him.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the futility of worldly possessions and attachments in the face of divine judgment. No amount of earthly wealth, power, or resources — even if one possessed the entirety of the world — could serve as a ransom or means of salvation on the Day of Judgment. True salvation lies not in material accumulation, but in sincere faith, righteous deeds, and the mercy of Allah. It is a profound reminder that human beings must orient their hearts toward the eternal rather than the temporal.

translation: No! Indeed, it is the Blazing Fire (Laza),
interpretation: This verse serves as a divine refutation and warning, cutting through human complacency and denial. The word 'Kalla' (No!) is a sharp rhetorical rebuke, jolting the listener out of any illusion that worldly distractions or false hopes can shield them from accountability. The fire called 'Laza' is not merely a punishment, but a manifestation of absolute divine justice — a reality that strips away all pretense. The verse urges humanity to abandon spiritual negligence and recognize that the consequences of one's choices are as real and inevitable as the fire itself.

translation: It shall strip away the scalp (or the extremities).
interpretation: This verse, from Surah Al-Ma'arij (70:16), uses visceral, physical imagery to convey the absolute destructive power of Hellfire. The mention of stripping away the scalp or extremities is not merely a description of physical torment, but a deeper indication that the punishment reaches the most sensitive and peripheral parts of a person — nothing is spared, nothing is left untouched. It serves as a warning that the consequences of rejecting faith and persisting in arrogance are total and all-encompassing, leaving no part of the soul or body unaffected by divine justice.

translation: Calling those who turned their backs and walked away.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the nature of divine invitation and human rejection. It reflects the sorrow embedded in the act of calling out to those who have consciously chosen to turn away from truth and guidance. The imagery of someone physically turning their back suggests not mere ignorance, but a deliberate and willful refusal. The verse invites us to reflect on the tragedy of a soul that has been reached by the call of truth, yet chooses estrangement over return, highlighting that the door of guidance remains open even for those who flee from it.

translation: And gathered and hoarded.
interpretation: This verse condemns the human tendency to accumulate wealth obsessively and withhold it from circulation or charity. It speaks to the spiritual disease of greed, where one's entire purpose becomes the gathering and storing of material possessions, leaving no room in the heart for gratitude, generosity, or awareness of God. The act of hoarding is presented not merely as a social harm but as a symptom of a soul that has become enslaved to the dunya, forgetting that wealth is a trust from God to be used in His cause.

translation: Indeed, mankind was created anxious (and impatient).
interpretation: This verse speaks to the fundamental nature of the human soul, revealing that restlessness, anxiety, and impatience are not merely behavioral flaws but are woven into the very fabric of human creation. This divine acknowledgment serves as both a compassionate recognition of human vulnerability and a call to self-awareness. Rather than condemning this trait, Allah informs us of it so that we may consciously struggle against its negative manifestations — such as panic in hardship and ingratitude in ease — and channel this innate intensity toward devotion, striving, and reliance upon God. It is a reminder that our weaknesses are known to our Creator, and that spiritual growth lies in acknowledging and transcending them through faith and patience.

translation: When adversity touches him, he is impatient and distressed.
interpretation: This verse highlights a fundamental weakness in human nature — that without faith and spiritual grounding, a person becomes overwhelmed and loses composure when faced with hardship. It is a reminder that true strength and patience in times of difficulty can only be achieved through a deep connection with God, and that those who lack this connection will inevitably succumb to anxiety and despair when trials arise.

translation: And when good touches him, he is withholding.
interpretation: This verse highlights a fundamental flaw in human nature — that when a person experiences prosperity, comfort, or blessing, they become stingy and reluctant to share with others. It is a reminder that wealth and good fortune are not personal achievements to be hoarded, but rather trusts from Allah that carry with them a responsibility toward the community. The verse calls us to examine our instinct toward self-preservation and to transcend it through gratitude, generosity, and remembrance that all good ultimately comes from Allah and should flow through us to benefit others.

translation: Except the ones who pray
interpretation: This verse serves as a powerful exception, suggesting that the path to salvation and escape from the punishment described in preceding verses lies in the establishment of prayer. It implies that prayer is not merely a ritual act, but a transformative practice that anchors the soul to its Creator, cultivates humility, and safeguards a person from the spiritual heedlessness and moral failings that lead to ruin. The verse invites reflection on whether one's prayer is truly lived and internalized, rather than performed as an empty habit.

translation: Those who are constant in their prayer
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that true believers do not merely perform prayer as a ritual obligation, but maintain it with consistency, dedication, and presence of heart. The word 'dā'imūn' (constant) implies a deep, unbroken commitment — suggesting that faith is not a fleeting or circumstantial act, but a steady, lifelong devotion that shapes one's entire existence. True worship is not measured by the number of prayers performed, but by the unwavering continuity and sincerity with which the believer returns to God, time after time, regardless of the circumstances of life.

translation: And those in whose wealth there is a recognized right
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that true believers acknowledge that their wealth is not entirely their own. It points to the spiritual reality that material possessions carry a moral and social obligation — that giving to others is not an act of charity born of generosity alone, but a duty that has been divinely ordained. Wealth, in the Islamic worldview, is a trust from God, and embedded within it is the right of others. By recognizing this 'known right,' the believer transcends the ego's attachment to material things and aligns themselves with a higher sense of justice and communal responsibility.

translation: For the beggar and the deprived.
interpretation: This verse reminds us that the fulfillment of our religious and social obligations does not end with ritual worship; true piety demands active engagement with the suffering of others. The mention of both the one who asks and the one who is too dignified to ask challenges us to look beyond the visible poor and extend our compassion and generosity to those whose need is hidden by their silence and pride.

translation: And those who believe in the Day of Judgment.
interpretation: This verse highlights that true faith is not merely an abstract belief but a transformative conviction that shapes one's entire conduct in life. To sincerely believe in the Day of Judgment means that one lives with a constant awareness of divine accountability, recognizing that every action, word, and intention carries eternal consequence. This belief instills in the believer a profound sense of moral responsibility and humility, anchoring their choices not in worldly gain or social approval, but in the pursuit of that which will stand before God on the ultimate Day of reckoning.

translation: And those who are fearful of the punishment of their Lord
interpretation: This verse highlights that true believers maintain a constant state of reverent fear and vigilance regarding divine accountability. Even those who are righteous and devoted in their worship do not become complacent or self-assured in their piety. This holy apprehension keeps the believer spiritually alert, preventing arrogance and self-righteousness, and serves as an ongoing motivation to remain steadfast on the path of righteousness. It is not a paralyzing fear, but rather a healthy, reverent awareness that purifies the soul and draws one closer to God.

translation: Indeed, the punishment of their Lord is not something to feel secure from.
interpretation: This verse serves as a profound reminder of the ever-present reality of divine accountability. It calls upon the human soul to maintain a state of spiritual vigilance and humility, warning against the dangerous trap of complacency in one's relationship with God. No matter how righteous one may believe oneself to be, a sense of absolute certainty about one's safety from divine consequence leads to arrogance and heedlessness. True faith is balanced between hope in God's mercy and a healthy fear of His justice, and it is this balance that keeps the believer grounded, morally conscious, and continuously striving toward righteousness.

translation: And those who guard their private parts
interpretation: This verse speaks to the virtue of chastity and self-restraint as a mark of true faith. It calls believers to exercise disciplined control over their sexual desires, recognizing that the body is a trust from God and that yielding to unlawful desires weakens the soul's connection to the Divine. True spiritual elevation requires not only ritual worship but also the mastery of one's lower impulses, making chastity an essential pillar of moral integrity and nearness to God.

translation: Except with their spouses or those their right hands possess, for then they are not blameworthy.
interpretation: This verse establishes that the guarding of one's private parts — a virtue praised in the preceding verses — is not an absolute prohibition on intimacy, but rather a channeling of human desire into lawful and sanctioned relationships. The exception is not a license for unchecked passion, but a divine recognition that human nature carries legitimate needs, and that Islam addresses these needs within a framework of responsibility, covenant, and dignity. The mention of 'blamelessness' subtly implies that outside these boundaries, blame and moral accountability do apply, reinforcing that sexuality in Islam is never morally neutral but is always situated within an ethical order.

translation: But whoever seeks beyond that, those are the transgressors.
interpretation: This verse draws a firm moral boundary around human desire and conduct, warning that any who seek to fulfill their desires beyond the lawful limits set by God have overstepped the bounds of what is righteous. It is a reminder that self-restraint within divine boundaries is not a restriction but rather a definition of what it means to be a truly upright and God-conscious human being. Transgression here is not merely a legal infraction but a spiritual deviation — a crossing of the line between the sacred order God has established and the chaos that results when human passion goes unchecked.

translation: And those who are guardians of their trusts and their covenants.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the moral obligation of faithfulness in all dimensions of human life. The believer is called not merely to honor explicit contracts and agreements, but to cultivate an inner disposition of trustworthiness that governs every relationship — with God, with fellow human beings, and even with oneself. The soul that truly submits to God becomes, by its very nature, a vessel of integrity, recognizing that every trust placed in it is ultimately a sacred responsibility before the Divine.

translation: And those who uphold their testimonies
interpretation: This verse calls believers to a standard of moral integrity and accountability in their interactions with others. Standing firm in one's testimony is not merely a legal obligation, but a reflection of one's inner truthfulness and commitment to justice. It implies that a true believer does not distort, conceal, or abandon what they know to be true out of fear, personal interest, or social pressure. Upholding testimony becomes an act of worship in itself, as honesty before people mirrors one's honesty before God.

translation: And those who carefully maintain their prayers.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that true believers do not merely perform prayer as a ritual obligation, but actively guard and preserve it with consistency, mindfulness, and devotion. It calls the believer to treat prayer not as a burden to be discharged, but as a sacred trust to be protected — ensuring it is performed at its proper times, with full presence of heart, and with the reverence it deserves. The use of the word 'maintain' or 'guard' suggests an ongoing, vigilant effort, implying that prayer is something that can be lost or diminished if one is not careful, and that the mark of the truly faithful is their unwavering commitment to preserving this connection with God throughout their lives.

translation: Those will be in gardens, honored.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the profound dignity that awaits the righteous in the afterlife. True honor does not lie in worldly status, wealth, or power, but rather in one's relationship with God and adherence to His guidance. The honor bestowed in the gardens of Paradise is the ultimate validation of a life lived in faith and righteousness, suggesting that the soul's deepest longing is not merely for comfort or pleasure, but for divine recognition and esteem. It reminds the believer that every act of worship and sacrifice in this world is seen and will be met with a dignity that surpasses anything the material world can offer.

translation: So what is the matter with those who disbelieve, rushing toward you
interpretation: This verse challenges the arrogance and mockery of the disbelievers who would gather around the Prophet in haste, not out of sincere seeking of truth, but out of ridicule and opposition. The rhetorical question 'what is the matter with them?' exposes the absurdity of their behavior — that they would rush toward the light of divine guidance only to reject it, reflecting a profound spiritual blindness where proximity to truth ironically deepens their heedlessness rather than awakening them to it.

translation: From the right and from the left, in groups.
interpretation: This verse calls attention to the way people gather around the Prophet in scattered, curious clusters rather than as sincere, unified believers. The imagery of people crowding from both sides in separate groups reflects a fragmented, superficial engagement with the truth — drawn by spectacle or social pressure rather than genuine faith. It serves as a subtle rebuke of those whose outward proximity to revelation does not translate into inner commitment or spiritual cohesion.

translation: Does every one of them hope to enter a garden of bliss?
interpretation: This verse challenges the arrogance of those who reject faith yet still expect divine reward. It serves as a rebuke to those who live in heedlessness and denial while harboring an unfounded sense of entitlement to God's mercy and paradise. True hope for paradise must be grounded in sincere belief, righteous deeds, and accountability — not in wishful thinking or self-delusion. The verse invites deep self-reflection, urging every person to examine whether their actions are truly aligned with the expectations they hold of God's reward.

translation: No! Indeed, We created them from that which they know.
interpretation: This verse serves as a divine rebuke to those who deny resurrection or mock the power of God. The reminder that humans were created from a humble, well-known substance — namely a drop of seminal fluid — is meant to silence arrogance and disbelief. If God was capable of bringing forth a complex human being from something so insignificant, then surely He is fully capable of recreating and resurrecting that same being after death. The verse challenges human pride by pointing back to the very origins of existence, urging reflection on the miracle of creation itself as proof of God's unlimited power over life and death.

translation: So I swear by the Lord of the Easts and the Wests, indeed We are capable.
interpretation: This verse calls upon the magnificent power of God as demonstrated through His mastery over the rising and setting of the sun across countless points on the horizon throughout the seasons. The oath is not merely astronomical; it is a profound affirmation that the same Divine power governing the vast cosmic order of the universe is equally capable of resurrection and the seemingly impossible. The verse thus challenges human skepticism about the afterlife by redirecting attention to the undeniable and observable grandeur of creation, implying that He who controls the movements of celestial bodies with such precision is certainly capable of recreating human beings after death.

translation: To replace them with better than them, and We are not to be outdone.
interpretation: This verse asserts the absolute and unchallenged sovereignty of Allah over creation. It serves as a reminder to humanity that no one can outpace or outmaneuver the divine will. When Allah decrees the replacement or transformation of a people or a situation, no force in existence can prevent or delay it. The verse instills both awe and humility, reminding human beings that their existence, their continuation, and their standing are entirely contingent upon Allah's will, and that He is fully capable of bringing forth something better whenever He chooses, without any limitation or obstacle.

translation: So leave them to plunge into vain discourse and play until they meet their Day which they are promised.
interpretation: This verse conveys a sense of divine forbearance and ultimate justice. God instructs the Prophet not to exhaust himself in grief over those who persistently reject the truth. Their indulgence in idle amusement and trivial disputes is not a sign of their escape from accountability, but rather a rope they are given before the inevitable arrives. The verse reminds us that heedlessness in this life is itself a form of punishment, as those who choose play over purpose are spiritually lost even before the final reckoning. It is a call for the believer to remain focused and steadfast, undistracted by the mockery of those who refuse to reflect, trusting that divine justice will unfold at its appointed time.

translation: The Day they will come forth from the graves rapidly, as if they were rushing toward an erected goal (or idol).
interpretation: This verse draws a striking comparison between the urgency of the resurrection and the frantic eagerness of those who once rushed toward idols and objects of false worship. The simile serves as a profound irony: the same heedless speed with which the heedless devoted themselves to worldly vanities and false gods will characterize their inevitable emergence from the graves on the Day of Judgment. It reminds us that the energy and devotion we invest in this life will ultimately be redirected toward our standing before the Divine, suggesting that the direction of one's rush in this world reflects the orientation of one's soul, and that no soul can escape the swiftness of that final summoning.

translation: Their eyes humbled, overwhelmed by humiliation. That is the Day which they were promised.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the ultimate accountability that awaits those who denied the truth. The imagery of downcast eyes and enveloping humiliation serves as a powerful reminder that arrogance and denial in this worldly life will be met with profound abasement in the Hereafter. The Day they were repeatedly warned about but chose to dismiss or mock will arrive with absolute certainty, and no soul will be able to escape its reckoning. The verse is a stark warning that the promises of Allah are not empty, and that those who lived in heedlessness and pride will find themselves utterly stripped of any pretense of dignity when they stand before their Creator.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Indeed, We sent Noah to his people, [saying], 'Warn your people before there comes to them a painful punishment.'
interpretation: This verse establishes the divine pattern of mercy that precedes judgment: God never punishes a people without first sending them a warner. The very act of sending Noah reflects God's compassion, as He gives humanity an opportunity to turn back before consequences become inevitable. The urgency embedded in the command — to warn *before* the punishment arrives — reveals that divine retribution is not arbitrary or sudden, but is always preceded by a period of grace, guidance, and choice. This serves as a reminder that accountability is rooted in fairness, and that human beings are never left without guidance.

translation: He said, 'O my people, I am a clear warner to you.'
interpretation: This verse highlights the profound responsibility of the prophetic mission — that a messenger's primary duty is not to compel or force belief, but to deliver a transparent and unmistakable warning. The use of the word 'mubeen' (clear) suggests that the truth being conveyed leaves no room for ambiguity, meaning that those who reject it do so not out of ignorance but out of willful choice, thereby bearing full moral responsibility for their decision.

translation: That you worship Allah, fear Him, and obey me.
interpretation: This verse reflects the fundamental covenant between the Divine and humanity — that true worship is not merely ritualistic devotion, but a comprehensive orientation of the soul toward God through reverence and conscious awareness of His presence. The call to obey the messenger alongside worshipping and fearing God illustrates that divine guidance cannot be received in abstraction; it must be embodied through a living example. The sequence is deliberate: worship establishes the relationship, fear (taqwa) refines and purifies the heart, and obedience translates both into righteous action in the world.

translation: He will forgive you your sins and reprieve you until an appointed term. Indeed, when the term of Allah comes, it cannot be delayed, if only you knew.
interpretation: This verse carries a profound urgency rooted in the reality of divine mercy paired with the finality of death. The forgiveness offered is not unconditional in its timing — it is tied to the window of life that remains. The phrase 'if only you knew' is a gentle but piercing rebuke of human complacency, suggesting that people act as though they have unlimited time to repent and reform. The appointed term — death — waits for no one, and once it arrives, the door of repentance is sealed. The verse thus invites us to recognize that the mercy of God is vast and available now, but the window through which it can be received is limited by the inescapable appointment with death. The true wisdom being called for is not merely intellectual knowledge of this fact, but a lived awareness that transforms one's daily choices and priorities.

translation: He said, 'My Lord, indeed I have called my people night and day.'
interpretation: This verse captures the essence of prophetic perseverance and devotion to one's mission. Noah's declaration to his Lord reflects not merely a report of his actions, but a profound acknowledgment that his relentless effort, spanning both the darkness of night and the light of day without rest, was ultimately in service of God alone. The verse teaches that true dedication to a noble cause requires exhausting every opportunity and moment available, and that when human effort reaches its limits, one turns to God not in defeat, but in complete trust, surrendering the outcome to the One who holds all results in His hands.

translation: But my calling them has increased them not except in flight.
interpretation: This verse, spoken in the voice of Prophet Nuh (Noah), reveals a profound spiritual truth: that divine invitation, when met with a hardened heart, can paradoxically deepen one's resistance. The act of turning away from truth is not a neutral choice but an active flight — a willful running — suggesting that those who reject the call do so not out of ignorance, but out of a deep-seated aversion to accountability and transformation. The more the truth is presented, the more it exposes what lies within the soul, and those unwilling to confront themselves will flee further into denial.

translation: And indeed, every time I called them so that You might forgive them, they put their fingers in their ears, covered themselves with their garments, persisted, and were arrogant with great arrogance.
interpretation: This verse reveals the profound tragedy of willful spiritual blindness — that the greatest barrier to divine mercy is not ignorance, but deliberate rejection. The people did not simply fail to hear the truth; they actively blocked it out, using their fingers and garments as shields against guidance.
