It serves as a powerful warning to reflect on one's deeds before facing a reality whose scale is beyond human imagination.

translation: As if they were yellow camels/ropes.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah Al-Mursalat (77:33), uses the vivid imagery of yellow or tawny camels to describe the sparks thrown off by the fire of Hell. The comparison serves to emphasize the overwhelming and terrifying scale of Hell's flames — its sparks are not small embers but massive, surging entities, like a herd of enormous camels stampeding through the sky. This imagery is meant to shake the human soul out of complacency, urging reflection on the consequences of denying God's truth and rejecting accountability in the Hereafter.

translation: Woe on that Day to the deniers!
interpretation: This powerful divine warning serves as a recurring refrain of accountability, reminding humanity that denial of truth is not a neutral act but a moral choice with profound consequences. The repetition of this phrase throughout Surah Al-Mursalat is itself a rhetorical device meant to awaken the conscience, suggesting that each moment of denial compounds one's spiritual recklessness, and that the Day of Judgment will be a moment of unavoidable confrontation between one's choices and divine justice.

translation: This is a Day when they will not speak.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the absolute silence and helplessness of the disbelievers on the Day of Judgment. Unlike in this world, where people can argue, justify, and defend themselves with words, on that Day all excuses will be stripped away. The silence is not merely physical but represents a profound state of utter powerlessness — a recognition that no words can alter what has already been decreed. It serves as a stark reminder that the time for speech and repentance is now, in this life, before the arrival of a Day when no voice can intercede without Divine permission.

translation: And they will not be permitted to make excuses.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the absolute and irreversible nature of divine judgment on the Day of Resurrection. Unlike in this worldly life, where people can offer justifications, rationalizations, or pleas for forgiveness, the wrongdoers in the Hereafter will not even be granted the opportunity to present their excuses. This signifies that all chances for repentance and explanation have already passed, having been available throughout one's earthly life. It serves as a powerful reminder that the time to seek forgiveness and make amends is now, in this world, before the door of excuse and repentance is permanently closed.

translation: Woe on that Day to the deniers!
interpretation: This verse serves as a divine warning and a repeated refrain of accountability. The phrase 'woe on that Day' is not merely a statement of punishment, but a profound call to reflection in the present moment. God is drawing attention to the inevitable reality of Judgment, urging human beings to reconsider their denial before it is too late. The repetition of this verse throughout Surah Al-Mursalat functions as a rhetorical device to awaken the conscience, reminding us that denial of truth — whether of God's signs, His messengers, or the Day of Reckoning — carries ultimate consequences. It is an invitation disguised as a warning, urging the human soul to turn back toward truth while there is still time.

translation: This is the Day of Separation; We have gathered you and the former peoples.
interpretation: This verse underscores the ultimate accountability that awaits all of humanity across time. The term 'Day of Separation' (Yawm al-Fasl) suggests that this is the moment when all ambiguity is resolved, all truth is distinguished from falsehood, and every soul receives its just recompense. By emphasizing that both the current and all former generations are gathered together, the verse reminds us that no one escapes this reckoning regardless of when they lived, reinforcing that divine justice is universal, timeless, and all-encompassing. It serves as a powerful warning to reflect on one's deeds in this life, knowing that the Day of Separation will bring an unavoidable and perfectly just judgment.

translation: So if you have a plan, then plan against Me.
interpretation: This verse is a direct divine challenge to those who deny or oppose God, emphasizing His absolute and unchallengeable sovereignty. It is an expression of God's infinite power and supremacy, highlighting the utter futility and impotence of any human or created being who might attempt to resist or outwit the Divine Will. The rhetorical boldness of this challenge is meant to awaken the human soul to the reality of its own powerlessness before its Creator, inviting deep humility and sincere submission.

translation: Woe on that Day to the deniers!
interpretation: This powerful refrain serves as a divine warning that reverberates throughout Surah Al-Mursalat, emphasizing that the consequence of persistently rejecting truth is not merely intellectual error but a profound moral failure that carries ultimate accountability. The repetition of this phrase is itself a rhetorical act of mercy, giving the denier multiple opportunities to reflect before the Day arrives when reflection will no longer avail.

translation: Indeed, the righteous will be among shades and springs.
interpretation: This verse invites us to reflect on the profound spiritual reward that awaits those who live a life of God-consciousness and piety. The imagery of shade and flowing springs speaks to a deeper truth: that the one who disciplines their soul in this world, enduring its heat and hardships through devotion and righteousness, will find ultimate rest and refreshment in the next. Just as shade offers relief from the scorching sun and springs quench the deepest thirst, the Divine promises that no act of sincere piety goes unrewarded. The verse is an encouragement to persevere in taqwa — mindful awareness of God — by reminding us that the apparent sacrifices of this life are nothing compared to the eternal comfort and beauty that God has prepared for those who remain faithful.

translation: And fruits of whatever they desire.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the boundless generosity of Allah in Paradise, where the believers will not merely be given what is available, but precisely what their hearts long for. It reflects the idea that divine reward is perfectly attuned to the individual soul — a fulfillment so complete that even the subtlest desires are met without the need to ask. This is a reminder that true contentment, which eludes us in this world, will be perfectly realized in the next.

translation: Eat and drink with ease, for what you used to do.
interpretation: This verse serves as a divine proclamation of reward, reminding believers that the pleasures of Paradise are not arbitrary gifts but the direct fruit of their earthly striving. It encourages us to understand that our deeds in this world are seeds planted for the next, and that God's justice is not merely punitive but deeply merciful and affirming — every act of faith, patience, and righteousness will be fully recognized and celebrated in the most tangible and joyful of ways.

translation: Indeed, thus do We reward the doers of good.
interpretation: This verse serves as a divine reassurance that righteousness never goes unnoticed or unrewarded. It reflects the profound justice and mercy of Allah, affirming that every act of goodness, no matter how small, is meticulously observed and will be met with a worthy recompense. It invites the believer to remain steadfast in virtue, not out of fear of punishment, but out of the hopeful certainty that Allah's generosity toward those who strive to do good is an unwavering and eternal promise.

translation: Woe on that Day to the deniers!
interpretation: This powerful divine warning serves as a recurring refrain throughout Surah Al-Mursalat, functioning as a hammer of emphasis upon the conscience. The repetition of this phrase is itself a rhetorical act of mercy — God does not condemn without first warning repeatedly, giving humanity every opportunity to reflect and turn back. The 'woe' here is not merely a statement of future punishment, but a present moral alarm, urging the listener to reconsider their stance of denial before the Day arrives when reconsideration will no longer be possible.

translation: Eat and enjoy yourselves for a little while; indeed, you are criminals.
interpretation: This verse serves as a divine admonition that worldly pleasures and indulgences are fleeting and temporary. It is a stern reminder that those who persist in sin and transgression may revel in the comforts of this life, but such enjoyment is inconsequential and short-lived in the grand scope of eternity. The verse warns that no amount of worldly gratification can shield the wrongdoer from divine accountability. It underscores the Islamic principle that this life is merely a transient passage, and those who squander it in heedless pleasure and criminality will ultimately face the consequences of their deeds in the Hereafter.

translation: Woe on that Day to the deniers!
interpretation: This verse serves as a powerful divine warning, emphasizing that those who reject the truth — whether it be the signs of God, the message of the Prophet, or the reality of the Day of Judgment — will face severe consequences. The repetition of this phrase throughout Surah Al-Mursalat functions as a rhetorical hammer, meant to awaken the heedless soul and shake it out of its complacency. It reminds us that denial is not a passive act but a willful turning away from evident truth, and that such a choice carries ultimate accountability before God.

translation: And when it is said to them, 'Bow down,' they do not bow down.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the profound nature of arrogance and its spiritual consequences. The act of bowing (rukoo') is not merely a physical gesture but a symbol of complete submission and humility before Allah. When the disbelievers refuse to bow, they are not simply rejecting a ritual act — they are revealing the deep-seated pride within their hearts that prevents them from surrendering their ego to the Divine. True faith requires the breaking of one's arrogance, and this refusal to bow illustrates that the greatest barrier between a human being and God is not intellectual doubt, but the unwillingness of the self to humble itself before its Creator.

translation: Woe on that Day to the deniers!
interpretation: This verse serves as a divine warning and expression of grief for those who persistently reject the truth. The word 'woe' (ويل) carries a profound sense of destruction and sorrow, and its repetition throughout Surah Al-Mursalat functions as a rhetorical hammer, driving home the gravity of disbelief. The verse reminds us that denial is not merely an intellectual position but a moral failure with ultimate consequences. It challenges us to reflect on our own relationship with truth, urging sincere self-examination before the arrival of a Day when denial will no longer be possible.

translation: Then in what statement after it will they believe?
interpretation: This verse serves as a profound rhetorical challenge, suggesting that if the Qur'an — with all its clarity, wisdom, and divine eloquence — fails to move a person to faith, then no other speech or message, however compelling, could ever reach their heart. It points to a spiritual hardness that no external word can penetrate, implying that the barrier to belief lies not in the absence of evidence, but in the willful closure of the heart itself.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. About what are they asking one another?
interpretation: This opening verse of Surah An-Naba serves as a rhetorical device to capture the listener's attention and provoke deep reflection. The question is not asked out of ignorance, for God knows all things, but rather it is directed at the disbelievers of Mecca who disputed and debated among themselves about the Day of Resurrection. By posing this question, God draws our focus to the gravity and certainty of what is being denied, implying that the matter they so casually question is of the utmost seriousness and consequence. It is a divine challenge that invites humanity to pause, reflect, and reconsider their skepticism about ultimate accountability.

translation: About the great news
interpretation: This verse refers to the Day of Resurrection and the Quran itself as the 'great news' — a momentous reality that humanity is deeply divided over, yet cannot escape. It serves as a dramatic opening that commands attention and signals that what follows is of ultimate cosmic significance, urging the listener to reflect seriously on what they have been heedlessly disputing.

translation: That about which they differ.
interpretation: This verse points to the nature of divine revelation as the ultimate arbiter of human disputes. It suggests that the Qur'an or the truth of the Day of Judgment serves as the definitive resolution to the deep ideological, theological, and moral disagreements that divide humanity. Human beings, left to their own devices, will endlessly dispute matters of faith, existence, and morality, and only through divine guidance can such fundamental divisions be truly resolved.

translation: No! They will come to know.
interpretation: This verse serves as a divine warning, asserting that those who are heedless, arrogant, or in denial of truth will ultimately face the consequences of their actions and disbelief. It is a reminder that human ignorance and defiance are temporary, and that the reality of divine judgment will become undeniably clear to everyone, whether in this life or the next. The brevity and sharpness of the verse itself mirrors the certainty and swiftness of that inevitable reckoning.

translation: Then, no! They will come to know.
interpretation: This verse serves as a divine warning emphasizing the certainty of accountability. The repetition of 'no' intensifies the seriousness of the admonition, suggesting that human heedlessness and denial of truth are grave mistakes. Allah is asserting that those who are negligent or who deny the reality of their purpose and ultimate return to Him will inevitably come to a full and undeniable realization of the truth — but this realization will come too late, on the Day of Judgment, when knowledge will no longer benefit those who ignored the warnings given to them in this life.

translation: Have We not made the earth a resting place?
interpretation: This verse invites human beings to reflect on the profound gift of the earth as a stable, nurturing cradle for life. It is a rhetorical question that draws attention to the divine wisdom embedded in the very foundation of our existence — that the earth was not created arbitrarily, but was deliberately fashioned as a place of comfort, sustenance, and security for humanity. The verse calls us to gratitude and awareness, reminding us that what we often take for granted — the ground beneath our feet — is itself a sign of God's mercy and intentional care for His creation.

translation: And the mountains as pegs
interpretation: This verse invites us to reflect on the divine wisdom embedded in the natural world. Just as tent pegs anchor a structure to the earth, mountains serve as stabilizers for the Earth's crust, preventing it from shifting and trembling beneath us. The verse thus points to the profound care and intentionality of the Creator in designing a world that is habitable and stable for humanity, urging us to recognize that what we may take for granted in our physical surroundings is in fact a deliberate act of divine mercy and provision.

translation: And We created you in pairs.
interpretation: This verse invites deep reflection on the divine wisdom embedded in the nature of creation. Beyond the literal pairing of male and female, it points to the fundamental principle of duality and complementarity that underlies all of existence. Everything in creation is designed to find wholeness through its counterpart, suggesting that incompleteness is not a flaw but a divine invitation toward union, harmony, and mutual dependence. Human beings are thus reminded that their nature is inherently relational, and that seeking connection is not merely a social impulse but a reflection of how God has fashioned the very fabric of creation.

translation: And We made your sleep a rest.
interpretation: This verse invites us to reflect on the profound mercy of Allah in designing sleep as a biological and spiritual mercy for humanity. Sleep is not merely a physical necessity, but a divine gift that restores the soul, quiets the mind, and reminds us of our dependence on Allah. Just as we surrender consciousness each night, we are reminded of our ultimate surrender to our Creator, and that all renewal and restoration comes from Him alone.

translation: And We made the night a garment.
interpretation: The verse invites us to reflect on the profound mercy embedded in the natural order. Just as a garment wraps and conceals the body, the night envelops the world in darkness, offering rest, concealment, and relief from the toils of the day. This is not merely a physical phenomenon, but a divine gift — a reminder that Allah has thoughtfully designed the rhythms of existence to nurture and protect the human soul, and that in every natural cycle there is evidence of His boundless care and wisdom.

translation: And We made the day for livelihood.
interpretation: This verse points to the divine wisdom embedded in the natural order: the light of day is not merely a physical phenomenon, but a purposeful gift from God enabling human beings to pursue their sustenance and fulfill their responsibilities in the world. It invites reflection on how even the most ordinary aspects of existence — the rising of the sun, the brightness of day — are deliberate acts of divine mercy and provision, reminding us that our ability to work and provide for ourselves is ultimately dependent on God's grace rather than our own efforts alone.

translation: And We built above you seven strong [heavens].
interpretation: This verse invites humanity to reflect on the magnificent power and creative mastery of Allah, who has constructed the heavens as a firm, structured, and enduring canopy over all of creation. The emphasis on the strength and solidity of these heavens serves as a reminder that the universe is not a product of chance, but rather a deliberate and meticulously designed edifice, sustained by divine will. It calls the human being to humility, recognizing that above them exists a reality far greater and more enduring than anything they can construct or comprehend.

translation: And We made a blazing lamp.
interpretation: This verse draws attention to the divine act of creating the sun as a brilliant, intensely burning source of light and heat. The use of the word 'wahhāj' — meaning blazing or intensely luminous — invites reflection on the awe-inspiring power of God, who fashioned such a magnificent celestial body to illuminate and sustain life on earth. It is a reminder that what humanity may take for granted — daylight, warmth, the rhythm of days — is in fact a deliberate and magnificent gift from the Creator, meant to inspire gratitude and acknowledgment of His omnipotence.

translation: And We sent down from the rain-laden clouds pouring water
interpretation: This verse draws our attention to the divine orchestration behind the natural phenomenon of rainfall. Allah reminds us that nothing in nature is accidental or self-sustaining — even the most ordinary and taken-for-granted blessing, such as rain, is an act of divine will and mercy. By emphasizing that it is He who 'sends down' the water, the verse invites us to move beyond a purely materialistic understanding of nature and recognize the hand of God in every drop of rain that falls. It is a call to gratitude and mindfulness, urging us to see the universe not as an autonomous system, but as a continuous manifestation of divine generosity and power.

translation: That We may bring forth thereby grain and vegetation
interpretation: This verse invites reflection on the divine generosity embedded in the natural world. The sending down of rain is not a random act of nature, but a deliberate and purposeful mercy from Allah, designed to sustain life. The verse calls us to recognize that every grain of food we eat and every plant that grows is a direct result of divine provision. It is a reminder that our sustenance is not ultimately in our own hands, but in the hands of Allah, and that gratitude and humility are the appropriate responses to this constant, life-giving blessing.

translation: And dense gardens
interpretation: This brief yet vivid phrase evokes the lush abundance of Paradise, suggesting that true fulfillment and reward lie not in the fleeting pleasures of worldly life, but in the intertwined and overflowing blessings that await the righteous — a fullness so complete that even the gardens themselves are densely interwoven, leaving no emptiness or lack.

translation: Indeed, the Day of Separation is an appointed time.
interpretation: This verse serves as a solemn reminder that the Day of Judgment is not a distant abstraction or mere theological concept, but a precisely appointed moment in the divine plan that is absolutely certain to arrive. Just as every worldly appointment carries weight and demands preparation, this ultimate appointment demands that humanity take its moral and spiritual preparation seriously, for on that day all distinctions between truth and falsehood, righteousness and wickedness, will be decisively and permanently separated.

translation: The Day when the Trumpet is blown, and you will come forth in multitudes.
interpretation: This verse draws our attention to the overwhelming and inevitable nature of the Day of Resurrection, reminding us that no soul can escape or delay its coming. The image of people arriving in crowds or waves suggests that despite the vastness of humanity across all of time, every single person will be gathered and held accountable. It is a call to reflect on our collective responsibility before God, urging us not to be deceived by the comfort of numbers or social belonging, for on that Day, each soul will ultimately stand alone before its Creator.

translation: And the sky is opened and becomes gateways.
interpretation: This verse evokes the complete dissolution of the cosmic order on the Day of Judgment, suggesting that even the heavens — which humanity has long regarded as a fixed, impenetrable barrier — will yield and open wide. The imagery of gateways implies not merely destruction, but a purposeful opening: the boundary between the seen and unseen worlds collapses entirely, and what was once hidden from human perception becomes fully manifest. It is a reminder that all of creation is subject to Allah's will, and that the apparent permanence of the physical universe is ultimately an illusion sustained only by divine permission.

translation: And the mountains will be set in motion and will become a mirage.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the complete dissolution of the physical world as we know it on the Day of Judgment. The mountains, which represent the most solid, permanent, and immovable things in human experience, will be reduced to illusions — things that appear to exist but have no substance. This is a powerful reminder that nothing in the material world is truly permanent or reliable, and that our attachment to earthly certainties is ultimately misplaced. Only God and the eternal realm endure, while everything we consider fixed and unshakeable will vanish like a desert mirage.

translation: Indeed, Hell has been lying in wait.
interpretation: This verse serves as a profound warning that divine justice is ever-vigilant and inescapable. The use of the word 'mursaad' — meaning a place of ambush or watchful waiting — suggests that Hell is not merely a destination but an active, observant force that stands ready for those who transgress. It conveys that no soul can slip past the awareness of God's justice, and that the consequences of one's deeds are not arbitrary or delayed by chance, but are waiting with certainty and precision for those who have earned them.

translation: For the transgressors, a place of return.
interpretation: This verse serves as a stark warning that those who exceed all bounds in their arrogance, oppression, and rebellion against God will inevitably face a predetermined destination of punishment. It reminds us that no matter how powerful or unchecked a tyrant may appear in this world, their ultimate return is not to freedom or triumph, but to divine accountability and retribution. The use of 'place of return' implies that this fate is inescapable and certain, as all journeys must come to an end.

translation: Remaining therein for ages (ahqab).
interpretation: This verse speaks to the concept of extended, immeasurable punishment for those who have gone astray. The use of the word 'ahqab' (ages or long stretches of time) suggests a duration so vast it defies human comprehension, emphasizing the gravity and weight of turning away from the truth. It serves as a profound warning to humanity that accountability is real and enduring, urging believers to reflect on their choices and realign themselves with righteousness before such a reckoning arrives.

translation: They will not taste therein any coolness nor any drink.
interpretation: This verse depicts the absolute deprivation experienced by the condemned in Hell. The denial of both 'coolness' and 'drink' is deeply significant in the Arabian context, where relief from scorching heat through shade and water represented the highest forms of comfort. The verse suggests that divine justice operates through the principle of cosmic inversion — those who refused to seek spiritual refreshment through faith and righteous deeds in this life will find themselves permanently denied any form of relief or comfort in the next. The soul that rejected the 'coolness' of divine guidance will find no substitute for it in the Hereafter.

translation: Except boiling water and purulent fluid,
interpretation: This verse serves as a stark reminder that those who reject divine guidance and persist in wrongdoing will find no true sustenance or comfort in the Hereafter. The contrast between the nourishment and refreshment that believers enjoy in Paradise and the scalding water and festering discharge given to the disbelievers illustrates that the soul which turns away from truth ultimately feeds on the fruits of its own corruption. What one nurtures in this life — whether righteousness or transgression — becomes the very substance of one's experience in the next.

translation: A fitting recompense.
interpretation: This phrase reminds us that divine justice is perfectly calibrated — neither excessive nor deficient. It invites deep reflection on the moral weight of our actions, urging us to recognize that every choice we make carries a consequence that mirrors it exactly. It is a call to accountability and mindfulness, reminding the human being that the universe operates under a precise and just order established by God, and that nothing done in this life is ever truly lost or overlooked.

translation: Indeed, they did not expect any reckoning.
interpretation: This verse points to the root cause of moral and spiritual failure: the absence of accountability consciousness. When a soul ceases to believe that its actions will be weighed and judged, it loses the most fundamental restraint against wrongdoing. The expectation of a reckoning is not merely a theological concept but a transformative force that shapes every choice and intention. To live without this expectation is to live in a kind of spiritual blindness, where the consequences of one's deeds in the ultimate sense are ignored, leading inevitably to heedlessness and transgression.

translation: And they denied Our signs with utter denial.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the deliberate and emphatic nature of rejection by those who refuse to acknowledge divine truth. The use of the intensified verbal noun 'kidhdhāban' signals that their denial was not born of ignorance or confusion, but was a willful, persistent, and absolute turning away from God's signs. It serves as a warning that such conscious rejection of divine guidance carries profound moral consequences, as it represents a hardening of the heart against truth that is plainly manifest.

translation: And everything We have enumerated in a written record.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the absolute and all-encompassing knowledge of Allah, emphasizing that nothing in creation escapes His awareness. It serves as both a reminder and a warning to human beings that every deed, thought, and moment is recorded with perfect precision in the divine ledger. This should inspire a sense of accountability in the believer, motivating them to be ever-mindful of their actions, knowing that the record kept by Allah is complete and will be presented on the Day of Judgment with absolute accuracy.

translation: So taste [the punishment], for We will never increase you except in torment.
interpretation: This verse delivers a chilling and irrevocable divine decree directed at the disbelievers in the Hereafter. The use of the future tense with the emphatic negation 'lan' (never) signals the eternal and ever-escalating nature of punishment for those who rejected the truth. The verse teaches that divine justice is not merely retributive but proportional and continuous — the punishment grows in accordance with the magnitude of one's rejection and arrogance. It serves as a profound warning to the living that there is no relief, negotiation, or end to the consequences of willful disbelief, urging reflection and accountability before that final and irreversible moment arrives.

translation: Indeed, for the righteous there is a place of triumph/success.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the ultimate reward awaiting those who live with God-consciousness and moral integrity. The promise of 'mafaza' — a place of triumph and deliverance — is not merely a physical destination, but a testament to the divine justice that vindicates those who endured patience, resisted temptation, and remained steadfast in their devotion. It reminds the believer that worldly sacrifice and righteousness are never in vain, for the true measure of success is not found in this fleeting life, but in the eternal victory that God has reserved for those who feared and loved Him above all else.

translation: Gardens and vineyards
interpretation: This verse draws attention to the deliberate and purposeful nature of divine creation by highlighting the variety and abundance of what has been provided for humanity. The specific mention of gardens and vineyards serves as an invitation for reflection, urging human beings to recognize that the blessings surrounding them are not accidental, but are signs pointing to the existence and generosity of their Creator. By contemplating these gifts, one is led to gratitude and a deeper awareness of one's dependence on God.

translation: And full-breasted maidens of equal age
interpretation: This verse, found in Surah An-Naba (78:33), is part of a description of the rewards awaiting the righteous in Paradise. It serves as a representation of ultimate fulfillment and pleasure in the afterlife, using imagery that was deeply appealing to the 7th-century Arabian audience. The verse should be understood within the broader Quranic framework that Paradise is a state of complete joy and satisfaction, where every longing of the soul is met. Classical scholars often interpret such descriptions allegorically, suggesting that the physical imagery points to a deeper spiritual reality of perfect contentment and bliss that transcends human comprehension, as the true nature of Paradise is ultimately beyond what words can fully express.

translation: And a full, overflowing cup.
interpretation: This verse points to the spiritual reality that divine generosity is never measured or withheld — it flows abundantly and without restraint. The overflowing cup symbolizes that the rewards of the righteous in the hereafter are not merely sufficient, but exceed all expectation, reflecting the boundless nature of God's mercy and grace toward those who have strived faithfully in this life.

translation: They will not hear therein any ill speech or falsehood.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the perfection of Paradise as a place of absolute truth and dignity. It invites us to reflect on how much of our worldly suffering stems from the hurtful, false, or meaningless words of others. Paradise is not merely defined by its physical pleasures, but by the profound peace that comes from an environment entirely free of deception and vain discourse — suggesting that true spiritual rest is found not just in comfort, but in the complete absence of moral corruption in our surroundings.

translation: A reward from your Lord, a gift more than sufficient.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that the rewards granted to the believers in the afterlife are not merely what they have earned through their deeds, but rather a generous and abundant gift from Allah that far exceeds any measure of accounting. It reflects the boundless mercy and generosity of God, reminding believers that divine grace goes beyond strict justice, and that the ultimate recompense is an expression of Allah's infinite giving rather than a transaction based solely on human effort.

translation: The Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them, the Most Merciful — they possess no power of speech with Him.
interpretation: This verse establishes the absolute sovereignty and transcendence of God over all creation, while simultaneously emphasizing His attribute of mercy (Al-Rahman). The juxtaposition of His dominion over the heavens, earth, and all that exists between them with the inability of any being to address Him without His permission reveals a profound theological truth: true mercy does not imply familiarity or equal access. Rather, it is a mercy that flows entirely from His will and grace. No creature can approach God or intercede on their own initiative or authority — any communication with the Divine is entirely contingent upon His allowance. This instills in the believer both awe and humility, recognizing that even speech directed toward God is itself a gift granted by Him, not a right possessed by creation.

translation: The Day when the Spirit and the angels will stand in rows, they will not speak except for one whom the Most Merciful permits, and he will say what is correct.
interpretation: This verse impresses upon us the absolute and unchallenged sovereignty of God on the Day of Judgment. Even the mightiest of spiritual beings — the angels and the Spirit (understood to be the archangel Gabriel) — will stand in complete submission and silence, unable to utter a single word without divine permission. This teaches us that intercession on that Day is not a matter of entitlement or presumption, but entirely dependent on God's grace and will. It is a profound reminder that no one, regardless of their station, possesses independent authority before God, and that the only speech of value will be that which is both divinely authorized and rooted in truth.

translation: That is the Day of Truth. So whoever wills may take a path back to his Lord.
interpretation: This verse serves as a profound invitation to human free will and accountability. Allah affirms the certainty of the Day of Judgment as an absolute reality, and then — rather than issuing a command — opens the door of choice to humanity. The use of 'whoever wills' underscores that the return to God is not forced, but is a path consciously chosen through one's deeds and intentions in this life. Every righteous act, every prayer, every turning of the heart toward God is in essence a step along this path of return. The verse reminds us that we are already in the process of making our way back to our Lord, and that the choices we make now are shaping the nature of that return on the Day that is inevitable and true.

translation: Indeed, We have warned you of a punishment that is near - the Day when a man will observe what his hands have put forth, and the disbeliever will say, 'Oh, I wish that I were dust!'
interpretation: This verse confronts us with the terrifying clarity of the Day of Judgment, where every soul will be forced into a moment of absolute self-reckoning with no possibility of denial or deflection. The disbeliever's desperate wish to be dust is profoundly ironic - the very earth he walked upon, which he may have considered beneath him, becomes the object of his most fervent desire. This reflects the ultimate inversion of worldly pride and arrogance: the one who rejected God's truth would rather cease to exist entirely than face the consequences of his choices. The verse serves as a wake-up call to humanity while there is still time to act, reminding us that the deeds of our hands - both what we did and what we neglected to do - will stand as irrefutable witnesses against us, making the present moment the only true opportunity for redemption and righteous action.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. By those [angels] who extract with violence,
interpretation: This verse invites deep reflection on the certainty and inevitability of death. The oath sworn by the angels who forcefully extract souls serves as a powerful reminder that no soul can escape its appointed time. The intensity implied by the word 'gharqa' — meaning to extract deeply or violently — suggests that for those who clung to this world with arrogance and disbelief, the separation of the soul from the body will be a profound and overwhelming experience. It is a call to humanity to prepare for that inevitable moment by living righteously, so that the transition may be one of peace rather than anguish.

translation: And those who move swiftly, swimming swiftly
interpretation: This verse, part of Surah An-Nazi'at, is understood to refer to the angels who carry out divine commands with great speed and eagerness. The 'swiftness' described here points to the effortless and energetic manner in which angels execute Allah's will, suggesting that the divine order of the universe is maintained through beings of remarkable zeal and dedication. It invites reflection on the unseen forces that operate in perfect obedience to God, contrasting with human hesitance and negligence in fulfilling divine obligations.

translation: By those [stars or angels] that glide swiftly through space
interpretation: This verse is an oath sworn by that which moves through existence with effortless, fluid grace — whether angels descending through the heavens or celestial bodies swimming through their orbits. The imagery invites us to reflect on the perfection of divine order: nothing in creation moves haphazardly, but rather every entity glides along a path precisely ordained by Allah. The oath itself draws our attention to the miraculous nature of motion and purpose embedded within creation, reminding us that even in the unseen mechanics of the universe, there is a sublime, intentional harmony that points unmistakably to its Creator.

translation: And those who race forward, racing ahead
interpretation: This verse refers to the souls or angels that hasten with great speed and precision to carry out the divine will of God, illustrating that in the spiritual realm, there is an eager and swift movement toward righteousness and obedience. It serves as an encouragement for believers to similarly race toward good deeds and not delay in their pursuit of closeness to God.

translation: And those who arrange/manage affairs.
interpretation: This verse refers to the angels entrusted by Allah with the administration and execution of divine decrees throughout the universe. The oath sworn by these angels emphasizes that the affairs of creation — from the movement of celestial bodies to the sustenance of living beings — are not governed by chance or chaos, but are meticulously ordered and managed under divine will. It serves as a reminder that behind the apparent natural order lies a profound and purposeful spiritual governance, urging humans to reflect on the precision of creation and the sovereignty of Allah over all things.

translation: On the Day the Shaker shakes
interpretation: This verse invites deep reflection on the absolute certainty and overwhelming power of the Day of Resurrection. The use of the active participle 'al-raajifa' (the Shaker) rather than simply describing the shaking itself suggests that this cosmic trembling is an entity of immense, purposeful force — not a random geological event, but a divinely ordained upheaval that will dissolve the very foundations of the world as we know it. It serves as a wake-up call to humanity to recognize the fragility of the material world we cling to, urging us to anchor our hearts in what is eternal rather than what merely appears stable.

translation: Followed by the subsequent [blast].
interpretation: This verse, continuing from the preceding mention of the first trumpet blast, emphasizes the inexorable and sequential nature of divine decree on the Day of Judgment. The two blasts are not random or chaotic events, but a precisely ordered unfolding of God's will, reminding humanity that the end of the world is a structured and purposeful event fully under divine control, leaving no room for escape or delay.

translation: Hearts on that Day will be trembling
interpretation: This verse speaks to the profound existential reckoning that awaits every soul. The trembling of hearts on the Day of Judgment is not merely a physical sensation but a complete spiritual upheaval, as the certainty of divine accountability becomes undeniable. It reminds us that no matter how composed or confident a person may be in this worldly life, the ultimate truth of standing before God will strip away all pretense and arrogance, leaving the heart in a state of raw vulnerability. This serves as a call to cultivate humility and God-consciousness now, so that the heart may find some measure of peace on that otherwise terrifying Day.

translation: Their eyes cast down in humility
interpretation: This phrase speaks to the state of the soul when it stands before divine truth — that true humility is not merely an outward posture but a surrender of the inner gaze. The lowering of the eyes signifies the relinquishing of pride and self-assertion, acknowledging that in the presence of the Almighty, one's own vision and judgment are insufficient. It is a reminder that spiritual clarity begins not with looking outward, but with turning the gaze inward in submission and awe.

translation: They say, 'Are we really to be restored to our former state?'
interpretation: This verse captures the incredulity and mockery of the disbelievers toward the concept of resurrection. The use of the interrogative form reflects their dismissive attitude — they find it absurd that after death, human beings could be returned to a living state. The verse invites the reader to recognize the spiritual blindness that comes from measuring divine power by human limitations. Just as they could not conceive of creation from nothing, they reject the idea of recreation, failing to understand that the One who originated life is fully capable of restoring it. Their question, meant as a taunt, ironically affirms the very truth they seek to deny.

translation: When we are decayed bones?
interpretation: This verse captures the incredulous question of the disbelievers who mockingly deny the possibility of resurrection. It reflects the deeply rooted human tendency to measure possibility by material observation alone — seeing only dust and decay, and failing to perceive the infinite creative power of God who brought all things into existence from nothing in the first place. The verse challenges us to expand our conception of divine power beyond the limits of what our eyes can witness.

translation: They said, 'That would then be a losing return.'
interpretation: This verse captures the dismissive and cynical attitude of the disbelievers toward the concept of resurrection. Their use of the word 'losing' reveals that their rejection is not merely intellectual skepticism, but stems from a deeper unwillingness to accept accountability. They frame resurrection as a bad deal for themselves, unconsciously acknowledging that if it were true, they would indeed be on the losing side — thus exposing the reality that their denial is rooted in fear of judgment rather than a genuine search for truth.

translation: It will be only a single blast
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the absolute and effortless power of Allah over all of creation. The resurrection of all mankind, an event of incomprehensible magnitude, will require nothing more than a single command or cry. This serves as a reminder to humanity not to be deceived by the apparent permanence and solidity of this world, for its end and the transition to the next life will occur in an instant, by the will of Allah alone.

translation: And at once they will be on the surface of the earth.
interpretation: This verse captures the sudden, instantaneous nature of the resurrection. The use of 'إذا' (suddenly/at once) emphasizes that the transition from death to resurrection will happen in a single, overwhelming moment, with no gradual awakening. It serves as a powerful reminder that human beings have no control over this event, and that the promise of Allah regarding the Day of Judgment is absolute and inevitable. The 'al-sahira' (the open plain) signifies a new, leveled existence where all of humanity stands equal before their Creator, stripped of the worldly distinctions they once held.

translation: Has there come to you the story of Moses?
interpretation: This rhetorical question is not merely an inquiry about knowledge, but a divine invitation to attentiveness. God is drawing the listener — and through the Prophet, all of humanity — into a state of heightened awareness and receptivity, signaling that what follows carries profound spiritual weight. The phrasing implies that this is not ordinary news, but a sacred narrative worthy of deep reflection, urging us to approach the account of Moses with fresh ears and an open heart, as though hearing it for the very first time.

translation: When his Lord called him in the sacred valley of Tuwa
interpretation: This verse draws our attention to the intimate and direct nature of divine communication, reminding us that God's call to a human soul is not bound by ordinary circumstances of place or time. The specification of the sacred valley of Tuwa suggests that holiness is not an inherent property of geography, but rather a sanctity conferred upon a place by the divine presence itself. The deeper lesson is that when God chooses to speak to the human heart, the very ground upon which one stands becomes transformed into sacred space, urging us to remain perpetually attentive and receptive to the call of our Lord, wherever we may find ourselves.

translation: Go to Pharaoh, for he has transgressed.
interpretation: This divine command to Moses carries a profound spiritual lesson: no matter how powerful, arrogant, or tyrannical an oppressor may become, God does not abandon the oppressed. The verse reminds us that earthly power, no matter how absolute it may seem, is always subject to divine accountability. It also teaches that confronting injustice is not merely a human responsibility but a sacred duty — one that requires courage rooted in divine support rather than personal strength.

translation: And say, 'Would you [be willing to] purify yourself?'
interpretation: This verse reflects the gentle and inviting nature of the divine message. Rather than issuing a command or a threat, God instructs the Prophet to approach even the most hardened of hearts — in this context Pharaoh — with a question, an open invitation. This teaches us that true guidance must be offered with humility and respect for human free will. The path to purification is never forced; it is extended as an offer, reminding us that spiritual growth is ultimately a personal choice that no one can make for another. The verse also implies that purification — of the soul, of one's conduct, of one's relationship with God — is always possible, no matter how far one has strayed.

translation: And I will guide you to your Lord so that you may fear Him.
interpretation: This verse, spoken by Moses to Pharaoh, reveals that the ultimate purpose of prophethood and divine guidance is not merely intellectual knowledge of God, but the cultivation of a living, trembling awareness of His majesty. True guidance does not end at information — it ends at transformation of the heart into one that stands in awe before its Creator. The goal of all spiritual direction is khashya, a reverential fear born not of terror but of intimate recognition of God's greatness and one's own smallness before Him.

translation: So He showed him the greatest sign.
interpretation: This verse points to the profound moment when Allah revealed to Moses a miraculous demonstration of divine power, signifying that true authority belongs solely to God. The 'greatest sign' serves as a reminder that no matter how powerful earthly rulers like Pharaoh may appear, they are ultimately insignificant before the infinite power of the Creator. It is an invitation for all people to reflect on the undeniable evidence of God's existence and supremacy, and to submit willingly to His will rather than to the transient powers of the world.

translation: But he denied and disobeyed.
interpretation: This verse serves as a stark warning about the ultimate consequence of rejecting divine truth and defying God's commands. The pairing of denial and disobedience highlights that disbelief is not merely an intellectual position, but is always accompanied by a willful turning away from righteousness. The two acts are inseparable — when the heart rejects truth, the body follows in transgression. This verse invites reflection on the dangerous spiritual state of one who, despite being presented with clear signs and guidance, chooses arrogance over submission.

translation: Then he turned away, striving.
interpretation: This verse captures the arrogance and heedlessness of one who, after being presented with divine truth, deliberately chooses to walk away from it and actively pursue worldly concerns or opposition to it. The combination of turning one's back and hastening away suggests not merely passive rejection, but a willful and energetic flight from guidance — a profound spiritual blindness where a person's ambition and striving are directed entirely away from God rather than toward Him.

translation: So he gathered [his people] and called out
interpretation: This verse speaks to the nature of arrogant leadership, illustrating how those in power who reject divine truth resort to mobilizing their followers and raising their voices in defiance. The act of gathering and calling out represents the desperate attempt of a tyrant to consolidate influence and resist the call of God, demonstrating that worldly power and loud proclamation are ultimately futile against divine truth.

translation: And said, 'I am your highest lord.'
interpretation: This verse recounts the declaration of Pharaoh, who in his arrogance and tyranny proclaimed himself the supreme deity over his people. It serves as a profound warning against the sin of pride and the ultimate folly of humans who allow power to corrupt them into denying the sovereignty of God. The verse illustrates that the gravest form of oppression is spiritual — when a ruler not only subjugates the bodies of people but also attempts to enslave their souls by diverting their worship away from the Creator to himself. It is a timeless reminder that no matter how great a person's earthly power may seem, such blasphemous claims are the height of self-delusion and lead only to inevitable destruction.

translation: So Allah seized him with exemplary punishment in the Hereafter and the first [life].
interpretation: This verse serves as a profound warning that divine justice is all-encompassing and transcends the boundaries of time. The punishment of Pharaoh is presented not merely as a historical event, but as a timeless lesson — a demonstration that no amount of worldly power, arrogance, or denial of truth can shield a person from Allah's reckoning. The pairing of 'the Hereafter and the first life' suggests that true accountability is twofold: there are consequences that manifest in this world, and there are consequences that await beyond it. The verse invites the reader to reflect on the futility of rebellion against divine truth, and to recognize that the fate of those who persist in tyranny and disbelief is sealed across both dimensions of existence.

translation: Indeed in that is a lesson for whoever fears [Allah].
interpretation: This verse calls upon those who possess a God-conscious heart to look beyond the surface of events and perceive the deeper divine wisdom embedded within them. True reflection and the drawing of lessons from the signs of Allah is not accessible to everyone, but only to those whose hearts are softened by the fear and reverence of their Creator. It is this inner state of khashya — a profound, awe-filled awareness of Allah — that unlocks the capacity for genuine understanding and moral transformation. Without this spiritual disposition, even the most dramatic of divine signs will pass before a person's eyes without leaving any trace upon their soul.

translation: Are you a more difficult creation, or is the heaven? He constructed it.
interpretation: This verse challenges human beings to reflect on their own insignificance in the face of divine power. By contrasting humanity with the vastness of the heavens, God invites us to recognize that if He is capable of constructing something as immense and magnificent as the sky and all it contains, then the resurrection of human beings — which some deny — is a far simpler matter. It is a call to humility, urging us to abandon our arrogance and denial of the afterlife by contemplating the far greater act of creation that surrounds us every day.

translation: He raised its ceiling and proportioned it.
interpretation: This verse invites deep reflection on the perfection of divine creation. The raising and proportioning of the sky is not merely a description of physical architecture, but a profound reminder that nothing in the universe exists by accident or chance. The deliberate, balanced, and harmonious nature of the heavens serves as a sign pointing toward the intentionality and wisdom of the Creator, urging the observer to move from contemplating the creation to recognizing the majesty of the One who created it.

translation: And He darkened its night and brought out its forenoon light.
interpretation: This verse draws our attention to the divine orchestration of the natural world, reminding us that the alternation between darkness and light is not a random cosmic occurrence, but a deliberate and purposeful act of Allah. The contrast between the darkness of night and the brilliance of the morning light serves as a profound sign of Allah's absolute power and control over creation, inviting the human being to reflect deeply on how every moment of their existence — both the trials that feel like darkness and the blessings that feel like light — are equally under His command and wisdom.

translation: And after that, He spread out the Earth.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the divine act of preparing the Earth as a habitable and functional place for creation. The spreading out (dah) of the Earth signifies not merely a physical expansion, but the purposeful arrangement of conditions necessary for life, sustenance, and order. It reminds us that the universe was not created haphazardly, but with intentional design and care, inviting us to reflect on the wisdom and power behind every element of our existence, and to feel a deep sense of gratitude for the Earth that has been made a cradle for humanity.

translation: He brought forth from it its water and its pasture.
interpretation: This verse invites us to reflect on the divine generosity embedded in creation itself. The earth, in its apparent stillness and silence, carries within it hidden treasures of sustenance — water that gives life and vegetation that nourishes. The act of 'bringing forth' suggests that all provision is not accidental but intentionally drawn out by God, reminding humanity that the sources of their survival are not of their own making, but are gifts continuously unfolded from a higher will. It calls us to gratitude and humility before the One who designed the earth as a vessel of bounty.

translation: And the mountains, He anchored them.
interpretation: This verse invites us to reflect on the profound wisdom of divine design — the mountains are not merely geological formations, but serve as stabilizing forces for the earth, preventing it from shaking and trembling beneath our feet. The use of the verb 'arsāhā' (anchored) draws a powerful nautical image, likening the mountains to anchors of a ship, suggesting that without this divine act of fastening, the earth would be in a state of perpetual instability. This is an invitation to humility, reminding human beings that the very ground they stand on with such confidence is held firm only by the will and mercy of God.

translation: A provision for you and your livestock.
interpretation: This verse reminds us that the blessings of the earth — its vegetation, water, and natural resources — are not solely for human benefit. God's mercy and provision extend to all living creatures, inviting us to reflect on our responsibility as stewards of creation and to recognize that the divine care encompassing even animals should inspire in us a sense of humility, gratitude, and compassion toward all beings that share this world with us.

translation: So when the Greatest Catastrophe comes
interpretation: This verse instills a profound sense of awe and urgency about the Day of Judgment, reminding humanity that no matter how consumed we are by the affairs of this world, there is an inevitable and overwhelming event approaching that will dwarf all earthly concerns. The use of 'the Greatest Catastrophe' serves as a wake-up call, urging us to reflect on our deeds and prioritize our spiritual preparedness over worldly distractions.

translation: The Day when man will remember what he strove for.
interpretation: This verse draws our attention to the profound moment of accountability on the Day of Judgment, where every soul will be confronted with full clarity and perfect memory of all their earthly deeds and intentions. The emphasis here is not merely on actions, but on what one truly *strove for* — the deepest motivations and goals that drove a person's life. In this world, we often forget, rationalize, or obscure the true nature of our pursuits, but on that Day, the veil of self-deception will be lifted entirely. This serves as a powerful reminder that we should reflect *now*, in this life, on what we are truly working toward, because the remembrance that comes on that Day will be too late to change anything — it will only serve as witness against or for us.

translation: And Hellfire will be made visible to whoever sees.
interpretation: This verse serves as a stark reminder that on the Day of Judgment, the consequences of one's deeds will no longer be a matter of faith or unseen reality, but will become a tangible and undeniable truth laid bare before all. The unveiling of Hell is meant to emphasize the absolute certainty of divine accountability — that which people may have doubted or dismissed in their worldly lives will be fully manifest, leaving no room for denial or escape. It is a call to reflect and reform before that day arrives.

translation: As for one who transgresses
interpretation: This verse marks the beginning of a divine distinction between two categories of people on the Day of Judgment. The use of 'transgresses' (طغى) points to a fundamental attitude of rebellion and excess — not merely committing sins, but crossing the boundaries set by Allah with arrogance and willful defiance. It implies a state of spiritual overstepping, where a person elevates their own desires above divine guidance, much like floodwaters that exceed their bounds and cause destruction. This verse serves as a solemn warning that such a disposition carries inevitable consequences, reminding us that our inner orientation toward God defines our ultimate fate.

translation: And preferred the life of this world
interpretation: This verse serves as a warning against the seductive pull of worldly existence. It speaks to a fundamental human weakness: the tendency to prioritize immediate, tangible pleasures and comforts over the eternal and spiritual. When a person 'prefers' this life, they are not merely making a casual choice, but are committing an act of profound spiritual negligence — placing the temporary above the permanent, the illusory above the real. It is a reminder that our attachment to worldly gains, whether wealth, status, or pleasure, can blind us to our higher purpose and ultimate accountability before God.

translation: Indeed, Hellfire is the refuge (abode).
interpretation: This verse serves as a solemn divine warning, emphasizing that for those who have transgressed and turned away from the path of righteousness, the consequences of their choices are absolute and inescapable. The use of the word 'refuge' or 'abode' is deeply ironic — a place ordinarily associated with shelter and comfort becomes the ultimate destination of punishment, suggesting that those who rejected God's guidance have, through their own free will, led themselves to a dwelling place of suffering. It is a reminder that every soul bears responsibility for the path it chooses in this life.

translation: But as for he who feared the standing before his Lord and restrained the soul from [unlawful] inclination,
interpretation: This verse points to the transformative power of God-consciousness — when a person truly internalizes the reality of standing before their Lord on the Day of Judgment, that awareness becomes a moral compass that disciplines the soul. The fear spoken of here is not a paralyzing dread, but a reverential awe that produces self-mastery. The greatest jihad, as the tradition teaches, is the struggle against one's own desires, and this verse suggests that the motivation for winning that inner battle is not willpower alone, but a living, felt sense of divine accountability. It is the remembrance of God's presence that gives the soul the strength to say no to itself.

translation: Then indeed, Paradise is the refuge.
interpretation: This verse serves as a divine reassurance that for those who strive in righteousness and restrain themselves from worldly temptations, the ultimate destination is not merely a reward but a true home — a place of belonging and eternal rest. The use of the word 'refuge' (مأوى) suggests that Paradise is not just a prize to be won, but a sanctuary where the soul finally finds the peace and security it was always searching for in this transient world.

translation: They ask you about the Hour: when will it come to anchor?
interpretation: This verse highlights the fundamental limitation of human knowledge in contrast to divine omniscience. The use of the word 'mursaha' (anchoring, like a ship dropping anchor) is deeply evocative — it suggests that the Hour is already in motion, sailing through time, and only God knows the precise moment it will dock. The question posed by the people reflects a deeply human impulse to control and predict the unknown, yet the verse subtly rebukes this impulse by framing the Hour as something beyond any human calculation or foresight. It is a reminder that certainty about ultimate events belongs solely to Allah, and that our role is not to know when the end will come, but to be perpetually prepared for it.

translation: In what position are you regarding its remembrance (the Hour)?
interpretation: This verse challenges the Prophet ﷺ — and by extension all of humanity — to reflect on the futility of preoccupying oneself with pinpointing or predicting the timing of the Day of Judgment. The rhetorical question implies that no human being, regardless of their station or knowledge, has any real standing or access to the knowledge of when the Hour will arrive. It is a divine reminder that some matters are entirely beyond human reach, and that our role is not to speculate about what Allah has kept hidden, but rather to remain in a state of readiness and moral preparedness at all times.

translation: To your Lord is its finality (its end or ultimate knowledge belongs to your Lord).
interpretation: This verse speaks to the absolute sovereignty and omniscience of God regarding the Day of Judgment. It reminds the human being of their fundamental limitation — that no matter how much one seeks to know, calculate, or predict the ultimate realities of existence, there are matters that belong solely to God. It is a call to humility, urging the believer to surrender the illusion of total control and knowledge, and to place their trust in the One who holds the beginning and the end of all things.

translation: You are only a warner to those who fear it (the Hour).
interpretation: This verse highlights the selective nature of prophetic guidance — the Prophet's warnings are not universally received, but take root only in hearts already predisposed to awe and reverence. It suggests that true spiritual readiness is a prerequisite for transformation; the message finds fertile ground only in those who carry within them a consciousness of accountability. Rather than diminishing the Prophet's role, this frames his mission with precision: he is not responsible for the guidance of all, but is a catalyst for those whose souls are already inclined toward the truth.

translation: On the Day they see it, it will be as though they had not tarried [in the world] except for an evening or its morning.
interpretation: This verse reveals the profound insignificance of worldly life when confronted with the eternal reality of the Hereafter. No matter how long a person lives — decades filled with struggles, ambitions, and attachments — the entire span of their earthly existence will feel, in the light of resurrection, as fleeting as a single afternoon or a single morning. The verse serves as a powerful call to reorient one's priorities: if this life is ultimately experienced as no more than a brief moment, then clinging to it at the expense of the next life is the greatest of misjudgments. The soul's true home lies beyond, and this world is nothing but a short passage.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. He frowned and turned away.
interpretation: This opening verse serves as a divine rebuke directed at the Prophet Muhammad, illustrating that no human being, regardless of their status or mission, is above accountability before God. The frowning and turning away refer to a moment when the Prophet showed displeasure toward a blind man who interrupted him while he was engaged with influential leaders of Quraysh. God's willingness to correct His own beloved Prophet in such a direct and public manner demonstrates that in Islam, spiritual sincerity and the humility to receive all seekers of truth equally are of greater value than social strategy or worldly influence. It is a reminder that divine guidance belongs first and foremost to those whose hearts are open and yearning, not to those who appear powerful in the eyes of men.

translation: That there came to him the blind man.
interpretation: This verse, part of Surah Abasa, serves as a divine rebuke and a reminder that no human being, regardless of their worldly status or perceived importance, should be dismissed or overlooked in spiritual matters. True worth in the sight of God is not measured by social standing, wealth, or influence, but by sincere desire for guidance and purity of heart. Leaders and those in positions of authority must remain accessible and humble, recognizing that the most earnest seekers of truth may come from the most unexpected places.

translation: And what would make you know? Perhaps he might be purified.
interpretation: This verse is a divine rebuke directed at the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), reminding him that true spiritual worth and receptivity cannot be judged by outward appearances or social status. It teaches that the human heart's capacity for growth, purification, and guidance is known only to Allah, and that no person — regardless of how lowly or insignificant they may seem to others — should ever be dismissed or overlooked in the pursuit of spiritual truth. The verse calls us to humility in our judgments of others and to recognize that divine guidance may take root in the most unexpected of souls.

translation: Or he may remember and the reminder may benefit him.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the profound uncertainty inherent in the act of spiritual guidance. No soul can be written off as beyond redemption, for the heart is in constant flux and only Allah knows its ultimate trajectory. The verse urges us never to abandon hope in another person's capacity for awakening, reminding us that a single moment of genuine reflection can transform an entire life. It is a call to humility for those who deliver the message — their role is only to convey, not to judge who is worthy of receiving it.

translation: As for he who is self-sufficient (wealthy and indifferent),
interpretation: This verse draws our attention to a fundamental human tendency: when people feel materially secure or socially powerful, they often become heedless of spiritual guidance. The 'self-sufficiency' referred to here is not merely financial wealth, but an inner attitude of arrogance and independence from God — a state where a person believes they have no need for divine guidance or correction. It serves as a warning that worldly abundance, if it breeds spiritual negligence, becomes a veil between the soul and truth.

translation: But you attend to him
interpretation: This verse gently rebukes the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) for turning his attention toward the wealthy and influential, reminding him that true spiritual priority lies not in seeking the approval of the powerful, but in responding to the sincere seeker of guidance, regardless of their social status. It teaches that divine work must never be compromised by worldly considerations of prestige or influence.

translation: And it is not upon you [to be concerned] if he does not purify himself.
interpretation: This verse addresses the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), reminding him that his sole responsibility is to deliver the divine message. He is not accountable for whether people choose to accept guidance and purify their souls or not. The burden of spiritual growth and moral rectification lies with each individual, and no messenger, however sincere, can force transformation upon another soul. This is a profound reminder that the role of the teacher, guide, or caller to truth is limited to conveyance, and the outcome belongs entirely to God and the free will of the individual.

translation: But as for one who came to you striving eagerly
interpretation: This verse serves as a gentle but firm rebuke, reminding us that true spiritual leadership means prioritizing those who are sincerely seeking guidance and knowledge, regardless of their worldly status. The one who 'comes striving' represents the earnest seeker whose hunger for truth and spiritual growth should never be overlooked in favor of those who appear more socially influential. It teaches us that in the sight of God, sincerity and genuine effort outweigh social standing, and those entrusted with conveying divine guidance must remain attuned to the hearts that are truly receptive rather than being distracted by outward prestige.

translation: And he fears
interpretation: This fragment, often understood in the context of Surah Abasa (80:9), points to the profound spiritual principle that sincere fear of Allah — not social status or worldly prestige — is the true measure of a person's worth before God. It serves as a divine reminder that those who come with humility, awareness of their own accountability, and genuine reverence for the Creator deserve the utmost attention and respect, even when the world might overlook them.

translation: But you are distracted from him (by others).
interpretation: This verse serves as a divine rebuke directed at the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), reminding him — and by extension all believers and leaders — that true spiritual worth is not measured by worldly status or social standing. The one who comes seeking guidance with sincerity and humility, however lowly they may appear in the eyes of society, deserves our full attention and care. It is a call to reorient our priorities away from the powerful and influential, and toward those who genuinely seek truth and nourishment for their souls, for it is in serving such souls that the real mission of guidance is fulfilled.

translation: No! Indeed, it is a reminder.
interpretation: This verse serves as a divine rebuttal to those who treat the Qur'an with indifference or dismissiveness. The emphatic 'No!' (كلا) functions as a sharp correction, asserting that the Qur'an is not something that can be ignored or taken lightly. Its designation as a 'reminder' (تذكرة) suggests that its truths are not foreign to the human soul — rather, they awaken something already embedded within human consciousness, a primordial awareness of God and moral responsibility. The verse thus challenges humanity to recognize the Qur'an not as an imposition, but as a restoration of what we inherently know to be true.

translation: So whoever wills, let him remember it (or take heed of it).
interpretation: This verse is a profound declaration of human free will and divine respect for individual autonomy. Allah does not compel anyone to accept guidance or remember His message, but rather leaves the choice to the human being. It is a subtle but powerful reminder that true faith cannot be forced — it must arise from a sincere and willing heart. At the same time, the verse carries an implicit weight of responsibility: the opportunity to remember and reflect has been given, and what one does with that opportunity defines one's spiritual standing before God.

translation: In honored scrolls
interpretation: This verse points to the noble and exalted status of divine revelation itself. The message of God is not merely spoken words that fade away, but is preserved in writings of great honor and dignity. This emphasizes that what has been revealed to humanity carries an intrinsic sanctity and worth that demands reverence and careful attention, reminding believers that engaging with scripture is not a casual act but an encounter with something profoundly sacred.

translation: Exalted and purified
interpretation: This verse points to the divine elevation and sanctity of the Quran itself, suggesting that its nature transcends the physical and mundane world. Its exaltation is not merely in status but in essence — it exists in a realm of absolute purity, untouched by falsehood, distortion, or corruption. This serves as an assurance to the believer that what they hold in their hands is not merely ink on paper, but a preserved and sacred trust from the Divine, worthy of the utmost reverence and careful engagement.

translation: In the hands of scribes (noble and virtuous).
interpretation: This verse points to the elevated status and sanctity of divine revelation — that the words of God are not carried carelessly or by just anyone, but are borne by noble, purified beings (the angels), reminding us that what we receive as scripture is the result of a sacred and meticulous chain of transmission that demands our utmost reverence and respect.

translation: Noble and righteous
interpretation: This phrase, often used in the Qur'an to describe the angels who record human deeds, reminds us that the divine system of accountability is administered with the utmost integrity and honor. It suggests that the recording of our actions is not a cold, bureaucratic process, but one carried out by beings of noble character, implying that every human soul is worthy of such distinguished attention and that our deeds carry profound cosmic significance.

translation: Perish the human! How ungrateful he is!
interpretation: This verse is a divine expression of profound astonishment and condemnation at the deeply rooted tendency of human beings to deny and reject the countless blessings and favors bestowed upon them by their Creator. It serves as a stark reminder that ingratitude is not merely a social failing, but a spiritual disease that blinds humanity to the reality of their dependence on God, and that such willful denial of truth carries within it the seeds of one's own spiritual destruction.

translation: From what substance did He create him?
interpretation: This verse provokes human reflection and humility by challenging mankind to contemplate the humble and insignificant origin of their own creation. It serves as a rhetorical reminder that the very being who often becomes arrogant and forgetful of God was fashioned from something lowly and base, urging a return to gratitude and awareness of one's dependence on the Creator.

translation: He created him from a drop of fluid, then proportioned him.
interpretation: This verse invites deep reflection on the humbling origins of human existence. Despite the greatness that mankind often attributes to itself, the reminder of being fashioned from something as insignificant as a drop of fluid is meant to cultivate humility and gratitude. The word 'proportioned' points to the divine precision and intentionality behind creation — nothing about the human form is accidental. God's act of measuring and shaping suggests that every human being carries within them a deliberate divine design, urging us to recognize our dependence on God rather than take pride in our own perceived self-sufficiency.

translation: Then He made the path easy for him.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the divine facilitation of the human journey through life. Allah, in His infinite mercy, does not leave humanity to navigate existence alone or without guidance. After creating the human being and fashioning him in the most complete form, Allah eases the way — providing revelation, reason, and innate disposition (fitrah) as tools to find truth and righteousness. It is a reminder that the path to fulfillment, both in this world and the next, is not an impossible burden, but one made accessible through divine grace. The verse invites reflection and gratitude, urging humans to recognize that every faculty they possess and every guidance they receive is a gift, and that the road to God, though requiring effort, has been cleared and illuminated by the One who created them.

translation: Then He caused him to die and provided a grave for him.
