interpretation: This verse highlights the complete sovereignty of Allah over the entire arc of human existence. The deliberate pairing of death with burial is significant — it is not merely that man dies, but that Allah, in His mercy and dignity, ordains that the human body be honored even in death through proper burial. This reflects the Islamic understanding that divine care for the human being does not cease at the moment of death, and that the sanctity of the human form is preserved even after the soul has departed. It is a reminder that every stage of our existence, including its end, is held within the purposeful will of God.

translation: Then when He wills, He will resurrect him.
interpretation: This verse underscores the absolute sovereignty of God over life and death, reminding humanity that resurrection is not a matter of natural law or human agency, but purely an act of divine will. The use of 'when He wills' emphasizes that the timing and occurrence of resurrection are entirely within God's dominion, instilling in the believer both humility before God's omnipotence and certainty that the promise of the afterlife will be fulfilled on His terms alone.

translation: No! He has not yet accomplished what He commanded him.
interpretation: This verse serves as a rebuke to the human being who is ungrateful and neglectful of his duties. It reminds us that despite being given all the faculties, blessings, and guidance necessary to fulfill our purpose, we consistently fall short of truly fulfilling the obligations that God has placed upon us. It is a call to self-reflection and accountability, urging us to examine whether we are truly living up to the covenant and responsibilities that come with our existence as conscious, moral beings endowed with reason and free will.

translation: Let man look at his food.
interpretation: This verse invites human beings to engage in deep reflection and contemplation about the origins of their sustenance, recognizing that the intricate process by which food is brought forth — from rain, soil, seeds, and sunlight — is not a product of chance or human ingenuity alone, but rather a manifestation of divine providence and power. By meditating on something as ordinary and daily as food, man is drawn toward gratitude and acknowledgment of his utter dependence on God.

translation: We poured down water in abundance
interpretation: This verse draws attention to the miraculous and deliberate nature of rainfall as a divine act. The emphatic use of 'We poured' reflects Allah's direct and purposeful intervention in sustaining life on earth, inviting human beings to reflect on their utter dependence on divine mercy for their very existence and nourishment. The abundance of water is not accidental, but a carefully measured blessing that calls for gratitude and recognition of the Creator's ongoing providence.

translation: Then We split the earth, splitting it open.
interpretation: This verse draws attention to the miraculous and deliberate act of God in causing the earth to crack and break open to bring forth vegetation and sustenance. It invites the human being to reflect on the divine power behind something as ordinary as the growth of plants from soil, reminding us that what we take for granted is in reality a sign of God's continuous providence and care for His creation.

translation: And We caused to grow therein grain
interpretation: This verse invites us to reflect on the divine generosity embedded in the natural world. The use of 'We caused to grow' emphasizes that the act of cultivation is not merely a human achievement, but a manifestation of God's sustaining power. Every grain that emerges from the earth is a sign of divine providence, reminding humanity that its survival and nourishment are entirely dependent on God's will and mercy. The verse calls us to gratitude and humility, recognizing that even the most basic elements of life are gifts from the Creator.

translation: And grapes and clover,
interpretation: This verse, part of a larger passage describing the blessings of provision that God has created for humanity, draws attention to the deliberate and purposeful nature of divine sustenance. By enumerating specific fruits and fodder, the verse invites the reader to reflect on the intricate care with which God arranges the natural world — not only providing for human needs but also for the animals that serve humanity. It is a reminder that every element of creation, even the most ordinary plant, is a sign of divine generosity and intentionality, calling us to gratitude and awareness of our utter dependence on God.

translation: And olive trees and palm trees
interpretation: This verse invites us to reflect on the divine generosity embedded in creation. The olive and the palm are not merely plants, but symbols of sustenance, blessing, and civilization. By singling out these two trees, the Qur'an draws our attention to the deliberate and purposeful nature of God's provision — that the earth was not randomly furnished, but carefully equipped with what humanity needs to thrive, both physically and spiritually. The mention of these specific trees calls us to gratitude, reminding us that every fruit we enjoy is a sign of divine care and intentionality.

translation: And dense gardens,
interpretation: This verse alludes to the abundant and lush rewards awaiting the righteous in Paradise, symbolizing that divine generosity knows no scarcity. The density of the gardens suggests that the blessings of God are not sparse or limited, but rather overflowing and overwhelming, reflecting the infinite nature of His mercy and care for those who remain steadfast in their faith.

translation: And fruit and herbage (abba).
interpretation: This verse draws our attention to the interconnectedness of divine provision, reminding us that Allah's sustenance encompasses not only what directly nourishes the human soul and body, such as fruit, but also what sustains the broader created order, such as pasture for animals. It invites us to reflect on the completeness and balance of Allah's design, where every living creature — human and animal alike — is provided for within an intricate, harmonious system that we did not create and cannot replicate, thus calling us to gratitude and humility before the Creator.

translation: A provision for you and your livestock.
interpretation: This verse reminds us that divine mercy extends beyond humanity to encompass all living creatures. God's provision is all-encompassing and deliberate, and we are called to recognize that the blessings of the earth are not ours alone to exploit, but are shared sustenance for all beings under our care. This invites a sense of responsibility and stewardship toward the animals entrusted to us, as their welfare is intertwined with our own in the eyes of God.

translation: So when the Deafening Blast comes
interpretation: This verse draws our attention to the certainty and overwhelming power of the Day of Judgment. The use of the word 'Sākhkhah' — meaning a blast so loud it deafens — is not merely a description of sound, but a metaphor for an event so absolute and shattering that it will render all worldly concerns utterly insignificant. The use of 'when' rather than 'if' affirms its inevitability, inviting the reader to reflect on their preparedness for that moment rather than question its arrival.

translation: The Day a man will flee from his own brother,
interpretation: This verse speaks to the absolute terror and self-absorption of the Day of Judgment, where the bonds of brotherhood — among the most sacred in human society — will be completely severed by fear. It reveals that on that Day, every soul will be so consumed by its own reckoning and fate that even the most cherished earthly relationships will offer no comfort or refuge, reminding us that the only true security lies in our relationship with Allah, not in our worldly connections.

translation: And his mother and his father
interpretation: This verse fragment emphasizes the profound bond and duty owed to one's parents. It serves as a reminder that recognition of one's origins — the mother who bore and nurtured, and the father who provided and guided — is integral to gratitude, humility, and moral accountability. The mention of parents in the Qur'an is frequently linked to the acknowledgment of divine blessings, suggesting that honoring one's parents is not merely a social obligation but a spiritual one, reflecting the recognition of the chain of care and sacrifice through which human life is sustained.

translation: And his wife and his children
interpretation: This verse highlights that on the Day of Judgment, every soul will be so overwhelmed by its own accountability that even the closest and most beloved of human bonds — the spouse and children — will be of no consequence. It serves as a powerful reminder that worldly attachments, no matter how deep, will not intercede or provide refuge on that ultimate Day, urging believers to focus on their individual spiritual accountability before God.

translation: Every person that Day will have matter to preoccupy him.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the absolute isolation of the human soul on the Day of Judgment. No matter how strong the bonds of love, kinship, or friendship were in this world, on that Day every soul will be so overwhelmed by its own reckoning and fate that it will have no capacity to concern itself with anyone else. It is a profound reminder that the relationships and social connections we rely upon in this life will offer no refuge on that ultimate Day, urging us to focus on our own accountability before God rather than placing false hope in the intercession or company of others.

translation: Faces on that Day will be bright,
interpretation: This verse speaks to the spiritual reality that one's inner state will be made manifest on the Day of Judgment. Those who lived a life of faith, righteousness, and sincere devotion to God will have their inner light reflected outwardly in their faces. The radiance described is not merely physical beauty, but the luminosity of a soul that has been purified through worship, good deeds, and closeness to the Divine. It serves as a reminder that nothing can be hidden on that Day, and that the true measure of a person lies in the condition of their heart and soul.

translation: Laughing, rejoicing
interpretation: This phrase speaks to the ultimate state of the blessed souls in the Hereafter — one of pure, uninhibited joy. True laughter and delight here are not merely emotional states, but rather the outward manifestation of a soul that has been fully relieved of all worldly burden, fear, and uncertainty. It suggests that the highest reward is not merely safety from punishment, but an active, radiant happiness — a joy so complete that it shines upon the face. This is a reminder that the goal of a believer's journey is not just survival in the Hereafter, but genuine flourishing and bliss.

translation: And faces on that Day will be covered with dust,
interpretation: This verse evokes the image of humiliation and despair that will befall those who have rejected faith on the Day of Judgment. The dust upon their faces is not merely a physical description, but a symbol of utter disgrace and defeat. Just as a person thrown to the ground in defeat is covered in dust, so too will the disbelievers wear their spiritual failure visibly upon their faces, unable to hide their shame before God and all of creation.

translation: Darkness will cover their faces
interpretation: This verse speaks to the spiritual and physical consequence of rejecting God's truth. The darkness that covers the faces of the wrongdoers is not merely an external punishment, but a reflection of the inner darkness they carried in their hearts during their earthly lives. Just as they turned away from the light of divine guidance, their faces in the Hereafter will bear the mark of that turning away, making visible what was once hidden within their souls.

translation: Those are the disbelievers, the wicked.
interpretation: This verse delivers a severe moral and spiritual judgment, linking disbelief with moral corruption to show that the rejection of divine truth is not merely an intellectual stance but inevitably manifests in immoral and sinful conduct. True faith and righteous behavior are inseparable, and the absence of one leads to the corruption of the other.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. When the sun is wrapped up [in darkness].
interpretation: This verse opens Surah At-Takwir and serves as a profound warning to humanity about the impermanence of the physical world. The image of the sun — the most dominant and life-sustaining force in our observable universe — being 'wrapped up' or extinguished is a deliberate divine reminder that nothing in creation, no matter how vast or powerful it may seem, is eternal or independent. God is drawing our attention away from our attachment to the material world and toward the reality of accountability. If even the sun, upon which all earthly life depends, will cease to exist, then human beings must reflect on their own fragility and ultimate return to their Creator. The verse invites deep humility and a reorientation of priorities toward what is truly everlasting.

translation: And when the stars lose their light and fall scattered
interpretation: This verse invites us to reflect on the utter fragility of what we consider permanent and eternal. The stars, which humanity has gazed upon across millennia as symbols of constancy, guidance, and grandeur, will themselves be extinguished and cast away. If even the stars — those magnificent celestial bodies — are subject to annihilation, then how can a human being place ultimate trust or attachment in anything of this world? The verse calls us to reorient our hearts away from the transient and toward the only true permanence, which is God Himself.

translation: And when the mountains are set in motion
interpretation: This verse speaks to the absolute transformation of the physical world at the end of times. The mountains, which we consider to be the most immovable and permanent fixtures of our earthly existence, symbols of stability and permanence, will be uprooted and moved as though weightless. This serves as a powerful reminder that nothing in this world is truly permanent or beyond the power of Allah. What we place our trust and security in — wealth, status, even the solid ground beneath our feet — will all be dissolved. It invites the believer to redirect their attachment away from the transient world and toward that which is eternal.

translation: And when the pregnant she-camels are abandoned
interpretation: This verse, set within the cataclysmic events of the Day of Judgment (Surah At-Takwir), uses the abandonment of the pregnant she-camel — the most prized possession in Arabian society — as a powerful symbol of total worldly collapse. The fact that something so valuable and carefully tended would simply be left behind signals that on that Day, all earthly attachments and material concerns will become utterly meaningless, as the terror and magnitude of what unfolds will override every human instinct toward possession and survival.

translation: And when the wild beasts are gathered together
interpretation: This verse invites deep reflection on the total dissolution of the natural order at the end of time. The gathering of wild beasts — creatures that in this world scatter, hunt, and roam in fear of one another — serves as a powerful symbol that even the laws of nature that govern this world will be completely overturned. If even the animals are resurrected and assembled, it underscores the absolute and all-encompassing nature of Divine Justice, reminding humanity that nothing in creation, however small or seemingly insignificant, falls outside the scope of God's awareness and authority on the Day of Judgment.

translation: And when the seas are set ablaze
interpretation: This verse speaks of one of the cataclysmic signs of the Day of Judgment. The igniting or overflowing of the seas symbolizes the complete unraveling of the natural order as we know it. Just as water is the very opposite of fire, this impossible transformation signals that on that Day, all worldly certainties and constants will be shattered, reminding humanity that nothing in this existence is permanent or beyond the power of Allah. It serves as a powerful warning to reflect on our deeds before that inevitable moment arrives.

translation: And when the souls are paired
interpretation: This verse speaks to the divine justice of the Day of Judgment, where every soul will be reunited with its counterpart — matched with those of like nature and deed. The righteous will be joined with the righteous, and the wicked with the wicked. It suggests that our choices and actions in this life are not isolated, but form a spiritual identity that will ultimately find its true company in the hereafter. We are, in essence, drawn toward what we resemble, and on that Day, no soul will be able to hide its true nature.

translation: And when the girl [who was] buried alive is asked
interpretation: This verse calls attention to the grave injustice of female infanticide practiced in pre-Islamic Arabia, where daughters were sometimes buried alive out of shame or fear of poverty. By declaring that on the Day of Judgment it is the victim — not the perpetrator — who will be questioned, God subverts the power dynamic of the oppressor and the oppressed. The verse implies that her innocent blood cries out for justice, and that the accountability for such a crime will be made manifest before the Divine. It is a profound affirmation of the sanctity of human life, especially the lives of the vulnerable, and a warning that no injustice, however normalized by society, escapes divine reckoning.

translation: For what sin was she killed?
interpretation: This verse, from Surah At-Takwir (81:9), refers to the Day of Judgment when the female infant who was buried alive — a common practice in pre-Islamic Arabia — will be asked for what crime she was killed. The verse is a profound moral indictment of those who took innocent lives, asserting that on the Day of Reckoning, all injustices will be brought to light and the oppressors will be held accountable. It affirms that no innocent soul can be taken without consequence before God, and it elevates the dignity and rights of the vulnerable, particularly women and children, who were historically marginalized and victimized. The rhetorical question is not directed at the victim, but serves as a divine condemnation of the perpetrators, making clear that such an act is utterly indefensible before the Creator.

translation: And when the scrolls are spread open
interpretation: This verse speaks to the absolute transparency and accountability that will define the Day of Judgment. The spreading open of the scrolls symbolizes that nothing in a person's life — no deed, intention, or secret — will remain hidden. Every action, however small or concealed, will be laid bare before God and before the individual themselves, leaving no room for denial or excuse. It is a powerful reminder that our lives are being recorded, and that we should be ever mindful of what we contribute to that record.

translation: And when the sky is stripped away,
interpretation: This verse invites deep reflection on the total dismantling of the familiar cosmic order on the Day of Judgment. The sky, which we perceive as a permanent and vast canopy above us, will be peeled back like a layer being removed, signifying that nothing in this world — no matter how immense or seemingly eternal — is beyond Allah's power to dissolve. It serves as a profound reminder that our attachment to the material world is misplaced, for everything we consider permanent is ultimately temporary and subject to the will of the Creator.

translation: And when the Hellfire is set ablaze
interpretation: This verse draws attention to the terrifying reality of the Day of Judgment, where the ignition of Hellfire serves as a cosmic sign that divine justice is being enacted. The passive construction implies that it is Allah who sets it ablaze, reminding humanity that the consequences of their choices in this life are real, inevitable, and ultimately in the hands of God. It is a call to moral consciousness and accountability before that day arrives.

translation: And when Paradise is brought near,
interpretation: This verse speaks to the immediacy and tangibility of Paradise on the Day of Judgment. The use of the passive construction 'brought near' suggests that Paradise is not something humans attain through their own power, but rather it is drawn close to the righteous as an act of divine grace and mercy. It implies that the reward of the believers is so certain and so real that it will be physically manifested before them, as if to honor them by coming to meet them rather than making them journey toward it. This reversal of effort reflects the ultimate dignity God bestows upon those who lived righteously.

translation: Every soul will know what it has brought forth.
interpretation: This verse serves as a profound reminder of individual moral accountability. Each person carries within them a complete and perfect record of their deeds, intentions, and choices made throughout their life. On the Day of Judgment, nothing will be hidden or forgotten — the soul itself will be the witness to its own actions. This awareness is meant to inspire mindfulness and conscientiousness in one's daily conduct, urging the believer to constantly reflect on what they are 'bringing' with them toward their inevitable meeting with God.

translation: So I swear by the retreating stars
interpretation: Allah swears by the stars that recede and hide themselves — drawing attention to the precision and grandeur of the cosmos as evidence of divine power and design. The oath serves to elevate the importance of what follows, urging humanity to recognize that the universe itself bears witness to the truth of the revelation being delivered, and that those who reflect deeply on the natural world will find in it undeniable signs of the Creator's sovereignty and wisdom.

translation: The stars that sweep along, sweeping (hide themselves)
interpretation: This phrase, found in Surah At-Takwir (81:15-16), refers to the stars in their courses — those that move swiftly across the sky and then disappear below the horizon. The deeper meaning is an invitation to reflect on the magnificent order and precision of the cosmos as a sign of Allah's power and sovereignty. Just as these celestial bodies move in perfect, ordained paths and then conceal themselves, so too does all of creation operate under divine command and control, humbling humanity before the grandeur of the Creator.

translation: By the night as it recedes,
interpretation: The oath sworn by the retreating night draws attention to the transitional moment between darkness and dawn, symbolizing the perpetual interplay between falsehood and truth. Just as the night inevitably gives way to light, this verse invites reflection on the temporary nature of obscurity and hardship, assuring that clarity and relief are always on the horizon for those who remain steadfast in faith.

translation: And by the dawn when it breathes
interpretation: The image of dawn 'breathing' is a profound metaphor that invites us to witness the divine artistry in the transition from darkness to light. Just as breath is the most intimate sign of life, the gradual spreading of morning light across the sky is portrayed as a living, breathing entity — a testament to Allah's continuous and intimate involvement in sustaining creation. This verse calls us to reflect on how even the most ordinary, recurring moments in nature are, in truth, sacred signs of divine power and mercy.

translation: Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the divine authenticity of the Qur'an by affirming that it is delivered through a noble and trustworthy messenger, reminding us that the channel through which revelation comes is as important as the message itself — God chooses only the most honorable and pure of His creation to bear and convey His word, so that no doubt may be cast upon its integrity.

translation: Possessed of power, with the Owner of the Throne, secure in position.
interpretation: This verse describes the Angel Jibreel (Gabriel), emphasizing that true authority and honor are not self-possessed but are derivative — existing only in proximity and submission to Allah, the Owner of the Throne. The verse reminds us that even the most powerful of creation derives its strength and standing entirely from its closeness to the Divine, teaching us that genuine honor for any being, whether angel or human, lies not in independent power but in one's nearness and faithfulness to Allah.

translation: Obeyed there, and trustworthy.
interpretation: This verse, referring to the Angel Jibreel (Gabriel), reminds us that true leadership and authority are built upon two inseparable qualities: the power to command obedience and the moral integrity to be trusted absolutely. It invites us to reflect that any position of influence, whether angelic or human, is only legitimate and noble when both strength and trustworthiness are united within it.

translation: And your companion is not mad.
interpretation: This verse serves as a divine defense of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), affirming his sound mind and rational judgment against the accusations of his opponents. It challenges the disbelievers to reflect honestly on their knowledge of the Prophet, whom they had lived with for years and knew to be a man of exceptional wisdom and moral integrity. The verse invites critical self-examination: if they truly knew him, how could they dismiss his message as the ranting of a madman? The accusation of madness was a desperate attempt to discredit a truth they could not rationally refute.

translation: And indeed, he saw him on the clear horizon.
interpretation: This verse refers to the Prophet Muhammad's vision of the Angel Jibreel (Gabriel) in his true angelic form on the clear, vast horizon. It affirms the authenticity and clarity of divine revelation — that the Prophet did not receive the Qur'an through delusion or imagination, but through a genuine, undeniable encounter. The 'clear horizon' signifies that this was not a hidden or ambiguous experience, but an open and manifest one, underscoring the certainty and transparency of the revelation brought to humanity.

translation: And he is not withholding of the unseen.
interpretation: This verse defends the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) against accusations that he was concealing divine revelation for personal gain. It affirms that the Prophet faithfully and generously conveyed everything revealed to him without holding back any portion of it, demonstrating his complete trustworthiness as a messenger. The verse thus establishes the integrity of the prophetic transmission, assuring believers that what they have received is the full and unaltered message from God.

translation: And it is not the word of a cursed devil.
interpretation: This verse serves as a divine refutation of the accusations made by the disbelievers who claimed that the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) received his revelations from evil or satanic sources. Allah here categorically denies any association between the Qur'an and the whispers of Satan, affirming that the noble words of the Qur'an are far too pure, guided, and truthful in their nature to have any connection with the accursed devil, who is fundamentally an enemy of humanity and a promoter of falsehood and corruption. The verse thus calls on the reader to reflect on the sublime nature of the Qur'anic message as evidence of its divine origin.

translation: So where are you going?
interpretation: This verse is a rhetorical challenge directed at those who turn away from the path of God. It implies that there is no escape from divine truth and no alternative path that leads to salvation or fulfillment. Human beings, despite being given clear guidance, often wander aimlessly in pursuit of worldly desires and false ideologies. The verse serves as a wake-up call, urging mankind to reflect on the direction of their lives and return to the straight path, for all other roads ultimately lead to loss.

translation: It is nothing but a reminder for all the worlds.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the universal and timeless nature of the Qur'an, asserting that its message transcends the boundaries of time, place, and people. It is not limited to a particular nation or era, but is a divine reminder addressed to all of humanity and creation. This universality reflects the all-encompassing mercy of God, who did not leave any people without guidance, and it places a collective responsibility upon all who receive this message to reflect upon it and heed its call.

translation: For whoever among you wills to walk straight.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the delicate balance between human free will and divine guidance. While God has laid out the straight path, the choice to walk upon it ultimately rests with the individual. It is a reminder that spiritual rectitude is not imposed but chosen — a conscious, ongoing act of the will. At the same time, this freedom is not absolute, as the very next verse clarifies that this willing is itself encompassed within the will of God, teaching us that our striving toward righteousness is itself a gift and a grace from the Divine.

translation: And you do not will except that Allah wills - Lord of the worlds.
interpretation: This verse addresses the fundamental relationship between human free will and divine sovereignty. While human beings possess the faculty of choice and volition, this capacity itself is entirely contingent upon and nested within the overarching will of God. It is not that human will is illusory or irrelevant, but rather that it operates within the boundless and all-encompassing will of the Lord of all creation. True freedom, in the deepest sense, is not independence from God, but rather the alignment of one's will with His — for our very ability to choose is itself a gift granted by Him. This verse humbles the human ego, reminding us that we are not self-sufficient masters of our own fate, but beings whose every inclination and decision unfolds within the embrace of divine wisdom and authority.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. When the sky is torn apart.
interpretation: This opening verse of Surah Al-Infitar uses the imagery of the sky being split open as a powerful metaphor to convey the complete unraveling of the familiar cosmic order on the Day of Judgment. It invites the reader to reflect on the impermanence of what appears most vast, stable, and eternal in our physical world. If even the heavens — which seem so infinite and unchanging — can be torn asunder, then nothing in creation is truly permanent, and only God's power and will endure. This is meant to instill a sense of awe and humility in the human heart, reminding us that our existence in this world is transient and that we must prepare for a reality far greater than what we currently perceive.

translation: And when the stars are scattered,
interpretation: This verse speaks to the total dissolution of the cosmic order at the end of time. The scattering of stars, which have always represented permanence, constancy, and celestial order in human experience, signals that even the most enduring and seemingly indestructible aspects of creation are subject to Allah's will. It invites the reader to reflect on the transience of all that we perceive as fixed and eternal, and to recognize that only Allah's existence is truly permanent and beyond dissolution.

translation: And when the seas are erupted (burst forth/exploded)
interpretation: This verse points to a profound transformation of the natural world at the end of time, suggesting that the seemingly fixed and permanent boundaries of existence — represented by the vast, contained oceans — will be violently undone. Just as the seas represent the deepest, most immovable forces of nature, their bursting apart signals that nothing in this world, no matter how grand or seemingly eternal, can withstand the Day of Reckoning. It is a reminder to humanity that our attachment to the permanence of this world is an illusion, and that true stability lies only in our relationship with the Divine.

translation: And when the graves are overturned (scattered and emptied)
interpretation: This verse draws our attention to the absolute certainty and totality of the resurrection. The use of the word 'bu'thirat,' meaning to be violently scattered or overturned, suggests that on the Day of Judgment, death itself will be undone with a force and finality that cannot be resisted. No grave, no matter how deep or ancient, can contain the soul when Allah decrees the resurrection. It serves as a powerful reminder that our earthly existence is temporary, and that accountability before Allah is inevitable. The imagery challenges us to reflect on how we live our lives now, knowing that the earth will one day yield back all that it has taken.

translation: Every soul will know what it has sent forth and what it has left behind.
interpretation: This verse serves as a profound reminder of individual accountability before God. Each person will be confronted with the complete record of their deeds — not only the actions they actively performed and presented in their lifetime, but also the lasting effects and consequences of those actions that rippled forward after them, as well as the good they neglected or delayed. It underscores that nothing escapes divine awareness, and that true self-reckoning must begin in this life before the ultimate reckoning in the next.

translation: O mankind, what has deceived you concerning your Lord, the Most Generous?
interpretation: This verse is a profound divine address that confronts the human soul with its own negligence and ingratitude. The rhetorical question is not one of anger but of gentle astonishment — God, in His infinite generosity, questions humanity about the audacity of disobedience despite receiving boundless blessings. The use of 'Al-Kareem' (the Most Generous) at the end is deeply intentional: it is precisely God's generosity and forbearance that humanity has mistaken for permission to sin, turning divine grace into a source of delusion rather than gratitude and devotion. The verse thus serves as a wake-up call, urging the human being to reflect on how they have allowed worldly distractions, ego, and false hopes to sever their awareness of accountability to the One who has given them everything.

translation: Who created you, proportioned you, and assembled you
interpretation: This verse invites deep reflection on the immense care and precision with which Allah fashioned the human being. It is not merely a statement about physical creation, but a reminder of the divine intentionality behind human existence. Every person has been deliberately shaped, balanced, and brought into a form that is uniquely their own. The progression of the three verbs — creating, proportioning, and assembling — suggests that human dignity is not accidental but divinely ordained, and that gratitude and humility are the natural responses of one who truly contemplates the miracle of their own being.

translation: In whatever form He willed, He assembled you.
interpretation: This verse invites deep reflection on the absolute sovereignty and creative will of God. It reminds the human being that their very existence, form, and constitution are entirely the result of divine choice — not chance, not personal merit, and not the will of any other being. The intended meaning is a call to humility: since God alone determined the shape, nature, and particulars of your being, any pride in one's physical form or innate qualities is misplaced. True gratitude and submission belong only to the One who fashioned you precisely as He willed.

translation: No! But you deny the Day of Judgment.
interpretation: This verse serves as a divine rebuke to those who reject accountability. The word 'Kalla' (No!) is a sharp repudiation, suggesting that the real root of human moral failure — neglecting the orphan, refusing to feed the poor, consuming inheritance greedily — is not ignorance or weakness, but a deliberate rejection of the concept of divine reckoning. When a person does not believe they will be held accountable for their actions, they lose the spiritual and moral restraint that faith provides. Denying the Day of Judgment is therefore not merely a theological error; it is the foundational corruption that enables all other injustices to flourish.

translation: And indeed, over you are appointed guardians (angels).
interpretation: This verse reminds us that human beings are never truly alone or unaccountable in their actions. Allah has assigned noble angels to watch over us, recording every deed we perform. This serves as a constant spiritual awareness that should inspire mindfulness and moral responsibility in every moment of our lives, encouraging us to align our actions with righteousness, knowing that nothing escapes the divine record.

translation: Noble scribes (angels) recording (deeds).
interpretation: This phrase reminds us that human beings are never truly alone in their actions — every deed, word, and intention is being observed and recorded by honorable angels appointed by God. This serves as a continuous moral reminder that accountability is woven into the very fabric of existence, encouraging mindfulness and ethical conduct in every moment of one's life.

translation: They know what you do.
interpretation: This verse serves as a reminder that human beings are never truly alone in their actions — noble angels have been appointed to watch over us and record our deeds with perfect accuracy. It calls us to a state of constant mindfulness and moral accountability, urging us to align our outward actions with our inner intentions, knowing that nothing escapes the awareness of those entrusted by God to bear witness to our conduct.

translation: Indeed, the righteous will be in bliss.
interpretation: This verse serves as a divine promise and assurance that those who live lives of virtue, righteousness, and obedience to God will be rewarded with eternal joy and comfort. It is not merely a description of paradise, but a motivation for the believer to remain steadfast on the path of goodness, reminding us that no act of sincere righteousness goes unnoticed or unrewarded by God. The use of the emphatic 'indeed' reflects the certainty of this promise, encouraging the faithful never to lose hope in God's ultimate justice and generosity.

translation: And indeed, the wicked will be in Hellfire.
interpretation: This verse serves as a stark moral warning, affirming the absolute justice of the Divine. The certainty expressed through the emphatic Arabic construction ('inna' and the lam of emphasis) suggests that the consequences of a life lived in wickedness and moral corruption are not arbitrary or uncertain, but are as real and inevitable as any physical law. It reminds us that our choices in this world carry profound spiritual weight, and that the path of transgression and heedlessness is not without ultimate consequence. The verse thus calls the human soul to accountability and self-reflection, urging us to examine the moral quality of our deeds before we stand before God.

translation: They will burn in it on the Day of Judgment.
interpretation: This verse serves as a stark warning about the inescapable consequences of one's deeds. The use of the future tense emphasizes the certainty of divine accountability — that no soul will escape the reckoning of the Day of Judgment. It reminds us that the choices we make in this transient world carry eternal weight, and that the Fire is not merely a punishment, but a manifestation of justice for those who persistently chose wrongdoing over righteousness.

translation: And they will not be absent from it.
interpretation: This verse serves as a stark warning that the disbelievers and wrongdoers cannot escape or hide from the punishment of Hellfire. There is no possibility of evasion, unconsciousness, or death that might offer them relief. Their suffering will be constant, conscious, and inescapable — a permanent state of accountability that underscores the absolute and uncompromising nature of divine justice.

translation: And what will make you know what the Day of Judgment is?
interpretation: This rhetorical question is not merely asking for information — it is an expression of the incomprehensible magnitude of the Day of Judgment. Allah addresses the Prophet, and through him all of humanity, to instill a profound sense of awe and humility. The implication is that the human mind, bound by its limited worldly experience, cannot fully grasp the weight, gravity, and reality of that Day. It is a divine invitation to reflect deeply and to approach the concept of divine accountability with reverence and seriousness, recognizing that what awaits transcends all human comprehension.

translation: Then what will make you know what the Day of Recompense is?
interpretation: This verse employs a rhetorical question to emphasize the incomprehensible magnitude of the Day of Judgment. The repetition of the question is a deliberate stylistic device to instill in the human mind a profound sense of awe and humility, suggesting that the reality of that Day far surpasses human imagination and comprehension. It is a divine reminder that no matter how much we think we understand about accountability and divine justice, the true weight and nature of that Day remains beyond our full grasp, urging us to take our moral and spiritual responsibilities seriously while we still have the opportunity.

translation: The Day when no soul will have power to do anything for another soul, and the command that Day will be entirely with Allah.
interpretation: This verse compels us to reflect deeply on the profound solitude of the Day of Judgment. In this worldly life, we often place our trust and hopes in social connections, wealth, status, and the intercession of others. We rely on family, friends, and influential figures to help us through difficulties. But this verse strips away every illusion of external salvation, reminding us that on the ultimate Day of Reckoning, every soul will stand utterly alone before its Creator. No parent can shield a child, no friend can carry another's burden, and no worldly power will hold any sway. The verse is not meant to instill despair, but rather to awaken a sense of urgent personal accountability — urging us to invest now in the only relationship that will matter on that Day: our direct, sincere, and unwavering bond with Allah, whose sole authority will reign supreme.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Woe to those who give less than due.
interpretation: This verse serves as a powerful divine warning against those who engage in dishonest dealings, particularly in commerce. The concept of 'tatfif' (shortchanging) is not merely about physical measurements but speaks to a deeper moral corruption — the self-serving tendency to demand full measure for oneself while deliberately depriving others of their rights. Allah opens this surah with a stern condemnation, signaling that justice in our dealings with others is not optional but a fundamental spiritual obligation. The 'woe' pronounced here reflects not just worldly consequence but divine displeasure, reminding us that every act of dishonesty, no matter how seemingly small, is witnessed and recorded by Allah.

translation: Those who, when they measure out against people, take full measure.
interpretation: This verse exposes a deeply rooted form of hypocrisy and moral corruption in business dealings. It highlights that those who cheat in trade are not merely committing an economic crime, but revealing a fundamental selfishness in their character — they are meticulous in securing their own rights while being careless or dishonest when fulfilling the rights of others. The verse invites us to reflect on how our treatment of others in everyday transactions is a mirror of our inner spiritual state, and that true faith demands we hold others' rights to the same standard we hold our own.

translation: And when they measure for them or weigh for them, they cause loss.
interpretation: This verse exposes a profound moral hypocrisy rooted in greed and self-interest: those who cheat others in trade represent a broader human tendency to apply double standards — demanding full measure for oneself while deliberately shortchanging others. The verse calls us to recognize that true integrity lies in treating others with the same fairness and completeness we desire for ourselves, and that any deviation from this principle is not merely an economic crime but a spiritual one, reflecting a heart that prioritizes personal gain over justice and divine accountability.

translation: Do they not think that they will be resurrected?
interpretation: This verse serves as a profound rhetorical rebuke, challenging those who deny accountability to reflect on the logical and moral consequences of their disbelief. The use of the interrogative form is not merely a question but an expression of astonishment that any rational being could live in heedlessness of the inevitable resurrection and divine reckoning. It implies that belief in resurrection is not only a religious obligation but a natural conclusion that sound reason and conscience should arrive at, and that denial of it reflects a deliberate turning away from truth rather than genuine intellectual uncertainty.

translation: For a Great Day
interpretation: This phrase serves as a divine warning, reminding humanity that all actions in this worldly life carry weight and consequence, as they will be accounted for on the Day of Judgment. It instills a sense of spiritual urgency and accountability, encouraging believers to remain conscious of their deeds and to align their lives with righteousness, knowing that a momentous reckoning awaits every soul.

translation: The Day when mankind will stand before the Lord of all the worlds.
interpretation: This verse serves as a profound reminder of ultimate accountability. Every human being, regardless of their status, wealth, or power in this life, will one day stand in complete humility and equality before their Creator. It strips away all illusions of worldly superiority and invites the reader to reflect on how they are living their life now, knowing that such a momentous standing awaits them. It is a call to conscious living, urging one to align their actions with what will matter most on that inevitable Day.

translation: No indeed! The record of the wicked is in Sijjeen.
interpretation: This verse serves as a stern divine warning, emphasizing that the deeds of the wicked are permanently and irrevocably inscribed in a lowly, confined register — Sijjeen — symbolizing that those who persist in sin and corruption have sealed their own fate. The use of 'Kalla' (No indeed!) is a rebuke, suggesting that the sinful wrongly believe they can escape accountability. The metaphor of a confined, sunken record reflects the spiritual descent of those who choose transgression, as their actions bind them to the lowest of destinations, both in this life and the next.

translation: And what will make you know what Sijjeen is?
interpretation: This rhetorical question is a divine emphasis on the incomprehensible nature of Sijjeen — the lowest register where the deeds and souls of the wicked are confined. Allah addresses the Prophet, and through him all of humanity, to convey that the reality of this place transcends ordinary human understanding. The use of this question is not an admission of ignorance, but rather a dramatic device to magnify the gravity and weight of what awaits those who deny truth and persist in wrongdoing. It is a call to reflect deeply on the consequences of one's choices before the final reckoning arrives.

translation: A written book (record).
interpretation: This phrase alludes to the idea that all human deeds, whether righteous or wicked, are meticulously and permanently recorded in a divine ledger, emphasizing that nothing escapes divine awareness and that every soul will be held accountable for what has been inscribed against its name on the Day of Judgment.

translation: Woe on that Day to the deniers!
interpretation: This verse serves as a powerful divine warning, emphasizing the severe consequences awaiting those who persistently reject the truth brought by the prophets. The repetition of this phrase throughout Surah Al-Mursalat functions as a rhythmic, solemn refrain that forces the human conscience to confront its own accountability. The word 'woe' (ويل) is not merely an expression of grief, but a declaration of divine justice, reminding us that denial of truth is not a passive act but an active moral failure that carries ultimate consequence. It calls the reader to honest self-reflection: are we among those who acknowledge the signs of God, or do we turn away from them?

translation: Those who deny the Day of Judgement
interpretation: This verse serves as a profound warning about the spiritual danger of rejecting accountability. When a person denies the reality of the Day of Judgement, they sever the moral compass that connects their actions to divine consequence. This denial is not merely an intellectual position, but a spiritual disease that leads to moral corruption, as one who believes there is no ultimate reckoning feels free to oppress, transgress, and indulge without restraint. The denial of the Day of Judgement is therefore the root of much evil in the world, as it removes the sense of divine responsibility that keeps the human soul aligned with righteousness and justice.

translation: And none deny it except every transgressor and sinner.
interpretation: This verse highlights a profound spiritual truth: that denial of divine truth is not merely an intellectual position, but a moral and ethical one. It is those who have already chosen a path of transgression and sin who are predisposed to reject the signs of God, because acknowledging them would require accountability and change. The rejection of truth is thus presented as a symptom of a corrupt inner state, suggesting that the heart's condition directly influences one's capacity to receive and accept guidance.

translation: When Our verses are recited to him, he says: 'These are legends of the ancients!'
interpretation: This verse reveals the timeless strategy of those who resist divine truth — not through reasoned argument or genuine inquiry, but through casual dismissal. By labeling the revelations as mere ancient myths and folklore, the arrogant soul seeks to deflate their sacred authority without engaging with their substance. The verse serves as a warning that the greatest obstacle to guidance is not ignorance, but the pride that causes a person to mock what they have not honestly considered, reducing eternal truth to mere human storytelling in order to justify their own refusal to submit.

translation: No! Rather, the stain has covered their hearts of that which they were earning.
interpretation: This verse points to the spiritual consequence of persistent sinful behavior. Every act of disobedience, when left unrepented, leaves a mark upon the heart. Over time, these marks accumulate and harden into a veil — a 'ran' — that prevents the light of truth, guidance, and divine awareness from penetrating. It is a warning that the heart is not merely a physical organ but a spiritual receptor, and its capacity to receive divine guidance can be gradually diminished through one's own choices. The verse thus calls humanity to vigilance over their deeds, for it is not God who seals the heart, but the individual themselves, through the cumulative weight of what they earn by their own hands.

translation: No indeed! On that Day they will be veiled from their Lord.
interpretation: This verse carries a profound spiritual warning: the greatest punishment for the disbelievers and the wicked on the Day of Judgment will not merely be physical torment, but the deprivation of the sight and nearness of Allah. Just as they chose to veil their hearts from God's truth and presence in this worldly life, they will be veiled from Him in the next. This implies, by contrast, that the believers will be granted the supreme blessing of beholding their Lord — suggesting that divine proximity and vision is the highest reward, and its denial the most devastating loss a soul can endure.

translation: Then indeed, they will be burning in Hellfire.
interpretation: This verse serves as a stern divine warning that those who persist in wrongdoing and disbelief will inevitably face the consequences of their choices. The use of 'thumma' (then) implies a temporal certainty — that no matter how long worldly life may seem, the reckoning will come. The emphatic particles in the Arabic ('inna' and the lam of emphasis) reinforce that this is an absolute, unalterable truth, reminding humanity that accountability before God is not a possibility but a guaranteed reality, urging reflection and return to righteousness before it is too late.

translation: Then it will be said, 'This is what you used to deny.'
interpretation: This verse serves as a moment of ultimate reckoning, where the denial of divine truth in this life is confronted with its full reality in the next. It reflects the profound consequence of willful rejection — that the very thing one chose to dismiss as false becomes the inescapable truth standing before them. The statement is not merely informational but carries within it a tone of profound accountability, reminding us that our choices in this world to accept or reject the truth are never without consequence, and that the Day of Judgment will strip away all illusions, leaving only the reality of what was always true.

translation: No indeed! The record of the righteous is in 'Illiyyun.
interpretation: This verse serves as a divine reassurance and contrast to the fate of the wicked, affirming that those who live virtuously and righteously will be elevated in rank and dignity before God. The term 'Illiyyun, derived from the root meaning 'high' or 'exalted,' suggests that the deeds and souls of the righteous are not merely recorded but are raised to the highest celestial register, implying that righteousness is never lost or diminished in God's sight but is eternally honored and preserved in the most exalted of stations. The verse thus invites the believer to aspire toward moral and spiritual elevation, knowing that every act of goodness ascends to God and is kept in a place of supreme honor.

translation: And what will make you know what 'Illiyyun is?
interpretation: This rhetorical question is used to emphasize the incomprehensible greatness and loftiness of 'Illiyyun — the highest register in which the deeds of the righteous are recorded. By posing the question in this way, Allah draws the reader's attention to the fact that human minds are incapable of fully grasping the honor and exaltation that awaits the righteous, suggesting that its reality transcends ordinary human comprehension and imagination.

translation: A written book (inscribed record).
interpretation: This phrase signifies that the divine record of human deeds is precise, permanent, and unalterable — written with absolute certainty and clarity. It serves as a reminder that nothing escapes the awareness of God, and that accountability is not merely a concept but a firmly established reality, sealed and preserved beyond any possibility of manipulation or denial.

translation: The near ones witness it.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the idea that the most elevated souls — the angels and the spiritually closest to God — are witnesses to divine truth and the recording of human deeds. It suggests that our actions do not go unnoticed, even if unseen by human eyes, implying a profound sense of accountability and the ever-present awareness of a higher realm observing our conduct.

translation: Indeed, the righteous will be in bliss.
interpretation: This verse serves as a divine promise and encouragement, affirming that those who live lives of virtue, integrity, and devotion to God will ultimately be rewarded with a state of complete joy and comfort in the Hereafter. It reassures the believer that righteous deeds are never lost or overlooked, and that the transient hardships of this world pale in comparison to the eternal bliss that awaits those who remain steadfast in goodness.

translation: On adorned couches, they will be gazing.
interpretation: This verse invites us to reflect on the ultimate reward of the righteous — not merely physical comfort, but the spiritual elevation of witnessing divine blessings from a place of honor and rest. The act of 'gazing' suggests a state of serene contemplation and gratitude, where the believers are granted the privilege of beholding the fruits of their faith and patience. It is a reminder that true repose belongs not to this world, but to the eternal realm where the soul finds its ultimate fulfillment in witnessing the mercy and generosity of Allah.

translation: You will recognize in their faces the radiance of bliss.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the idea that true inner joy and spiritual fulfillment inevitably manifest outwardly. The blessed in the hereafter will carry upon their faces an unmistakable luminosity — not merely physical beauty, but a glow born of divine contentment and eternal peace. It suggests that the soul's state is never fully hidden; just as suffering can etch itself into one's countenance, so too does proximity to God's grace illuminate the face in a way that requires no words. It is a reminder that the rewards of righteousness are not abstract, but deeply personal and visibly transformative.

translation: They will be given to drink of a pure wine, sealed.
interpretation: This verse invites the believer to persevere through the trials and deprivations of this world by painting a vivid picture of the exclusive and preserved reward awaiting the righteous in the Hereafter. The seal on the wine signifies that this divine gift has been kept untouched and protected solely for those who earned it through faith and good deeds, suggesting that true fulfillment and purity cannot be found in this worldly life but are being carefully held in trust by God for those who remain patient and steadfast.

translation: Its seal will be of musk. So for this let the competitors compete.
interpretation: This verse invites humanity to redirect its ambitions and rivalries toward what truly matters — the pursuit of the divine pleasure and the eternal reward of the hereafter. Just as people fiercely compete for worldly gains, status, and possessions, they are here urged to channel that same competitive energy and drive toward righteous deeds and spiritual excellence. The image of musk as a seal suggests that the ultimate reward is not only pure and precious, but that its very end and conclusion carries sweetness — a profound contrast to worldly pursuits whose endings often bring bitterness and regret. True and worthy competition, the verse implies, is not over the fleeting treasures of this world, but over the eternal and ever-fragrant bliss of the next.

translation: And its mixture is of Tasneem
interpretation: This verse elevates the status of the drink given to the righteous in paradise by attributing it to Tasneem, described elsewhere as the highest spring in paradise. The use of the word 'mixture' suggests that even the most exalted of heavenly springs is blended into the drink of the righteous, indicating that God's generosity to the believers is without limit, granting them access to the most sublime and pure of divine gifts. It speaks to the idea that the reward of the faithful is not merely sufficient, but overflowing with the finest that paradise has to offer, a reflection of God's boundless grace toward those who lived righteously in this world.

translation: A spring from which those brought near [to Allah] will drink.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the spiritual hierarchy of those closest to Allah, suggesting that proximity to the Divine is not merely a passive state but an active, living experience — symbolized by drinking from a living spring. The image of a flowing spring implies that nearness to Allah is not static but continuously nourishing, suggesting that the greatest reward for the righteous is not a distant, abstract paradise, but an intimate, ever-renewing closeness to the Divine presence itself.

translation: Indeed, those who committed crimes used to laugh at those who believed.
interpretation: This verse serves as a powerful reminder that worldly ridicule and social mockery directed at the faithful are not signs of truth or superiority, but rather indicators of moral corruption in those who mock. The laughter of the wicked at the believers reflects their spiritual blindness and arrogance, and implies that the ultimate reversal of fortunes in the Hereafter will render their mockery not only meaningless but a source of their own humiliation. Believers are thus encouraged to remain steadfast and undeterred by the scorn of others, trusting that their commitment to faith will be vindicated in the end.

translation: And when they passed by them, they would wink at one another.
interpretation: This verse highlights the arrogance and moral corruption of those who mock the believers. The act of winking or nudging one another in ridicule represents a deeper spiritual disease — the inability to recognize truth and virtue in others due to pride and contempt. It serves as a warning that such behavior is not merely a social failing, but a sign of a heart hardened against righteousness, and that those who indulge in mockery of the faithful will ultimately face accountability for their scorn.

translation: And when they return to their people, they return joyful.
interpretation: This verse exposes the moral hollowness of the hypocrites and mockers, revealing that their laughter and joy upon returning to their own kind is not a sign of genuine happiness or virtue, but rather a reflection of their spiritual blindness. Their amusement is rooted in arrogance and the false sense of superiority they feel over the believers, and this very joy becomes an indictment against them, for it shows how deeply their hearts have become hardened and disconnected from truth and accountability.

translation: And when they see them, they say, 'Indeed, these are truly misguided.'
interpretation: This verse captures the arrogance of the disbelievers who mock the believers in this worldly life, considering them foolish for abandoning worldly pleasures and social status in pursuit of faith. It serves as a reminder that the judgment of people is not the judgment of God — those who are mocked and marginalized for their faith may in truth be the ones who are rightly guided, while those who mock them are blind to their own spiritual misguidance. The verse invites the believer to remain firm in conviction, undisturbed by the ridicule of those whose measure of success is rooted in the dunya rather than in the sight of Allah.

translation: And they were not sent as guardians over them.
interpretation: This verse reminds believers that their role is not to police or force others into righteousness. Each soul is accountable only for itself, and the duty of the believer is to convey the message with sincerity and wisdom — not to coerce, control, or judge others. True faith cannot be imposed; it must be freely embraced, and God alone is the ultimate Guardian and Judge over all souls.

translation: So today those who believed are laughing at the disbelievers.
interpretation: This verse illustrates the divine principle of cosmic justice and the ultimate reversal of fortunes in the Hereafter. In this worldly life, the believers were often mocked, ridiculed, and scorned by the disbelievers for their faith and devotion. But on the Day of Judgment, the tables are turned completely. The laughter of the believers here is not one of cruelty or vengeance, but rather a manifestation of the ultimate vindication of truth. It serves as a powerful reminder that the judgment of this world is temporary and fleeting, while the judgment of Allah is eternal and absolute. Those who placed their trust in Allah will be honored, and those who mocked the truth will come to realize the gravity of their denial. The verse invites believers to remain steadfast in the face of ridicule, knowing that ultimate justice belongs to Allah alone.

translation: On thrones, they will be looking on.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the elevated station and restful repose granted to the righteous in Paradise. The image of reclining on thrones while gazing outward suggests not merely physical comfort, but a state of sovereign dignity and serene contemplation. The believers, having endured the trials of the worldly life, are now positioned as honored observers — perhaps witnessing the full scope of divine justice being realized, or beholding the beauty of Paradise spread before them. Their elevated position is a reflection of their elevated spiritual rank, and their gaze is one of peace, certainty, and gratitude rather than anxiety or longing.

translation: Is the reward of the disbelievers anything but what they used to do?
interpretation: This verse serves as a rhetorical warning, emphasizing the principle of divine justice: that every soul will be held accountable for its own deeds. The consequence that awaits those who reject faith is not an arbitrary punishment, but rather a direct reflection of their own choices and actions in this world. It reminds humanity that we are ultimately the architects of our own fate, and that turning away from truth and righteousness carries inevitable consequences — the reward one receives in the Hereafter is nothing more than the fruit of what one has sown in this life.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. When the sky is split asunder.
interpretation: This verse opens Surah Al-Inshiqaq and serves as a powerful eschatological warning. The splitting of the sky is presented as an inevitable cosmic event that signals the arrival of the Day of Judgment. By beginning with this dramatic image, God draws the human soul's attention to the fragility and temporality of the physical universe, reminding us that the seemingly permanent and vast heavens are subject to His will and command. The verse invites deep reflection on our own mortality and accountability, urging us to consider how we are preparing for the moment when the very fabric of creation will be torn apart and all will stand before their Lord.

translation: And it has listened to its Lord and was right to do so.
interpretation: This verse speaks of the sky's complete and willing submission to Allah. The deeper meaning here is that true submission to the Divine is not merely an act of obedience, but a natural and fitting response of all creation to its Creator. Just as the sky fulfills its purpose by surrendering entirely to Allah's command, human beings are reminded that their truest and most rightful state is one of conscious, willing surrender to God. The verse implies that submission to the Divine is not a burden but rather the most natural and correct state of existence for all things, and that resistance to this submission is what is unnatural.

translation: And when the earth is stretched out
interpretation: This verse invites us to contemplate the radical transformation that will occur on the Day of Judgment, when the familiar, mountainous, and uneven earth we know will be flattened and expanded infinitely. It serves as a reminder that nothing in this physical world is permanent or immovable, and that the very ground beneath our feet — which we take for granted as a source of stability — is entirely subject to the will of God. Our attachment to earthly things should therefore be loosened, as all that seems solid and enduring will ultimately be reshaped at His command.

translation: And it will cast out what is within it and become empty
interpretation: This verse speaks to the absolute surrender and submission of the earth to its Creator on the Day of Resurrection. Just as a vessel willingly empties itself, the earth will have no choice but to yield everything it has held within it — the dead, the secrets, and all that was concealed. It is a powerful reminder that nothing in this universe can withhold itself from the command of Allah, and that all things, animate or inanimate, are ultimately in complete obedience to Him.

translation: And it has listened to its Lord and was right to do so.
interpretation: This verse, referring to the sky on the Day of Judgment, reminds us that all of creation is fundamentally obedient to Allah. It invites us to reflect on how the heavens, without hesitation or resistance, submit completely to the will of their Creator. The verse serves as a powerful admonition to human beings: if the vast sky, in all its grandeur, willingly yields to its Lord, how much more should we — who have been gifted with reason, revelation, and free will — choose to submit ourselves to Allah's command? True and complete submission is not only natural but is the most fitting and correct response to divine authority.

translation: O mankind, indeed you are laboring toward your Lord with [great] exertion and will meet Him.
interpretation: This verse reminds us that the entirety of human life is not a leisurely stroll but a profound, effortful journey directed toward God. Every moment of struggle, hardship, joy, and striving is not random or purposeless — it is directional. We are all, whether we realize it or not, moving toward a divine encounter. The verse calls us to become conscious of this trajectory, so that we may align our efforts with intention and awareness. Life's toils and labors are not obstacles to meaning; they are the very path of return to our Creator. The inevitable meeting with God, described here not as a threat but as a fact, should inspire both mindfulness in how we live and hope in where we are headed.

translation: As for he who is given his record in his right hand,
interpretation: The right hand in this verse symbolizes honor, success, and divine favor. Receiving one's book of deeds in the right hand is a sign of salvation and acceptance before God. This imagery invites the believer to reflect on their daily actions and choices, reminding them that every deed is being recorded and that the ultimate measure of a life well-lived is not worldly success, but moral and spiritual accountability before the Creator.

translation: So he will be given an easy reckoning (account).
interpretation: This verse offers profound hope and reassurance to the believer, suggesting that God's mercy can transform the terrifying prospect of divine judgment into a gentle, gracious review. It implies that sincere faith and righteous deeds do not merely earn reward, but fundamentally alter the nature of one's encounter with God on the Day of Judgment — turning what could be a moment of severe scrutiny into one of divine tenderness and ease.

translation: And he will return to his family in happiness.
interpretation: This verse points to the profound spiritual truth that righteous deeds performed sincerely in this life will ultimately lead to a state of pure joy and reunion. The happiness described here is not merely emotional contentment, but a deep, transcendent fulfillment that comes from having lived a life aligned with divine purpose. It suggests that the soul's ultimate destiny, when it has walked the path of righteousness, is one of celebration and belonging — a homecoming in the truest and most complete sense.

translation: And as for he who is given his record behind his back,
interpretation: This verse speaks to the condition of the sinful soul on the Day of Judgment, where receiving one's book of deeds behind the back symbolizes shame, concealment, and the desperate wish to hide from one's own deeds. Unlike the righteous who receive their records in their right hands with joy and pride, the wicked are given theirs in a manner that reflects their spiritual blindness and willful turning away from truth during their earthly lives — just as they turned their backs on God's guidance, so too are their records handed to them from behind.

translation: He will call out for destruction.
interpretation: This verse serves as a stark warning about the overwhelming regret and despair that will consume the wicked on the Day of Judgment. When a person is handed their record of deeds in their left hand, their sins will be so apparent and their fate so horrifying that they will wish for their own annihilation, crying out for total destruction as an escape from the unbearable consequences of their worldly choices. It reminds us that the actions we commit in this life carry eternal weight, and that the desire for non-existence will be the ultimate expression of regret for those who rejected guidance.

translation: And he will burn in a Blazing Fire.
interpretation: This verse serves as a stark warning about the consequences of arrogance and rejection of truth. The imagery of burning in a blazing fire is not merely a physical punishment, but a reflection of the spiritual state of one who has allowed pride and denial to consume their soul in this life. Just as fire destroys what it touches, the rejection of divine guidance ultimately destroys one's inner being, and the punishment in the Hereafter is a manifestation of that self-inflicted spiritual ruin.

translation: Indeed, he used to be among his people very joyful.
interpretation: This verse serves as a cautionary reflection on the nature of worldly happiness and heedlessness. The joy described here is not inherently sinful, but it points to a person who was so absorbed in the pleasures and comforts of his family and social life that he became negligent of his spiritual responsibilities and his accountability before God. It is a reminder that excessive attachment to worldly ease and the comfort of one's social circle can blind a person to the deeper purpose of existence, leading to a reckoning in the Hereafter for a life lived without gratitude, humility, or devotion to the Divine.

translation: Indeed, he thought that he would never return.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the fundamental human tendency toward heedlessness and denial of accountability. The arrogant disbeliever, intoxicated by the pleasures and distractions of worldly life, convinces himself that there is no resurrection and no return to God. This self-deception is not merely intellectual doubt, but a willful rejection rooted in the desire to live without moral consequence. The verse serves as a warning that such presumption is itself a form of spiritual blindness, and that the certainty of return to God remains unchanged regardless of what one chooses to believe.

translation: Yes indeed! Surely his Lord was ever Seeing of him.
interpretation: This verse serves as a divine reassurance that no deed, whether righteous or sinful, goes unnoticed by Allah. It reminds us that God's all-encompassing sight is not merely a form of surveillance, but an expression of His intimate awareness of every soul's inner state, struggles, and intentions. The believer should find comfort in knowing that their sincere efforts are fully witnessed by Allah, while the wrongdoer should be sobered by the reality that no act of injustice is ever hidden from the One who sees all things.

translation: So I swear by the twilight glow
interpretation: Allah's oath by the twilight — that fleeting boundary between day and night — draws our attention to the profound significance of transitions and the signs embedded within the natural world. Just as the twilight is a threshold moment that cannot be held or reversed, our lives too are transient passages. The swearing by such a phenomenon invites us to reflect on the certainty of what follows the oath, urging us to recognize that the temporal beauty of this world is a testament to divine power and a reminder of our inevitable return to our Creator.

translation: By the night and what it envelops
interpretation: This verse is an oath sworn by Allah upon the night and all that it gathers and conceals within its darkness. The night, with its capacity to envelop all living creatures and draw them into rest, stillness, and vulnerability, serves as a reminder of Allah's power over cycles of existence. It points to the hidden dimensions of reality that lie beyond human perception, urging reflection on the forces that operate unseen, and calling humanity to recognize that just as the night inevitably envelops all things, so too does divine authority encompass all of creation without exception.

translation: And the moon when it becomes full
interpretation: This verse is an oath by the full moon, signifying that just as the moon reaches its complete and perfect state after a gradual process of growth, so too does the journey of the human soul toward its Lord follow a natural and divinely ordained progression. The fullness of the moon serves as a cosmic sign pointing to the certainty of completion and the fulfillment of God's promise regarding the resurrection and return of all souls to their Creator.

translation: You will surely pass through stage after stage.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the inevitable progression of the human soul through successive states of existence — from this worldly life, to death, to the grave, to resurrection, and ultimately to divine judgment. It is a reminder that no human being can escape this ordained journey, and that each stage brings one closer to standing before Allah. The verse calls humanity to awareness and accountability, urging people not to be deceived by the comfort of any single stage, for transformation and transition are the very nature of human existence.

translation: So what is wrong with them that they do not believe?
interpretation: This verse is a rhetorical rebuke directed at those who persistently reject faith despite being presented with clear signs and evidence. It reflects divine astonishment at human stubbornness, implying that there is no rational or justifiable excuse for disbelief when the truth has been made so plainly manifest. It serves as an invitation to self-reflection, urging people to examine their own resistance to faith and consider why they continue to turn away from what is evident.

translation: And when the Quran is recited to them, they do not prostrate.
interpretation: This verse exposes the arrogance of those who refuse to humble themselves before the divine word. True prostration is not merely a physical act but an expression of the soul's surrender to truth. The refusal to prostrate when the Quran is recited symbolizes a deeper spiritual disease — the hardening of the heart against guidance. It is a warning that intellectual exposure to divine revelation is not sufficient; what matters is whether the heart yields, submits, and is transformed by what it hears.
