The greatest veil between a person and God is not ignorance, but pride.

translation: But it is the disbelievers who deny.
interpretation: This verse points to the fundamental nature of disbelief as being rooted not in a lack of evidence or rational argument, but in a willful rejection of truth. The denial of the disbelievers is an active and deliberate act, suggesting that the problem lies not in the message itself, which is clear and consistent, but in the disposition of those who refuse to receive it. It is a reminder that guidance cannot be forced upon those who choose to close their hearts.

translation: And Allah is most knowing of what they conceal.
interpretation: This verse serves as a profound reminder that no secret of the heart or hidden intention escapes the knowledge of Allah. Human beings may conceal their true motives, doubts, and moral corruption behind outward appearances and words, but the Divine encompasses all that is stored within the chest. This should instill in the believer a constant awareness — a state of muraqabah — that sincerity must govern not only one's actions but the innermost chambers of one's soul, for it is ultimately before Allah that the full reality of a person's inner life will be laid bare.

translation: So give them tidings of a painful punishment.
interpretation: This verse employs the rhetorical device of bitter irony, using the word 'glad tidings' (بشرى), which is normally associated with joyful news, to announce a severe punishment. This contrast serves as a sharp rebuke to those who reject faith and hoard wealth without regard for others, highlighting the gravity of their actions by inverting the very language of joy and hope into one of warning and consequence. It is a divine reminder that the same certainty with which believers receive good news of reward, the transgressors will receive news of their retribution.

translation: Except those who believe and do righteous deeds; for them is a reward uninterrupted.
interpretation: This verse serves as a profound exception to the general state of human loss or decline, emphasizing that true fulfillment and an eternal, unceasing reward are attained only through the combination of sincere faith and righteous action. The pairing of belief with good deeds highlights that faith alone, without being manifested in conduct, is incomplete — and equally, deeds without the foundation of faith lack their ultimate spiritual worth. The promise of a reward that is 'uninterrupted' or 'without end' signals that such a person transcends the temporal limitations of worldly existence, entering into a state of perpetual divine grace that no worldly measure can diminish or cut short.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. By the sky containing great stars (constellations).
interpretation: God swears an oath by the vast, ordered heavens adorned with constellations, drawing our attention to the magnificent architecture of the cosmos as a testament to His power and precision. This oath invites us to reflect on the grandeur of creation as evidence of a Creator who governs all things with deliberate design, reminding us that the same divine authority that orders the heavens also governs human affairs and will hold all people accountable for their deeds.

translation: And the promised Day
interpretation: This verse refers to the Day of Judgment, a day that has been foretold and guaranteed by Allah. The use of the word 'promised' emphasizes the absolute certainty of its occurrence, reminding humanity that no matter how distant it may seem, it will inevitably come to pass. It serves as a call to accountability, urging believers to prepare themselves through righteous deeds, as they will stand before their Creator on a day that cannot be avoided or delayed.

translation: By the witness and the witnessed
interpretation: This oath invokes the dynamic relationship between that which observes and that which is observed, suggesting that the entirety of existence — both the perceiving and the perceived — stands as testimony to the absolute truth and justice of God. Nothing in creation escapes being either a witness or a subject of witnessing, implying that all of reality is held accountable within a divine framework of cosmic awareness.

translation: Cursed were the companions of the trench
interpretation: This verse invokes divine condemnation upon those who persecute the believers, reminding us that no act of oppression against the righteous goes unnoticed by Allah. The use of the passive curse form signals that such people have placed themselves outside the bounds of divine mercy through their own choices, and that ultimate justice — even when delayed in this world — is inevitable and absolute in the sight of God.

translation: The Fire with its fuel
interpretation: This verse alludes to the inescapable and self-sustaining nature of divine punishment. The emphasis on fuel suggests that the torment of the Hellfire is not arbitrary or fleeting, but rather a consequence that is continuously fed and maintained by the very deeds and disbelief of those who rejected the truth. It serves as a warning that wrongdoing carries its own consequence, stoking the flames of accountability that cannot be extinguished.

translation: When they were sitting over it (the pit of fire).
interpretation: This verse captures a moment of moral indictment, highlighting the callousness and cruelty of the oppressors who not only persecuted the believers but sat and watched their suffering without remorse. It serves as a reminder that passive witnessing of injustice, especially when done with satisfaction or indifference, is itself a grave sin deserving of divine accountability.

translation: And they were witnesses to what they were doing to the believers.
interpretation: This verse highlights the moral and spiritual blindness of the oppressors — not only did they commit heinous acts against the believers, but they did so openly, without shame or remorse, watching their own cruelty unfold before them. Their witnessing of their own deeds intensifies their guilt, as their persecution was not carried out in ignorance or secrecy, but with full awareness and deliberate intent. This serves as a powerful indictment: their presence as witnesses to their own wrongdoing removes any possibility of excuse on the Day of Judgment, and underscores the depth of their moral corruption.

translation: And they resented them for no reason except that they believed in Allah, the Almighty, the Praiseworthy.
interpretation: This verse highlights the profound injustice of religious persecution, revealing that the sole crime of the believers in the eyes of their oppressors was their faith in God. It serves as a timeless reminder that true faith may provoke hostility from those who reject it, and that the believer's steadfastness in holding to that faith — even under persecution — is itself an act of profound moral courage. The verse implicitly dignifies the suffering of the oppressed by affirming that their only 'fault' was the most noble of qualities: sincere belief in the All-Powerful and All-Praiseworthy God.

translation: He to Whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. And Allah is, over all things, Witness.
interpretation: This verse calls us to cultivate a profound awareness of divine omnipresence. The pairing of absolute sovereignty with absolute witnessing is not merely a theological statement, but an invitation to live with complete moral consciousness. Since Allah's dominion is total and His witnessing is perpetual, no human action, thought, or intention falls outside His awareness. This should inspire not fear alone, but a sense of accountability that elevates every mundane act into a spiritually meaningful one, reminding the believer that their entire existence unfolds under the watchful presence of the One who owns all of creation.

translation: Indeed, those who have tortured the believing men and believing women and then have not repented will have the punishment of Hell, and they will have the punishment of the Burning Fire.
interpretation: This verse serves as a solemn divine warning that those who persecute and oppress the faithful — whether through physical, psychological, or social harm — bear a profound moral responsibility before God. The emphasis on the absence of repentance reveals that God's mercy remains open even to oppressors, but those who choose to persist in their cruelty without seeking forgiveness will face a dual and intensified punishment. The repetition of punishment — both Hell and the Burning Fire — underscores that the severity of the consequence mirrors the gravity of deliberately harming those who have chosen faith, suggesting that the persecution of the innocent is among the gravest of transgressions in the sight of God.

translation: Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds will have gardens beneath which rivers flow. That is the great attainment.
interpretation: This verse invites us to understand that true success in this world is not measured by wealth, power, or status, but rather by the quality of one's faith and deeds. The image of gardens with flowing rivers represents not merely a physical reward, but the ultimate fulfillment of the human soul — a state of perpetual peace, beauty, and divine nearness. The phrase 'great attainment' challenges us to reconsider what we truly strive for in our lives, urging us to redirect our ambitions from the fleeting pleasures of this world toward an investment in our inner character and our relationship with the Divine. It is a reminder that every righteous act, no matter how small, is a seed planted for an eternal harvest.

translation: Indeed, the seizure of your Lord is severe.
interpretation: This verse serves as a profound warning about the overwhelming and absolute power of God's retribution. It reminds us that no matter how mighty or arrogant a person or civilization may become, they remain utterly powerless before divine justice. The verse invites deep humility and moral accountability, urging believers to reflect on the consequences of transgression and to never mistake God's patience for weakness or indifference.

translation: Indeed, it is He who originates and repeats.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the absolute and exclusive creative power of Allah, emphasizing that the cycle of creation and recreation — of life and death, of beginning and return — belongs solely to Him. It is a profound reminder that just as Allah initiated creation from nothing, He is equally capable of restoring and resurrecting it, which serves as both a proof of the resurrection and a call for humanity to place its trust and dependence entirely in the One who holds the beginning and the end of all existence.

translation: And He is the Forgiving, the Loving.
interpretation: This verse invites the believer to understand that divine forgiveness is not merely a cold legal pardon, but is inseparably bound to profound love. God's forgiveness flows not from indifference to sin, but from an intimate affection for His creation. The believer is thus encouraged not to approach God with mere fear of punishment, but with a heart open to a relationship of love and warmth, trusting that repentance will always be met with both mercy and genuine divine tenderness.

translation: [He is] the Possessor of the Glorious Throne.
interpretation: This verse draws our attention to the infinite majesty and sovereignty of Allah, reminding us that His authority and grandeur transcend all human comprehension. The 'Throne' here is not merely a physical seat of power, but a symbol of ultimate dominion over all creation. By describing it as 'Glorious,' we are invited to reflect on the fact that everything connected to Allah partakes in His glory — His rule is not one of tyranny or limitation, but one of boundless magnificence and perfection. Meditating on this attribute should inspire in the believer a profound sense of humility, awe, and trust, knowing that they are under the care of a Lord whose power and glory are without equal or end.

translation: He does whatever He wills.
interpretation: This verse points to the absolute and unrestricted sovereignty of Allah. Unlike creation, whose actions are bound by limitations, external forces, and consequences, Allah acts with complete freedom and perfect wisdom. His will is not subject to any higher authority, nor can any force prevent its fulfillment. This is not a statement of arbitrary power, but rather an affirmation that every action of Allah flows from His infinite knowledge and wisdom — meaning that whatever He wills is inherently just, purposeful, and perfect, even if human understanding cannot always perceive the wisdom behind it.

translation: Has there come to you the story of the soldiers?
interpretation: This verse serves as a rhetorical divine address to the Prophet Muhammad, drawing his attention to a profound narrative about to be revealed. The question is not one of ignorance but of emphasis, inviting deep reflection and anticipation. It implies that what follows carries immense weight and significance, reminding the believer that history is filled with lessons about those who opposed truth, and that God is fully aware of all events past, present, and future. The verse invites the listener to pause and prepare their heart for a lesson of great consequence.

translation: Pharaoh and Thamud
interpretation: This brief but powerful pairing serves as a stark reminder that arrogance and the rejection of divine guidance are not isolated events in history, but a recurring pattern among the powerful. By invoking these two civilizations together, the Qur'an draws attention to the universal law that no degree of worldly power, whether political like Pharaoh's or material like Thamud's, can shield a people from divine consequence when they willfully persist in oppression and denial of truth.

translation: But those who disbelieve are in denial.
interpretation: This verse points to the spiritual obstinacy that lies at the heart of disbelief. It is not merely an intellectual rejection of truth, but a deliberate and persistent state of denial. The use of the present continuous form suggests that this denial is not a single act but an ongoing condition — a hardening of the heart that becomes a defining characteristic of those who refuse to open themselves to divine guidance. The verse invites us to reflect on how pride, habit, and attachment to worldly certainties can trap a person in a cycle of rejection, making them unable or unwilling to receive truth even when it stands clearly before them.

translation: And Allah encompasses them from behind.
interpretation: This verse reminds us that no matter how powerful or cunning those who deny the truth may appear, they can never escape the absolute knowledge and authority of Allah. His encompassing presence means that all human plans, deceptions, and machinations ultimately fall within His divine grasp. It serves as a source of comfort for believers, assuring them that justice is never beyond reach, and a warning to those who oppose truth, reminding them that they are never beyond accountability.

translation: Rather, it is a Glorious Quran
interpretation: This verse serves as a divine rebuttal to those who doubt or dismiss the Quran. The use of 'Rather' signals a correction of false assumptions, asserting that what skeptics may belittle or reject is in fact nothing less than a scripture of immense majesty and honor. The attribute 'Glorious' elevates the Quran beyond human literary achievement, reminding believers that its worth is not diminished by the denial of the heedless, and that its grandeur stands independent of human recognition or acceptance.

translation: In a Preserved Tablet
interpretation: This verse points to the eternal and inviolable nature of divine knowledge and revelation. The Preserved Tablet symbolizes the absolute certainty and permanence of God's will and decree — nothing within it can be altered, corrupted, or lost. It reminds humanity that the Qur'an is not a product of human history or circumstance, but originates from a transcendent source beyond time and space, affirming that truth itself is ultimately protected by its very nature as divine.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. By the sky and the night-comer (Al-Tariq).
interpretation: God swears an oath by two magnificent creations — the vast expanse of the sky and the piercing star that appears in the darkness of night — to draw our attention to the profound truth that is about to be revealed. This oath invites us to reflect on the grandeur and order of the cosmos as evidence of divine power and intentionality. Just as the star penetrates the darkness with its sharp, unwavering light, the revelation itself pierces through the darkness of ignorance and heedlessness. The oath reminds us that nothing in creation is random or purposeless; every element of the universe operates under God's precise and watchful command, and humanity would do well to ponder these signs as a gateway to deeper faith and awareness.

translation: And what will make you know what the Nightly Visitor is?
interpretation: This rhetorical question is a divine technique used to elevate the listener's curiosity and attention, signaling that what follows transcends ordinary human knowledge. It implies that the truth of this phenomenon — the piercing star — cannot be grasped through mere human perception or reasoning alone, and that its full significance is only known through divine revelation. It humbles the intellect before the vastness of God's creation.

translation: The Piercing Star
interpretation: This phrase refers to a star of intense brilliance that penetrates through the darkness of the night sky. Spiritually, it serves as a metaphor for divine truth and guidance that cuts through the darkness of ignorance and falsehood. Just as a piercing star cannot be hidden by the night, the light of divine revelation cannot be suppressed or obscured by human darkness or disbelief. It reminds the believer that God's signs are ever-present and illuminating, capable of reaching even the deepest shadows of doubt.

translation: There is no soul but that it has over it a protector.
interpretation: This verse reminds us that every human being is under constant divine surveillance and accountability. No action, thought, or intention goes unrecorded or unnoticed. The 'protector' or guardian referred to here are the angels appointed by Allah to watch over each soul and record its deeds. This serves as both a comfort and a warning — a comfort in that we are never truly alone, and a warning that our deeds carry eternal weight. It calls the believer to a state of continuous mindfulness and God-consciousness (taqwa), knowing that every moment of one's existence is being witnessed and preserved.

translation: So let man observe from what he was created.
interpretation: This verse is a divine invitation for human beings to engage in deep self-reflection and contemplation of their own origins. By pondering the humble and insignificant substance from which they were formed, humans are guided toward a recognition of their dependency on their Creator, which in turn should cultivate humility, gratitude, and an acknowledgment of Allah's supreme power. The act of looking inward at one's own creation becomes a pathway to knowing God, dismantling arrogance and reminding the human being that true greatness belongs only to the One who brought them into existence from nothing.

translation: Created from a fluid, ejected.
interpretation: This verse draws human attention to the humble and insignificant origin of mankind, reminding us that despite our pride and arrogance, we were brought into existence from a lowly fluid. It serves as a call to humility, urging human beings to recognize that their greatness is not self-derived but entirely dependent upon the creative power of Allah, and that no one who originates from such modest beginnings has any right to be arrogant or to deny their accountability before their Creator.

translation: He is created from a fluid, ejected, emerging from between the backbone and the ribs.
interpretation: This verse invites humanity to reflect deeply on the humble and precisely orchestrated origins of human life. By pointing to the specific biological source of the fluid of creation, the Qur'an draws attention to the magnificent precision of Allah's design, reminding the arrogant human being that their existence began in a state of utter dependency and biological fragility. The verse serves as a call to humility — that one who begins in such a lowly and intricate physical process has no basis for pride or ingratitude toward their Creator.

translation: Indeed, He is able to bring him back.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the absolute power of Allah over creation and death. It serves as a reminder to humanity that just as Allah created us from nothing, He is fully capable of resurrecting us after death. The verse challenges those who doubt the resurrection by pointing to the undeniable evidence of Allah's creative power, urging reflection on human origins as proof that returning to life after death is well within Allah's infinite capability.

translation: The Day when secrets will be put to trial (exposed).
interpretation: This verse reminds us that on the Day of Judgment, no inner reality can be concealed. It is not merely our outward actions that will be examined, but the deepest intentions, hidden thoughts, and true motivations of the heart. This serves as a profound call to sincerity — to align our inner world with our outer conduct — for ultimate accountability lies not in what we showed to others, but in what we truly harbored within ourselves before God.

translation: So he has no power nor any helper.
interpretation: This verse serves as a profound reminder of the absolute helplessness of the human being who turns away from Allah. No matter how much wealth, status, or influence one accumulates in this world, none of it will provide strength or assistance in the face of divine reckoning. It strips away the illusion of self-sufficiency and reminds us that true power belongs only to Allah, and that any sense of security we derive from worldly means or human alliances is ultimately fleeting and deceptive. The believer is thus called to place their trust solely in Allah, for He is the only true source of strength and support.

translation: By the sky which returns (rain)
interpretation: This verse is an oath by the heavens, drawing attention to the divine cycle of giving and returning. The sky's repeated sending down of rain symbolizes God's perpetual mercy and sustenance — a reminder that divine blessings are not a one-time gift but a continuous, rhythmic outpouring that sustains all life. Just as the sky never ceases to return with rain, God's providence never ceases to return to His creation, inviting reflection on the constancy and reliability of divine generosity.

translation: And the earth that splits open
interpretation: This verse draws attention to the miraculous nature of the earth's capacity to crack and split, allowing seeds to germinate and vegetation to emerge from within it. It serves as an oath, directing the listener to reflect on the divine power embedded in natural phenomena, inviting contemplation of how life itself bursts forth from apparent stillness — a metaphor for resurrection and the inevitability of divine judgment.

translation: Indeed, it is a decisive word.
interpretation: This verse affirms the absolute authority and finality of the Qur'an as a criterion that distinguishes truth from falsehood. It is not merely speech or poetry, but a divine declaration that cuts through ambiguity and settles all matters with clarity and certainty. The verse calls upon the listener to recognize that what has been revealed carries ultimate weight, and that no human discourse can rival or diminish its decisive nature.

translation: And it is not a jest (or joke).
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the absolute seriousness and gravity of the Qur'an. It is a divine reminder that the revelations of Allah are not to be taken lightly or dismissed as entertainment or triviality. The Qur'an carries ultimate truth and consequence, demanding sincere reflection, reverence, and action from those who receive it. To treat it casually is to misunderstand the weight of divine communication and the responsibility it places upon humanity.

translation: Indeed, they are plotting a plot.
interpretation: This verse serves as a divine reassurance to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) and the believers, reminding them that the schemes and conspiracies of the disbelievers, no matter how elaborate or determined, are ultimately futile against the will of Allah. It calls the believer to remain steadfast and unafraid, recognizing that human plotting can never overpower divine providence.

translation: And I will devise a plan.
interpretation: This verse reflects the absolute and irresistible nature of divine strategy. While humans may plot and scheme against the truth, Allah's plan supersedes all human machinations. It serves as a reminder that no matter how elaborate the schemes of those who oppose righteousness may be, the divine will ultimately prevails, and those who plot against the truth are ultimately undone by their own devices.

translation: So give respite to the disbelievers; give them respite for a while.
interpretation: This verse serves as a divine reassurance to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) and the believers that the apparent success and comfort of the disbelievers is only temporary. Allah commands patience, reminding us that His justice is never absent, only delayed. The repetition of the command to grant respite emphasizes that every soul shall ultimately face accountability, and that the brief pleasures of this world enjoyed by those who reject the truth are nothing but a fleeting prelude to a reckoning that is absolute and inevitable. It is a call for believers not to despair at the seeming triumph of falsehood, for the timeline of divine justice transcends human perception.

translation: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High.
interpretation: This opening verse of Surah Al-A'la calls upon the believer to engage in active, conscious glorification of Allah, emphasizing that true worship begins with the tongue and heart recognizing the absolute transcendence of the Divine. The command to glorify not merely Allah Himself, but His 'name,' points to the sanctity of language itself — that the very words we use to address the Creator carry a sacred weight and must be treated with reverence and mindfulness. It is a reminder that spirituality is not passive, but a deliberate, ongoing act of orienting oneself toward the Most High in every moment of existence.

translation: Who created and proportioned
interpretation: This verse invites deep reflection on the divine precision embedded in all of creation. It points to the fact that God's creative act is not random or chaotic, but is characterized by perfect harmony and balance. Everything that exists has been brought into being with exact measure and symmetry, suggesting that the universe operates according to a deliberate divine will. The believer is thus urged to look at the order within themselves and the world around them as a continuous sign of God's wisdom and intentionality, fostering a sense of awe and gratitude toward the Creator.

translation: And who destined and then guided.
interpretation: This verse points to the divine harmony between divine decree and divine guidance—that Allah does not merely set a course for creation and leave it adrift, but actively provides the means, instincts, and revelations necessary for every created thing to fulfill its purpose. It is a reminder that nothing in existence is abandoned to chaos; rather, every soul has been given both its nature and the path to its fulfillment, and that this pairing of destiny and guidance is itself a profound mercy.

translation: And who brought forth the pasture
interpretation: This verse invites deep reflection on the divine act of sustaining life through the Earth's vegetation. It points to the miraculous nature of growth itself — that from seemingly barren soil, nourishment emerges for all living creatures. The verse calls humanity to recognize that the ability to feed and sustain life does not ultimately rest in human hands, but is a gift granted by God alone. It is a reminder of our dependence on a power greater than ourselves, urging gratitude and humility in the face of creation's bounty.

translation: And He made it dark, blackened debris.
interpretation: This verse invites us to reflect on the transience of worldly life. Just as lush green pasture is reduced to withered, blackened stubble, all that appears vibrant and flourishing in this world is ultimately impermanent. The verse serves as a reminder that attachment to worldly beauty and prosperity is misplaced, urging the believer to orient their heart toward that which is eternal rather than that which inevitably fades and perishes.

translation: We will make you recite, so you will not forget.
interpretation: This verse is a divine promise and assurance to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) that the revelation of the Qur'an is entirely under Allah's control and preservation. It reassures the Prophet that he need not anxiously rush to memorize the verses as they were being revealed, as Allah Himself guarantees their retention in the Prophet's heart. This reflects the broader theme of divine support and care for the Prophet in his mission, reminding him — and by extension all believers — that true knowledge and its preservation ultimately come from Allah alone, and that human effort must be accompanied by trust and reliance upon Him.

translation: Except what Allah wills. Indeed, He knows what is declared and what is hidden.
interpretation: This verse reminds us of the absolute sovereignty of Allah over all knowledge and memory. The exception 'except what Allah wills' serves as a profound reminder that even the Prophet's ability to retain and recite revelation is contingent upon divine will. Nothing occurs outside of Allah's permission or knowledge. The deeper spiritual lesson here is one of humility — human faculties, no matter how elevated, are ultimately dependent on Allah. Furthermore, the emphasis that Allah knows both the manifest and the concealed invites the believer to cultivate inner sincerity, recognizing that no hidden intention, secret thought, or concealed deed escapes divine awareness. It is a call to align one's inner and outer state, knowing that Allah perceives the totality of existence beyond what any human can observe or comprehend.

translation: And We will ease you toward ease.
interpretation: This verse is a divine promise that Allah will facilitate the path of righteousness and good deeds for the one who strives in His way. It suggests that spiritual and moral ease is not achieved through human effort alone, but is ultimately a gift from Allah granted to those who are sincere in their intentions and actions. The believer is thus encouraged to take the first steps toward goodness, trusting that Allah will remove obstacles and make the journey progressively lighter.

translation: So remind, if the reminder should benefit.
interpretation: This verse teaches that the duty of the Prophet, and by extension all believers, is simply to convey the message and remind others of the truth. The responsibility lies in the sincere effort of reminding, not in guaranteeing the outcome. It acknowledges that human hearts vary in their receptiveness, and that guidance ultimately belongs to Allah alone. The believer is therefore relieved of the burden of results and is only accountable for making the effort to remind when there is hope of benefit.

translation: He who fears will be reminded.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the selective nature of divine guidance — that true spiritual benefit and remembrance of God's message is only received by those whose hearts are already softened by a sense of reverence and accountability before their Creator. Fear of God, here, is not mere terror but a deep, conscious awareness of one's responsibility to the Divine, and it is precisely this awareness that opens the heart to receive and act upon guidance. Without this inner disposition of humility and God-consciousness, even the clearest reminders will fail to take root in the soul.

translation: And the most wretched will avoid it
interpretation: This verse speaks to the tragic nature of willful spiritual blindness. The 'most wretched' is not simply someone who lacks guidance, but one who actively turns away from it. True wretchedness lies not in ignorance, but in the deliberate rejection of truth and goodness when they are made plain. This serves as a profound warning that the greatest loss a soul can suffer is not external misfortune, but the self-chosen abandonment of the path to purification and divine mercy.

translation: He who will enter the Great Fire
interpretation: This verse serves as a solemn warning that there are those who, through their rejection of truth, arrogance, and persistent wrongdoing, will face the ultimate and most severe consequence in the Hereafter. The use of the word 'Great' to describe the Fire emphasizes the magnitude of divine justice, reminding humanity that no act of denial or transgression goes unaccounted for, and that the choices made in this life carry eternal weight.

translation: Then he will neither die therein nor live.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the ultimate state of hopelessness and perpetual suffering for those condemned to Hellfire. True death would bring relief, and true life would offer the possibility of change or redemption — but the condemned are granted neither. This suspended state between death and life represents the complete absence of mercy and the total futility of existence for those who rejected faith, suggesting that genuine life is only possible through connection to God, and without it, one is left in a state that cannot even be dignified with the name of either life or death.

translation: He has certainly succeeded who purifies himself.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the fundamental Islamic principle that true success and salvation are not measured by worldly achievements, wealth, or status, but rather by the purification of one's soul. This purification — known as tazkiyah — encompasses both the outward act of giving charity (zakah) to cleanse one's wealth and attachment to material things, and the inward spiritual work of cleansing the heart from pride, envy, and sin. The verse invites the believer to understand that the path to ultimate flourishing lies in constant self-refinement, a lifelong striving to align one's inner state with divine guidance, suggesting that human beings have both the capacity and the responsibility to actively participate in their own spiritual elevation.

translation: And he remembered the name of his Lord and prayed.
interpretation: This verse points to the inseparable connection between the remembrance of Allah and the act of prayer. True prayer is not merely a physical ritual — it is born from a heart that is first alive with the consciousness of God. When the soul genuinely remembers its Lord, it is naturally drawn to stand before Him in worship. The verse thus teaches us that the quality and sincerity of our prayer depends entirely on the depth of our remembrance, urging believers to cultivate an inner awareness of Allah that gives rise to prayer as a natural and heartfelt response rather than an empty obligation.

translation: But you prefer the worldly life
interpretation: This verse serves as a profound rebuke to the human tendency to prioritize immediate, tangible pleasures over eternal spiritual realities. It reflects the deep psychological truth that humans, despite knowing the transience of this world, consistently choose comfort, wealth, and status in this life over the preparation for the hereafter. The verse challenges us to examine our priorities and recognize that this preference for the dunya is not merely a neutral choice, but a fundamental spiritual misordering that keeps the soul anchored to what is fleeting rather than what is everlasting.

translation: And the Hereafter is better and more enduring.
interpretation: This verse invites us to reexamine our priorities and the values we place on worldly life. It reminds us that our attachment to material gains, pleasures, and status in this world is misplaced when compared to what awaits in the eternal life. The transient nature of worldly existence should motivate the believer to invest in actions and virtues that carry weight in the Hereafter, rather than sacrificing eternal reward for fleeting satisfaction. It is a call to spiritual wisdom — to see beyond the immediate and visible, and to orient one's heart toward what is truly lasting.

translation: Indeed, this is in the former scriptures.
interpretation: This verse affirms the continuity and universality of divine guidance, reminding us that the core truths revealed in the Qur'an are not novel or unprecedented, but have been part of God's eternal message delivered to humanity through earlier prophets and their scriptures. It invites reflection on the timeless nature of divine wisdom and calls us to recognize the unity of all revealed religions at their source.

translation: The Scriptures of Abraham and Moses
interpretation: This brief yet profound reference invites the believer to recognize that divine revelation did not begin with the Qur'an, but is part of a continuous and unbroken chain of guidance that God has extended to humanity throughout history. By mentioning Abraham and Moses together, the verse affirms the universality of the divine message and calls upon us to appreciate that all prophets were entrusted with the same essential truth, submission to God alone. It is a reminder that the Qur'an stands as the final link in this sacred chain, confirming and completing what came before it.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Has there reached you the report of the Overwhelming Event?
interpretation: This opening verse of Surah Al-Ghashiyah uses a rhetorical question not to seek information, but to arrest the listener's attention and create a sense of gravity and urgency. By addressing the Prophet — and through him, all of humanity — with 'has it reached you?', God draws us into a state of heightened awareness, compelling us to lean in and reflect deeply on what is about to be disclosed. The term 'Al-Ghashiyah,' meaning the Overwhelming Event, refers to the Day of Resurrection, and its very name signals that what is coming will envelop and overpower all of creation without exception. The verse thus serves as a divine summons to conscious reflection, reminding us that no soul will be exempt from that day, and that we ought to prepare for it with full seriousness.

translation: Faces on that Day will be humbled.
interpretation: This verse evokes the ultimate equalizing power of the Day of Judgment, where all pride, arrogance, and worldly status are stripped away. The humbling of faces — the most expressive and identity-bearing part of a person — symbolizes the complete surrender of the human ego before the absolute sovereignty of God. It serves as a reminder that whatever dignity or power one may possess in this life is entirely temporary and borrowed, and that true accountability awaits every soul.

translation: Laboring, exhausted.
interpretation: This verse points to the spiritual consequences of those who exerted effort in worldly pursuits or even acts of worship without proper faith and sincerity. Their toil was immense, yet it yielded nothing of eternal value, illustrating that effort alone, disconnected from truth and divine guidance, leads only to weariness and loss in the Hereafter.

translation: She will burn in a blazing fire.
interpretation: This verse serves as a divine warning that those who oppose truth, spread hatred, and persecute the believers will face ultimate and inescapable divine justice. The intense heat of the fire symbolizes the proportional consequence of the burning harm such individuals cause in the world through their malice and cruelty.

translation: It will be watered from a boiling spring.
interpretation: This verse serves as a stark warning about the nature of divine justice. The image of being forced to drink from a violently boiling spring is not merely a description of physical torment, but a profound metaphor for the consequence of rejecting truth and mercy during one's lifetime. Just as those in this world were offered the cool, nourishing waters of divine guidance and chose to turn away, in the Hereafter they will be given the opposite — a source that destroys rather than sustains. It illustrates the principle that punishment in the afterlife mirrors, in a fitting and just manner, the spiritual choices made in this world.

translation: They will have no food except from a poisonous thorny plant (Dari').
interpretation: This verse serves as a stark warning about the consequences of rejecting faith and living a life of heedlessness. The deprivation of nourishing food and its replacement with a toxic, harmful plant symbolizes the spiritual emptiness that results from a life devoid of divine guidance. Just as the soul that rejects truth feeds on falsehood and illusion in this world, in the Hereafter that same soul will be sustained only by what mirrors its worldly choices — something utterly devoid of benefit and full of harm. The punishment is not arbitrary, but a reflection of the inner state the person cultivated during their lifetime.

translation: It neither nourishes nor satisfies hunger.
interpretation: This verse uses the metaphor of food that provides no nourishment to illustrate the utter futility and worthlessness of the sustenance offered in Hell. Just as a starving person would find no relief from food that neither fills nor strengthens, those who denied God's truth will find that their existence in the afterlife offers no comfort, no relief, and no spiritual fulfillment. It is a profound reminder that only what is rooted in God's truth can truly nourish the soul, both in this life and the next.

translation: [Some] faces on that Day will be full of bliss,
interpretation: This verse points to the profound reality that the state of one's face on the Day of Judgment will be an outward reflection of one's inner spiritual condition. The radiance and softness described is not merely physical beauty, but the manifestation of a soul that lived in accordance with divine guidance and found its ultimate fulfillment in God's pleasure. The face, which in this life reveals our emotions and character, will in the next life reveal our eternal standing before God.

translation: Satisfied with its striving
interpretation: This verse speaks to the profound contentment that comes from wholehearted devotion and effort in one's spiritual journey. It suggests that the soul which strives sincerely in the path of God will find ultimate satisfaction not merely in the reward it receives, but in the very act of striving itself — implying that true fulfillment is found when one's deeds are aligned with one's deepest purpose and divine calling.

translation: In a lofty Garden
interpretation: This verse points to the elevated and exalted nature of Paradise, suggesting that true spiritual elevation is not merely a physical height but a moral and spiritual one. The believer is reminded that the reward for righteousness transcends the lowly concerns of worldly life, and that striving toward God lifts the soul to a station of dignity and honor that is incomparably greater than anything this world can offer.

translation: You will not hear therein any idle talk.
interpretation: This verse points to the perfection and purity of Paradise, suggesting that the quality of a place is reflected in the nature of its speech and conversation. Just as idle, vain, and frivolous talk is a hallmark of a corrupt and distracted worldly environment, its complete absence in Paradise signifies a realm of ultimate meaningfulness, where every word, interaction, and experience carries profound truth and purpose. It invites the believer to reflect on the weight of their own words in this life, as speech is a mirror of the soul's condition.

translation: In it is a flowing spring.
interpretation: This verse evokes the image of paradise as a place of perpetual, effortless sustenance and spiritual refreshment. The flowing spring symbolizes that divine blessings in the afterlife are not static or finite, but continuously renewed — unlike the fleeting and uncertain pleasures of this world, which require toil and effort to obtain. It invites the believer to redirect their longing from worldly comforts toward the eternal and abundant grace that awaits the righteous.

translation: In it are raised thrones.
interpretation: The elevated thrones described in Paradise symbolize the dignity, honor, and exalted status that the righteous will enjoy in the Hereafter. Just as a throne signifies authority and prestige in worldly life, these raised thrones represent the ultimate elevation of the believer's soul — a reward that contrasts with any humiliation or hardship they may have endured in the worldly life. It is a reminder that true honor belongs not to those who possess worldly power, but to those who are faithful and patient in their devotion to God.

translation: And cups set at hand
interpretation: This verse evokes the idea of divine generosity and effortless provision in Paradise, where every need is anticipated before it is even expressed. The cups being 'set in place' suggests that in the hereafter, the believer will live in a state of complete ease and honor, never having to seek or strive for comfort, as God's bounty will already be prepared and waiting — a stark and beautiful contrast to the toil and effort required to meet one's needs in this worldly life.

translation: And cushions set in rows
interpretation: This verse invites the believer to reflect on the immense comfort and hospitality that awaits the righteous in Paradise. The image of cushions arranged in perfect order suggests not only physical ease but a divine intentionality in the preparation of the heavenly abode, reminding us that Allah has thoughtfully and lovingly prepared every detail of Paradise for those who strive in this life, so that we should not become too attached to the fleeting comforts of this world but rather keep our eyes fixed on the eternal rest that lies ahead.

translation: And cushions/carpets spread about.
interpretation: This verse invites the believer to reflect on the incomprehensible generosity of Allah in the afterlife. The image of scattered cushions suggests an environment of complete ease and effortless comfort, where nothing needs to be sought or arranged — abundance is simply present all around. It serves as a reminder that the striving and hardship of this worldly life will give way to a state of perfect rest and dignity for those who are faithful, encouraging the believer to remain patient and steadfast in the present in anticipation of what Allah has prepared.

translation: Do they not look at the camels, how they are created?
interpretation: This verse invites human beings to engage in deep contemplative reflection upon the natural world as a pathway to recognizing the power and wisdom of God. By directing attention to the camel — an animal intimately familiar to the original audience, yet remarkably complex in its physical design and adaptation — the verse challenges people to move beyond passive observation toward conscious, purposeful thinking. The underlying message is that the signs of God's existence and creative mastery are not hidden in distant abstractions, but are present in the ordinary and familiar things surrounding us. True faith, the verse implies, is not blind but is grounded in thoughtful engagement with the world God has fashioned.

translation: And at the sky, how it is raised?
interpretation: This verse invites deep contemplation on the grandeur and perfection of divine creation. By drawing attention to the vastness and elevation of the sky, it challenges human beings to reflect on the incomprehensible power of God, who raised the heavens without any visible pillars or support. The rhetorical question is not seeking an answer, but rather awakening the human soul to recognize its own smallness and the magnificence of its Creator, pushing the observer from mere sight to spiritual insight.

translation: And at the mountains, how they are firmly set?
interpretation: This verse invites humanity to deeply contemplate the majestic stability of mountains, which serve as a profound sign of divine power and wisdom. The rhetorical question is not merely about physical geography, but rather a call to reflect on how Allah has established order, balance, and firmness in creation. Just as mountains anchor the earth and prevent it from shaking, this verse subtly reminds the believer that true stability and grounding come only through divine will, encouraging the human soul to seek its own spiritual anchorage in faith and surrender to God.

translation: And at the Earth, how it was spread out?
interpretation: This verse invites humanity to engage in deep contemplation of the natural world, specifically the earth beneath our feet. The rhetorical question is not merely an observation of a physical reality, but a call to awaken the human intellect and conscience. The spreading of the earth is presented as a divine sign, urging us to reflect on the purposeful design embedded in creation. The earth's vast, stable, and habitable surface — so perfectly suited for human life — is not accidental, but a deliberate act of divine wisdom and mercy. By directing our gaze downward to the ground we so often take for granted, the verse reminds us that the sacred is not only found in the heavens above, but in the very soil upon which we walk, and that gratitude and awareness of God's presence should permeate every aspect of our earthly existence.

translation: So remind, for you are only a reminder.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes that the Prophet's fundamental role is not to compel or force people into belief, but rather to convey the message and awaken the conscience of humanity. It is a divine reassurance that the burden of guidance does not rest solely on his shoulders — his responsibility ends at delivery of the truth. This reflects a broader Qur'anic principle that faith must arise from free will and inner conviction, not coercion, and that ultimately it is Allah alone who guides hearts.

translation: You are not over them a controller.
interpretation: This verse reminds the Prophet, and by extension all those who convey divine guidance, that their role is solely to deliver the message of truth — the responsibility of compelling others to believe or forcing them into faith is not theirs to bear. True faith cannot be coerced, and God alone holds authority over the hearts and ultimate accountability of human beings. This is a profound affirmation of human free will and a boundary set on the nature of religious authority.

translation: Except for the one who turns away and disbelieves.
interpretation: This verse serves as a divine warning that the freedom granted to humanity comes with accountability. God's role is not to compel belief, but those who willfully turn their backs on truth and choose denial will face the natural consequences of their own spiritual rejection. It is a reminder that indifference and disbelief are not neutral stances — they are active choices that carry profound weight before God.

translation: So Allah will punish him with the greatest punishment.
interpretation: This verse serves as a solemn warning that the ultimate and most severe consequence awaits those who turn away from divine guidance and choose arrogance over submission. The 'greatest punishment' is contrasted with the lesser trials of this world, reminding us that worldly suffering is nothing compared to the eternal reckoning that awaits those who consciously reject truth. It is a reminder that human accountability before God is absolute, and that no act of defiance or denial goes unnoticed or unanswered in the divine order of justice.

translation: Indeed, to Us is their return.
interpretation: This verse serves as a profound reminder that all human beings are ultimately accountable to God. It conveys that no soul can escape divine reckoning, and that every action, whether concealed or apparent, will be brought before the Creator. It instills in the believer a sense of awareness and responsibility, encouraging righteous conduct not out of fear of human judgment, but out of the deep conviction that one's final destination and ultimate accountability rests solely with Allah.

translation: Then indeed, upon Us is their account.
interpretation: This verse underscores the absolute sovereignty and omniscience of Allah, reminding us that while humans are given free will to make their choices in this life, ultimate accountability belongs entirely to God. It serves as both a warning to the heedless and a comfort to the oppressed, assuring that no deed — hidden or manifest — escapes divine reckoning. The verse relieves the Prophet, and by extension all believers, of the burden of forcing others to believe, redirecting that responsibility entirely to Allah, who alone is the perfect and just Reckoner.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. By the dawn.
interpretation: God swears by the dawn as a divine oath, drawing our attention to the profound significance of this moment of transition between darkness and light. The dawn is not merely a physical phenomenon, but a symbol of hope, renewal, and the ever-present mercy of God. Just as the dawn inevitably breaks through the darkness of night, so too does God's truth and justice inevitably prevail over falsehood and oppression. This oath invites us to reflect on the cyclical nature of existence and the certainty of divine promise, reminding us that no matter how deep the darkness, the light of God's guidance and mercy will always emerge.

translation: And by the ten nights
interpretation: The oath sworn by the ten nights signifies their immense spiritual weight and sacred value in the sight of God. Most scholars identify these as the first ten nights of Dhul-Hijjah, the holiest month in the Islamic calendar, during which acts of worship carry extraordinary reward. By swearing an oath upon them, God draws the attention of humanity to the profound opportunities these nights represent for devotion, reflection, and drawing closer to the Divine. The verse invites believers to recognize that time itself is not uniform — certain moments are charged with divine blessing and must be seized with intention and gratitude.

translation: By the even and the odd
interpretation: This oath by the even and the odd points to the fundamental structure of all creation — that existence itself is built upon duality and singularity. Everything in the universe can be understood through pairs and their resolution into oneness, ultimately pointing to the absolute oneness of God (tawhid), who alone is the singular without equal, while all of creation exists in complementary pairs. The oath invites deep reflection on the divine order embedded in the very fabric of reality.

translation: By the night as it passes (or journeys on)
interpretation: The oath sworn by the night as it moves and progresses reflects the dynamic, transient nature of time itself. God draws our attention to the night not merely as a period of darkness, but as a reminder that all things are in a state of passage and movement. Just as the night inevitably gives way to dawn, every hardship, trial, and phase of human life is temporary. The verse invites us to reflect on the purposeful flow of time as a sign of divine wisdom, urging us to remain conscious that our existence in this world is fleeting, and that we must use each passing moment in awareness of our accountability before God.

translation: Is there not in that an oath for one of sound mind?
interpretation: This verse challenges the rational mind to recognize the profound significance of the oaths God has sworn by the dawn, the ten nights, and other signs of creation. It implies that the evidence of God's power and wisdom embedded in these phenomena is so self-evident that any person of true intellect and sound reasoning should be able to perceive the divine truth without further elaboration. It is an invitation to reflect deeply, suggesting that the greatest proof requires no elaborate argument — only an awakened and unclouded mind.

translation: Have you not seen how your Lord dealt with 'Aad?
interpretation: This verse invites deep reflection and serves as a warning to those who witness or hear of the fate of past nations. By asking 'have you not seen?', God draws the reader into a moment of contemplation, urging them to look beyond the surface of history and recognize the divine justice that operates through time. The destruction of 'Aad was not merely a historical event but a living lesson — a demonstration that power, pride, and defiance of divine guidance ultimately lead to ruin. The verse challenges human arrogance by pointing to a civilization that was mighty yet fell, reminding us that no strength or civilization is beyond the reach of divine accountability.

translation: Iram of the Pillars
interpretation: This phrase refers not merely to a lost city of grandeur, but serves as a symbol of the ultimate futility of human power and architectural achievement. No matter how mighty a civilization builds itself — how tall its pillars, how vast its empire — it remains subject to divine will and the passage of time. The mention of Iram invites the reader to reflect on their own ambitions and attachments to worldly monuments, reminding us that true permanence belongs only to God.

translation: The like of which was never created in the lands.
interpretation: This verse, referring to the mighty civilization of 'Aad and their towering constructions, serves as a profound reminder that no matter how great a people's power, wealth, or architectural achievements may be, none of these worldly accomplishments can protect them from divine reckoning. True greatness lies not in material dominance, but in humility and submission to Allah, for all earthly power is fleeting and subject to His will.

translation: And Thamud, who carved out the rocks in the valley,
interpretation: This verse serves as a reminder of human arrogance and the ultimate futility of worldly power. The Thamud people, despite their extraordinary ability to carve entire dwellings from solid rock — a feat symbolizing the peak of human ingenuity and material mastery — were still destroyed when they transgressed against God's commands. The mention of this achievement is not one of admiration, but of irony: no matter how great humanity's technical and civilizational accomplishments may be, they offer no protection against divine judgment. It is a warning that strength, innovation, and worldly achievement must always be accompanied by moral and spiritual accountability.

translation: And Pharaoh, the owner of the stakes.
interpretation: The reference to Pharaoh as 'the owner of the stakes' serves as a powerful reminder that no matter how formidable worldly power appears — symbolized by the massive tent pegs or stakes used to anchor his great empire and perhaps the instruments of torture he used against his people — such power is ultimately transient and subject to divine justice. The verse invites reflection on the nature of tyrannical authority and its inevitable downfall before the absolute and eternal power of God.

translation: Those who transgressed in the lands
interpretation: This verse refers to those who, upon receiving power, wealth, or authority, exceeded all bounds of justice and moderation. It is a warning that arrogance and oppression in positions of influence are not merely political or social failures, but spiritual ones — a rebellion against the divine order that governs all of creation. The 'lands' here suggest that their transgression was not private or hidden, but public and widespread, corrupting communities and societies around them.

translation: And they spread much corruption therein.
interpretation: This verse serves as a divine indictment of those who, when granted power or prosperity, choose to abuse it by spreading disorder, moral decay, and injustice. It is a warning that the measure of a person or a nation is not found in their wealth or authority, but in whether they use such blessings to build or to destroy. True accountability before God lies in how one exercises influence in the world.

translation: So your Lord poured upon them a whip of punishment.
interpretation: This verse illustrates that divine retribution, when it falls upon those who persistently reject truth and oppress others, is both swift and overwhelming. The metaphor of a 'whip of punishment' conveys that God's chastisement is not merely a passive consequence but an active, precise, and purposeful response to human arrogance and transgression, serving as a warning to all generations that no civilization, regardless of its power or prosperity, is beyond accountability before its Creator.

translation: Indeed, your Lord is in wait.
interpretation: This verse serves as a profound reminder that God is ever-watchful over human conduct, not in a passive sense, but in an active, vigilant one. The imagery of 'lying in wait' suggests that no act of arrogance, oppression, or transgression goes unnoticed or escapes divine accountability. It is a warning that the fleeting nature of worldly power and pride is always under the gaze of a just and omniscient God, who will ultimately hold every soul to account for what it has earned.

translation: As for man, when his Lord tries him and honors him and favors him, he says, 'My Lord has honored me.'
interpretation: This verse exposes a fundamental flaw in human perception: we tend to equate worldly prosperity, comfort, and status with divine approval and favor. When God grants us wealth, health, or prestige, we quickly assume it is a sign of our own righteousness or God's special love for us. However, this is a dangerous misreading of reality. God's bestowal of worldly blessings is not necessarily a mark of honor in the spiritual sense — it may in fact be a test of gratitude, humility, and responsibility. The verse invites us to reflect on whether we are interpreting God's gifts correctly, warning us against the arrogance of assuming that material abundance is proof of divine endorsement.

translation: But when He tries him and restricts his provision, he says, 'My Lord has humiliated me.'
interpretation: This verse exposes a fundamental misunderstanding in human nature: that we equate material wealth with divine favor and poverty with divine punishment or humiliation. Allah is pointing out the error of measuring His love, care, or regard for a person through the lens of worldly provision. The restriction of sustenance is not a sign of God's contempt, but may itself be a form of divine wisdom, mercy, or test. True honor and humiliation are not determined by the abundance or scarcity of worldly resources, but by one's relationship with God, one's gratitude in times of plenty, and one's patience in times of hardship. The verse invites us to look beyond material circumstances to understand the deeper spiritual reality of our standing with our Creator.

translation: No! But you do not honor the orphan
interpretation: This verse is a divine rebuke directed at those who neglect their moral and social responsibilities. It reveals that the true measure of a society's spiritual health is not found in wealth or ritual, but in how it treats its most vulnerable members. The orphan here serves as a symbol of all those who are powerless and without a protector. God is pointing out a fundamental hypocrisy: people claim faith and virtue, yet fail to extend dignity and care to those who need it most. True honor before God is not achieved through self-glorification, but through the active and compassionate uplifting of those who have been left behind by the world.

translation: And you do not encourage one another to feed the poor.
interpretation: This verse is a condemnation of a deep moral failure — not merely the act of withholding food from the needy, but the abandonment of the communal responsibility to inspire and urge others toward generosity. True righteousness is not only personal; it demands that we actively cultivate a culture of compassion around us, holding one another accountable to care for the vulnerable. The silence of a person who witnesses poverty and says nothing is itself a form of participation in that poverty.

translation: And you consume inheritance, devouring it altogether.
interpretation: This verse condemns the greedy and indiscriminate consumption of inherited wealth, particularly that which belongs to vulnerable members of society such as orphans and women. It serves as a moral warning against the human tendency toward excessive materialism and selfishness, reminding believers that wealth carries ethical responsibilities and that one's relationship with worldly possessions must be governed by justice and restraint, not unbridled appetite.

translation: And you love wealth with an exceeding love.
interpretation: This verse serves as a profound spiritual mirror, revealing a fundamental human weakness: the tendency to place excessive attachment to material wealth above higher spiritual and moral obligations. The verse is not condemning the love of wealth outright, but rather warning against its excess — when the accumulation of worldly possessions becomes an all-consuming passion that distracts the soul from its true purpose, gratitude to God, and responsibility toward others. It is a call to self-awareness and balance, urging the believer to examine their heart and ensure that love of the divine and service to humanity takes precedence over the relentless pursuit of material gain.

translation: No! When the earth is shaken and pounded, pounded to dust,
interpretation: This verse serves as a divine refutation of human complacency and denial regarding the afterlife. The emphatic repetition of 'dakka dakka' (pounded, pounded) is not merely a description of physical destruction, but a rhetorical device meant to shake the human conscience awake. Allah is warning that the solid, stable earth — the very foundation upon which humanity builds its illusions of permanence, wealth, and power — will be utterly obliterated. The repetition emphasizes the totality and finality of this event, leaving no room for doubt or escape. It is a call to those who are heedless to reconsider their priorities before the moment arrives when the ground beneath their certainties is completely annihilated.

translation: And your Lord comes and the angels, rank upon rank.
interpretation: This verse points to the absolute sovereignty and majesty of Allah on the Day of Judgment. The coming of the Lord in a manner befitting His greatness, accompanied by angels arranged in orderly rows, signifies the establishment of divine justice and authority. It serves as a reminder that all worldly power and pretension will be rendered insignificant in that moment, and that nothing escapes the ultimate reckoning. The imagery of the angels standing in ranks emphasizes the solemn, awe-inspiring nature of that Day, urging humanity to reflect on their deeds and prepare for the moment when they will stand before their Creator.

translation: And on that Day, Hell will be brought forth. On that Day, man will remember, but what good will that remembrance be for him?
interpretation: This verse speaks to the tragic irony of delayed realization. Throughout his life, man was given countless opportunities to reflect, repent, and return to his Creator, yet he persisted in heedlessness. Only when Hell itself is brought forth as an undeniable, physical reality before his eyes does he finally awaken to the truth — but that moment of awakening comes too late. The verse serves as a profound warning to humanity: the capacity for remembrance and reflection is a gift given in this life, and to squander it through distraction, arrogance, or denial is the gravest of losses, for on the Day of Judgment, that same remembrance will bring nothing but anguish and regret.

translation: He will say, 'Oh, I wish I had sent ahead [something] for my life!'
interpretation: This verse captures the profound regret of a person on the Day of Resurrection, who realizes too late that the true and everlasting life is the Hereafter, not the worldly existence they prioritized. The exclamation reflects a moment of devastating self-awareness — that every deed, prayer, and act of charity left behind in the worldly life was in reality an investment for this eternal life, and the negligent soul wasted the opportunity. It serves as a powerful reminder to believers that the present moment is the only chance to prepare for what truly matters, urging them not to be deceived by the fleeting pleasures of the dunya at the expense of their eternal destiny.

translation: So on that Day, no one will punish as He punishes,
interpretation: This verse speaks to the absolute and unparalleled nature of divine justice on the Day of Resurrection. It serves as a profound warning that no earthly power, no matter how tyrannical or cruel, can come close to the magnitude of God's punishment. The verse invites deep reflection on accountability, reminding humanity that ultimate justice belongs solely to God, whose authority transcends all human comprehension. It is an invitation to take one's deeds seriously in this life, knowing that the reckoning of the Hereafter is incomparable to anything experienced in this world.

translation: And none can bind as He binds.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the absolute and unparalleled power of Allah in restraining and binding. No created being, no matter how mighty, can replicate or match the divine capacity to restrain. It serves as a reminder of human limitation and vulnerability before God, urging humility and awareness that ultimate control belongs solely to Allah. The verse calls us to recognize that any power or strength we perceive in creation is infinitely surpassed by the divine, and that on the Day of Judgment, no force in existence can intercede or release without His permission.

translation: O tranquil soul!
interpretation: This verse is an invitation and a divine address to the soul that has achieved inner peace through complete trust and surrender to Allah. It signals that true serenity is not found in worldly possessions or status, but is a spiritual station attained by those who have anchored their hearts in the remembrance and love of God. The soul being addressed here has transcended anxiety, doubt, and worldly attachment, reaching a state of contentment with whatever Allah has decreed — representing the highest aspiration of the human spiritual journey.

translation: Return to your Lord, well-pleased and pleasing [to Him].
interpretation: This divine address to the tranquil soul represents the ultimate moment of spiritual homecoming. It speaks to the soul that has journeyed through the trials of earthly life with patience, faith, and contentment, and has emerged in a state of mutual satisfaction — the soul is pleased with Allah's decree, and Allah is pleased with the soul. The verse invites us to understand that the goal of human existence is not merely survival or success in the worldly sense, but the cultivation of an inner peace so deep and so aligned with divine will that death itself becomes not a rupture, but a return — a joyful reunion with the Source from which we came.

translation: So enter among My servants
interpretation: This divine invitation signifies the ultimate honor and belonging granted to the righteous soul. It reflects the idea that true fulfillment and peace are found not in isolation, but in communion with those who have surrendered themselves to God. To be counted among His servants is not a diminishment but the highest distinction a soul can receive, representing complete acceptance, mercy, and eternal closeness to the Divine.

translation: And enter My Paradise.
interpretation: This verse represents the ultimate divine invitation and the culmination of a soul's journey. It signifies that true belonging and rest are found only with God, and that the righteous soul's entire earthly struggle finds its meaning and reward in this singular, intimate call from the Creator — a personal welcome into eternal bliss, expressed not as a collective decree, but as a direct and loving address to the individual soul.

translation: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. I swear by this city (Makkah).
interpretation: The use of the oath 'I swear by this city' is a rhetorical device that draws our attention to the profound sanctity of Makkah, the holiest city in Islam. God is reminding us that this blessed land — where the Prophet Muhammad was born and where the Kaaba stands — is a witness to the struggles and trials of humanity. The verse invites us to reflect on our own place in this world and the responsibilities we carry as human beings, grounding our existence in a sacred context that transcends the material and connects us to the divine purpose of our creation.

translation: And you are free of restriction in this city
interpretation: This verse honors the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) by declaring that Mecca, despite being a sacred city where conflict is generally forbidden, becomes a place where all things are made permissible for him. It signifies the unique and exalted status of the Prophet, suggesting that his presence itself sanctifies and transforms the rules of a place, reflecting the deep reverence and divine privilege bestowed upon him by Allah.

translation: By the father and what he begat
interpretation: This verse is an oath by God invoking the progenitor and his offspring, pointing to the sacred and primordial bond between parent and child as a reflection of divine creative power. It draws attention to the chain of human existence itself as a sign worthy of deep contemplation, reminding us that the very fact of our lineage and birth is a testament to God's sovereignty and the continuity of His creation across generations.

translation: We have certainly created man into hardship.
interpretation: This verse serves as a profound reminder that struggle and hardship are not accidental or punitive, but rather intrinsic to the very nature of human existence. Allah affirms that difficulty is woven into the fabric of human life by divine design, suggesting that our trials and toils are not signs of abandonment, but rather the very medium through which we grow, are tested, and ultimately draw closer to our Creator. To resist hardship is, in a sense, to resist the very condition of being human; the believer is therefore called to embrace difficulty with patience and trust, understanding that it is the path toward spiritual refinement and ultimate return to Allah.

translation: Does he think that no one has power over him?
interpretation: This verse serves as a stern warning against human arrogance and the delusion of self-sufficiency. It challenges the tendency of the human soul to behave recklessly or boastfully, as if one is beyond accountability or consequence. The verse reminds us that no matter how powerful, wealthy, or influential a person may become, they remain entirely within the grasp of Allah's omnipotence. True wisdom lies in recognizing one's own vulnerability and submission before the Almighty, rather than being deceived by temporary worldly power.

translation: He says, 'I have spent wealth abundantly.'
interpretation: This verse critiques the human tendency toward arrogance and boastfulness regarding material wealth. The statement reflects a misplaced sense of pride in one's spending, as though the mere act of expending great sums of money is itself a virtue worthy of recognition. The deeper lesson is that the value of wealth lies not in how much is spent, but in the sincerity and righteousness of the purpose behind it. Boasting about one's expenditure reveals a heart attached to worldly recognition rather than divine approval, exposing the spiritual emptiness that can accompany material abundance.

translation: Does he think that no one sees him?
interpretation: This verse serves as a profound reminder that Allah is the All-Seeing, ever-watchful over every action, intention, and moment in a person's life. It challenges the human tendency toward heedlessness and moral arrogance — the illusion that one can act freely without consequence simply because no other human is watching. True accountability transcends human observation; it is rooted in the divine awareness that encompasses all things, seen and unseen. The verse thus calls the believer to develop a consciousness of God (taqwa) that governs their conduct not out of social pressure, but out of an inner recognition that they are always in the presence of the Divine.

translation: Have We not made for him two eyes?
interpretation: This verse is a divine reminder to humanity of the profound gifts bestowed upon us by Allah. The mention of the two eyes is not merely a reference to the physical faculty of sight, but rather an invitation to reflect on the countless blessings we take for granted. Allah draws our attention to something as intimate and ever-present as our own eyes to awaken a sense of gratitude and awareness of our utter dependence on our Creator. It challenges us to recognize that even the most basic aspects of our existence are not self-made, but are gifts from Allah, and with such gifts comes a responsibility to use them in ways that are pleasing to Him.

translation: And a tongue and two lips
interpretation: This verse draws attention to the divine gift of speech and expression granted to human beings. The tongue and lips are not merely physical organs, but instruments of profound moral responsibility. God highlights these gifts to remind us that the faculty of communication — the ability to speak truth, offer comfort, recite His name, and guide others — is among the greatest blessings bestowed upon humanity, and with it comes the obligation to use it righteously and with gratitude.

translation: And We guided him to the two paths.
interpretation: This verse speaks to the divine gift of moral discernment granted to every human being. God has embedded within human nature the innate ability to distinguish between good and evil, virtue and vice. It is not merely an external guidance but an internal compass — a fitrah — placed within the soul itself. The two paths represent the clear fork every person faces in life: the path of righteousness leading to elevation, and the path of corruption leading to ruin.
